#8719. $656,000 of Frugal Things I Still Love Doing

“Until he got all rich and fancy so that he no longer understands the common person’s plight.

Stash probably doesn’t even practice any of these money-saving things he preaches any more!”

When I read things like this, I can’t help but laugh. Because on the one hand, when you put a bunch of personal life details online like this, being misunderstood is just part of the package. But on the other hand, if the critics could peek in and see our real lives – not just mine but those of all the Mustachians – they would have to give up their conspiracy theories and accept the fact that this stuff just works.

Because really, not much has changed when it comes to the basics. Like many MMM readers over the past twelve years, my total wealth level has increased pretty regularly.  But also like many of us, I haven’t felt the need to change very much about my spending because I was doing my best to live an enjoyable life in the first place.

How have so many people found such great success? I think we Mustachians have something that’s a bit more rare and special than standard financial advice, which is what makes it work so well:

Standard Advice: Slash your spending and make sacrifices until you reach a certain savings percentage, and beyond that it doesn’t matter, it’s all personal choice. More income? Great, that means you don’t have to sacrifice as much! FatFIRE for everyone!

Mustachianism: Cultivate a love of efficiency, creativity, self awareness, and self improvement. Use this knowledge to improve your life in all ways, including those which help you live better even as your monthly expense rate drops over time.

Well, I’ll give you some examples from my own present-day life. Things I do because I happen to enjoy them, which also happen to save a lot of money. Some of these are normal, some are silly and may end up in some future gossip magazine hit piece, but all of them happen to work for me, so the critics can be damned.

As I list each item, I’ll include an estimate of how much the activity saves me per decade, because you should always think at least in terms of decades. To make that calculation yourself, just use the “rule of 172” – take a monthly expense and multiply it by 172 to estimate how much it would compound into over ten years, if invested.

1) Fixing my own House (and everybody else’s too)

I’m a big believer in self-sufficiency, and working to build up the skills to manage the most important parts of your own life without depending on too many things (or people) that are outside of your control. In other words, one giant recipe for a happy life is simply to Become a Producer of the Things You Most Enjoy Consuming.

And in my case, I happen to love houses. I like living in beautiful, functional spaces and sharing them with friends. But most houses are ugly and poorly designed when you buy them, so I realized that I also love solving problems and redesigning old buildings to become new again. I enjoy this process so much that I spend most of my free time doing it – on both my own properties and the homes of friends.

And I love teaching other people to gain power over their own houses too. It’s amazing how great people feel as they lose their fear and dependence on outside contractors, and gain the ability to fix and maintain things with their own two hands.

Savings: An average of $20,000 per year = $287,000 per decade

You know what’s great? Having so much money that you can buy whatever you want – high quality things which get delivered to your front door the very next day.

You know what’s even better? Not buying some of those new things, and instead finding ways to share, repurpose and buy equally high quality items from other people who don’t need them any more. All while building up your own community and creating new friendships in the process.

Craigslist, Facebook Marketplace, and even NextDoor all have Buy Nothing groups for most areas. In the MMM-HQ community, we run a Discord server with about 200 local people, who chat around the clock on a wide range of subjects. They help each other with major projects in one channel called #diyhowto, and give away and sell things on #forsale and #buynothing.

Although our private Discord group is my favorite, I also use Craigslist regularly, and probably save (and earn) a few thousand every year thanks to the habit:

We all know that Mr. Money Mustache’s biggest contribution to personal finance is to insist that bike transportation is the best way to get around. And I still feel this way. As we learned in The True Cost of Commuting, cars cost at least 50 cents per mile to operate, while bikes are much cheaper, mainly due to reduced depreciation and maintenance costs (which are even bigger than the gas savings).

I do still use bikes (or walking) for at least 95% of my local trips these days, but because I live in the center of a small city, my life is pretty local. So this still only adds up to about 2000 miles per year, a savings of “only” $14,000 per decade.

But when you choose active transportation, there’s much more to the picture than just cutting your car expenses. You’re changing everything about your physical and mental health picture for the better, which brings us to the next point of…

Although I’m no competitive athlete, whenever I see an option to make my body work a bit harder, I usually take it. Stairs instead of elevators, running the golf course instead of using a golf cart, moving my own furniture and appliances instead of calling a mover, shoveling snow and raking leaves instead of using a machine.

When I face a decision like this, I simply ask myself the question: “Well, Mustache. Do you want MORE health and fitness, or LESS?” Putting it in that context makes the answer obvious.  Every bit helps, because when it comes to your body, the rule is pretty much use it or lose it.

But how much money does this save? There’s no real way to calculate it exactly, but I like to think of it this way: The US average health care spending is about $13,000 per person per year. My lifetime costs due to illness or medication so far have been just about zero, plus I know I’ve had more energy and greater productivity due to being healthy. Let’s just put it very conservatively and set the estimated savings and benefits at $10k per year which means

5) Saving Energy by Running my home like a Glamping Retreat

Here’s where things get a bit silly, but my level of joy is actually at its greatest.

My personality type is probably a weird combination of an engineer, a carpenter, an artsy hippie, and a mad scientist. Oh, and a devoted homebody too. Because of this, my favorite activity most days is to just run around my house taking care of things and trying new little experiments and improvements.

Sometimes I’ll cut a few big holes on on the South side of the house and install sliding doors and big windows to allow nice sunbeams and passive solar energy to get into my house and give me free heat in the winters. Other times it’s just smaller things to save energy and live more at at one with the seasons of my area:

Even taken all together, these things are pretty small – the average combined gas and electric bill for my area is about $250 per month, while my usage adds up to about $75. So while we’re only saving about $30,000 per decade for what sounds like a lot of work to most people, I consider this to be the biggest win because I enjoy living in “MMM’s Energy Efficiency Playground” so much.

“Hey, we’re having a big back yard pool party next weekend to celebrate Amy’s graduation from kindergarten, can you make it?”

“OH NOOOO!!! We will be off in at Disneyland that whole week! We planned the trip months ago, I wish we could make it!

As I type this in the height of the summer season, I really feel this effect at its fullest: almost all of my friends are off on trips, and my guest suite here at home is almost constantly full. People are traveling a lot, and many of them sound like they wish they could spend a few more of their precious summer weeks and weekends at home.

I’ll let you in on a little secret: you can! The trick is saying, “no thanks” more often to plans that involve you being away, and “yes please” to things that let you stay at home. The benefits are numerous:

Estimated Savings: Even if you replace just two weeks of travel for a family of four, with equivalent time at home you might save $5,000 per year in direct costs and a further $5,000 per year in incidental benefits like the health and local friendships. This would work out to a shocking $143,000 per decade of wealth increase!

Of course, travel is generally a good thing for broadening the life experience of you and your kids. It’s worth spending on, lavishly at times. But the key is to balance it out and be discerning, keeping the most enriching trips and pruning a few off the bottom of the list. And remembering that home time is valuable and healthy too.

And Whoa! We’ve already built up a huge list and I feel like I was just getting started.

Taken all together, we’ve already detailed things that compound to $656,000 every decade, which already more than double the median wealth that most American seniors have as they cruise nervously into their retirement years – after over 40 years of work!

And now that I’ve been writing this blog for over ten years myself, I can safely say that over $656,000 of even my most recent worth increases are directly attributable to these simple habits. The same ones many of us have been enjoying and preaching about all along, both before and after our retirement dates.

If money is in genuinely short supply, you could go a lot further than the examples in this article. And indeed, there’s a lot more laid out in this blog or the MMM Boot Camp email series.

But one of the points of Mustachianism is that you usually don’t have to try all that hard. Just tweaking your lifestyle to be slightly less ridiculous and more efficient than average is usually all it takes.

In the comments: what are your quirks and frugal indulgences? The things you do now to save money, or things you still do even after it’s no longer about the money? I often wonder how widespread this frugality-just-for-fun is. But since we Humans are a naturally curious and problem solving species in our natural state, I suspect there are many more of us out there.

I think his first point “Fixing my own House” is invaluable advice for any homeowner in HCOL areas. I live in a very HCOL city (a conscious decision that currently is worth the tradeoff for me) and bought a modest “fixer upper” for well below my neighborhoods average home price during COVID.

Boy did I quickly hit the “find out” part of that decision. I’d never touched renovations or building or fixing a home / apartment beyond mounting bike racks on my rented apartments walls. I received insane quotes for electrical, plumbing, HVAC, and all the drywall repairs required for that kind of work. I did the math out for many of these projects based on the number of people and days the companies told me it would take and in many cases these companies were pulling in $300 per man-hour.

So I didn’t hire any of them. I spent an entire year learning the plumbing and electrical code for my city / state / country. I bothered the hell out of my city inspectors with questions. Made dozens of trips (sadly mostly via car) to the big box stores – eventually even started accounts with supply houses and lumber yards for better variety and deals.

In the two years I spent renovating the house, I’ve saved myself more than $300,000 (estimating the value of my time at $50/hour).

If anybody on here is considering buying a home, but isn’t willing to learn to do this stuff themselves, I think renting might be the more Mustachian decision if the alternative is paying for somebody else to do this work. I also don’t think there’s anything wrong with that.

Thanks for the post MMM! Like those above, I resonated with your article. A lot of these were things I have “always just done” (like hang dry clothes) so a few more that “I just have always done”

(1) My grad school room mate and I loved new clothes but really couldn’t afford them. So we would challenge ourselves to keep our apartment as cold as we could tolerate in Ann Arbor, Michigan and “reward” ourselves in cost savings from our heating bill by buying a new sweater to keep us warm. That $50/month difference meant we were stoked by our new sweater and usually pocketed the savings the other months.

(2) Buy wool clothing. It’s more durable, needs to be washed less, and you can have a smaller wardrobe (which takes up less space, saving you money in storage/heating costs). Even better buy used wool clothing.

(3) Books. I love reading and go through upwards of 50+ books a year. Buying those new at a bookstore would be $30-$50 a month! Instead, I use Libby through my library and constantly have a multitude of books on hold. So yes, I need to wait, but honestly, it’s not that bad if you just had a great book come up that you’ve been waiting for. Slow gratification :)

(4) Shampoo / Conditioner. I’ve experimented a lot with this over the years. Especially for women, there is an expectation to have clean, styled, long hair. There just is. I have finally settled on washing hair 2-3x a week, using tiny amounts of shampoo and conditioner only when necessary means I can save 5 bottles of each a year.

(5) Buying the clearance veggies and cooking them that day. I’m also vegetarian. Both of these things save a TON of money, especially eating out (it’s about 10-15% less to be a vegetarian consistently when ordering out).

My last thought to add to your post is to be adaptable. My partner and I are throwing a large wedding in a month. Weddings are crazy expensive if you let them be. But instead, we’ve found “opportunity” in many unexpected objects left on the side of the road (like an old ladder that became a wine shelf rack) or sold at a huge discount (like silverware from another wedding for $20 for 50 people when it cost $1.25 to rent a single fork!!!) .

It may not be planned and perfectly coordinated, but we’ve created a wedding we’re proud of – both financially and visually. Most of it comes in, as you said, finding joy in the opportunities, not being frustrated with “what we don’t have”. We know we “could” have it, but honestly, that doesn’t bring me joy. Fixing up the old ladder and hearing people gasp when they see the before and after pictures does :)

#8717. Debt And Physician Finances

Have you ever had a termite infestation? You likely didn’t realize you did until it was too late. For months or sometimes years, you go about your life without the faintest idea that something is afoot, because after all, the house looks just fine from the driveway.

By the time you notice that sagging floorboards, the structure is already compromised.

Debt is that termite infestation. You don’t realize the damage it’s doing until it’s too late. It gnaws through your income, unnoticed, until the day a job change, a market downturn or an unplanned expense reveals just how rickety the foundation has become.

More than a third of Americans earning $200,000 or more say they’re living paycheck to paycheck. Nearly a third of six-figure earners describe themselves as financially stretched, struggling, or drowning.

Physicians are not exempt from this. A high income means nothing on its own. It can open up opportunities, yes but those options feel out of reach when debt takes away the majority of your paycheck.

Student loans and a primary mortgage are fixtures of adulthood. If you’re a physician and have never had to carry these, you’re extremely lucky. Or you know something I don’t— in which case, please share your secret with the rest of us.

The median education debt for the class of 2025 was $215,000— not including undergraduate loans. Many physicians carry this into their 40s and 50s.

Nobody becomes a doctor debt-free unless family money covers the tab. In return you get to enjoy a career in medicine earning good money with plenty of lucrative options for supplementing that income.

The mortgage on a primary residence is an equally unavoidable aspect of adult finances. In return you get a place to call home and an asset that (usually) appreciates. Mortgage is debt, yes, but paying it down builds equity that would otherwise go to someone else in the form of rent.

This type of debt cannot be categorized as termites. This is the foundation you build on top of and most physicians manage it fine once attending income kicks in. There are also ways to significantly ease the burden on this type of debt.

Discover legitimate, IRS-recognized tax strategies physicians can use to potentially reduce their tax bills, which options high earners qualify for, and which aggressive approaches could attract IRS scrutiny.

Ideal for: Physicians and high-income professionals looking to understand their tax-saving options before speaking with their CPA.

Sat, Nov 14  ·  1:00 pm ET  ·  10:00 am PT

Credit card balances, car payments beyond what a reliable car would cost, a second home bought at the top of a market, an extravagant vacation you didn’t save for but financed instead— I could go on. These are all examples of bad debt. Not because they aren’t “profitable” but also because the ROI they provide is short-lived.

Having a lake house feels great but not if you have to put up with a toxic workplace in order to pay it off. Jetting off to Switzerland feels like freedom but not if you have to skimp on your 401(k) contributions for the following years in order to pay it off.

In the second quarter of 2026, the average APR on credit card accounts that carry a balance was 22.15%, up from 21.52% in Q1. Total U.S. credit card debt reached $1.26 trillion in Q2 2026, closing in on the all-time high of $1.28 trillion set at the end of 2025. Roughly 60% of cardholders carry a balance month to month rather than paying in full.

A $15,000 balance at 22% APR costs over $3,300 a year in interest alone, money that produces nothing, builds nothing and simply vanishes. Extended across a decade of minimum payments, the total interest paid can exceed the original purchase several times over.

A 43-year-old high-earner drowning in debt posted his story on Reddit. Let’s call him Bill.

“On the outside, I probably look like a success. On the inside, I feel like I’m slowly breaking — just getting through one day at a time,” he wrote.

Him and his spouse carry close to $1 million in combined loans. Both work high-paying jobs. On paper, they look fine. In practice, their special-needs son’s therapy costs $3,000 a month. Before his diagnosis, that $3000 was the extra income they had planned to put towards paying down debt. These are the kind of curveballs life can throw at you. Out of nowhere, unannounced— thwack.

Bill tried his hand at several side businesses which failed and added more debt on top. He describes feeling trapped in a career he doesn’t enjoy with no visible exit.

Close to $1 million is debt may sound insane but in New York, D.C. or California, that number is an easy target. HCOL is no joke and Bill’s situation isn’t unique. Debt can be enticing even to the best of us.

Bill’s failure stems from the fact that he had thought nothing would ever go wrong and he would be able to pay off

the debt from the extra income. It was that years of “should be fine” income had never been forced into a written plan, so a single disruption ate the entire buffer.

That’s the sinkhole version of debt. It doesn’t look like reckless spending from the outside. It looks like a normal life that happens to be standing on ground with nothing underneath it.

Also read: Is Driving a Honda Smarter Than Flexing a Ferrari?

We love compound interest but not when it’s on the other side. Compound interest grows our savings the same way it grows balances— with indifferent efficiency.

Every month a balance carries over at 20%+ APR, that growth compounds against the borrower. Over 20 years, that comes out to 52.83x of the original number which could easily mean the difference between a paid-off house and a large credit card bill that never seems to shrink.

Every debt payment carries two costs. The first is obvious: the dollars leaving the account each month. The second almost never gets counted, because it never shows up anywhere: opportunity cost.

The cost of what you give up when your dollars go towards debt when they could’ve gone towards something profitable.

Consider a physician making aggressive payments on $215,000 in student loans during the first years as an attending.

Once the balance hits zero, that monthly cash flow can now go towards investment instead of paying a loan servicer. It can now be invested in index funds, a retirement account or a rental property that produces income instead of consuming it.

Also read: Building Wealth: Lessons In Sustainable Investment for Physicians

That’s what makes debt a double hit. Stretched across a 30-year investing timeline, missed growth frequently outweighs the interest itself, sometimes by a wide margin.

That’s why many advisors suggest building a straightforward financial foundation before reaching for anything advanced. Boring, broadly diversified investing beats clever debt-servicing strategies almost every time because it lets compounding start earlier instead of later.

The next time you sit down to fine-time your financial plan, consider the following:

Learn more: Is Diversification Finally Working Again?

After a decade of deferred spending, attending income brings much-need relief. But with it, comes the temptation to catch up all at once.

Those one-third of six-figure households that feel “stretched, struggling, or drowning” I mentioned earlier?

Their biggest downfall is precisely the fact that every income jump they are blessed with gets absorbed by a bigger house, a nicer car and a few thousand extra dollars a year in subscriptions and shopping. The brokerage accounts become the stepchildren that never get any love or attention.

Don’t be the evil stepmother. Do this instead:

Everyone takes stress as a given. As children we’re conditioned to worry about our homework and grades, as we grow older, we worry about fitting in, dating and winning the rat race.

The joys of parenthood are symbiotic with the worries of how to raise and protect our children in a world like ours. Being alive is, in essence, being stressed.

Debt adds in another layer of stress to all of that. But this is one we usually push away to the back of our minds so much so that it stops registering as stress at all.

Anyone carrying a meaningful balance knows what I’m talking about. Unexpected car repairs make us flinch. Due dates feel heavy but they arrive and we pay; then do it again the following month. Progress feels theoretical.

A systematic review of 39 U.S. studies found that debt is consistently linked to higher rates of stress and even suicide. The authors pointed to financial strain and the pressure of collection as the major drivers. Some debt, such as a mortgage, was labeled as “secure” which proves the point that not all debt is bad.

Another study reports that over-indebted consumers have lower life satisfaction and poorer health due to a diminished sense of control.

Eventually the discomfort becomes the baseline, and that’s when people take on more debt, because an actual plan to eliminate it no longer feels realistic.

Financing makes this worse by design. Nearly every major purchase now arrives with a monthly payment option built in, because a payment feels smaller than a price tag even when the total cost is higher.

47% of Buy Now, Pay Later users have been late on at least one loan in the past year. That percentage had been rising steadily, as it was 41% in 2025 and just 34% in 2024.

More alarmingly, 54% of consumers say that they wouldn’t be able to make ends meet without these loans. 29% say they use them to pay for groceries.

Financial well-being research consistently finds that experiences with debt and credit correlate directly with how secure people feel about their finances, independent of income.

So the relief once you’re on the other side? It’s exhilarating.

A Gallup study found that among recent graduates, only 25% of those with more than $50,000 in debt were thriving financially compared to 40% of debt-free grads.

Physicians who’ve finished paying off credit cards or student loans, especially after years of aggressive payments alongside PSLF, will know what I’m talking about. The financial change is expected but the psychological weight lifting is what often catches you off guard.

If you want to experience that relief sooner rather than later, stick to aggressive repayment and steer clear of financing anything marketed by its monthly payment instead of its total cost.

Debt is sneaky like that. It can make you feel like you’re living your best life, doing better than ever— doing better than those around you. It’s a costly little dog and pony show.

Home equity products are the easiest way to explain this. A physician spends years building equity in a primary residence, then starts seeing offers to unlock that equity through a HELOC (home equity line of credit) or cash-out refinance for a kitchen remodel, debt consolidation, etc.

The homeowner is essentially being gaslit into converting equity that already belongs to them into a new long-term loan that accrues interest all over again.

These ventures can make sense in rare, high-planned situations tied to high-returns but not in cases where the motive is discretionary. Saving for a large purchase takes longer than financing it yes, but it also provides security which a new, bigger loan just cannot.

No matter how fancy it looks. Debt servicers know how to market their products well. They disguise shackles as flexibility, but really they’re coming for the wealth you’ve already built while claiming to make more for you.

Your home equity is your net worth, not spendable cash. Unless “unlocking it” funds something that generates income or measurable value.

A fee-only advisor is your best friend when it comes to dealing with offers for HELOC or cash-out refinancing. Before you decide anything, compare the total interest cost to how much you could save in 12–24 months for the same purchase before signing anything. The number might surprise you.

Debt is not a moral failing. Nobody builds a career in medicine— or anything for that matter,  without borrowing something along the way. But building wealth that lasts (preferably for generations) requires you to differentiate between good and bad debt.

Student loans, a reasonable mortgage and car payments aside, if you find yourself dreading the monthly payments you know will eat chunks out of your salary, maybe a new plan is what you’re missing.

If any of this hits close to home, you don’t have to figure it out alone. The PoF community is here to help. Drop a comment or take a look at the resources on our site made specifically for this.

And if you’ve already beaten your debt, I want to hear from you. What actually worked? What almost derailed you? Share your story in the comments. Someone reading this today is looking for proof it’s possible— you’re it.

The median for the class of 2025 was $215,000. That number doesn’t include undergraduate loans, so many physicians carry more once you add those in.

Yes. Almost nobody finishes medical school and residency debt free unless family money paid for it. The debt itself isn’t the red flag. What you do with your income once you start earning is.

Match your employer’s 401(k) contribution first, then pay off anything charging more than 6-7% interest. After that, split extra cash between debt and investing based on your rate.

Debt tied to something that produces income or builds equity. A mortgage or a loan on a rental property qualifies. A financed vacation or a car loan on something you can’t actually afford does not.

Yes, for those who qualify. Ten years of qualifying payments while working for a nonprofit or government employer wipes out the remaining balance. Confirm your employer and loan type qualify before counting on it.

As fast as possible. Average APR on carried balances sat at 22.15% in Q2 2026. At that rate, minimum payments can take over a decade and cost more in interest than the original purchase.

Absolutely. Over a third of people earning $200,000 or more report living paycheck to paycheck. Income buys options. Debt takes them away just as fast.

Rarely, unless the money goes toward something that generates income or real value. Most of the time it just converts equity you already own into a new loan with new interest.

The scariest thing on a physician’s desk this October is the fourth-quarter estimated tax worksheet, propped against a 403(b) statement that hasn’t moved since spring.

Most retirement articles are written for someone worried about running out of money. You should worry about that too. On top of it, you carry a problem the average saver never meets: a tax code that takes 37 cents of every married dollar above $768,700, trims your itemized deductions once you get there, shrinks your SALT break somewhere past $505,000, and reaches two years backward to set your Medicare premiums.

Every mistake on this list costs a little more in that bracket.

This list is built for physicians with six figures before the comma, including those who collect some or all of it on a 1099.

Physicians are one of the few groups positioned to collect the maximum Social Security benefit, because most of you clear the taxable wage base ($184,500 in 2026) months before December. That makes claiming age a bigger lever for you than for almost anyone.

According to AARP, a worker at the 2026 maximum who files at 62 collects about $2,969 a month; the same worker gets $4,152 at full retirement age and roughly $5,181 by holding out until 70. Claiming early trims the benefit permanently (5/9 of 1% per month for the first 36 months, 5/12 of 1% per month beyond that), and every year you wait past full retirement age adds 8%.

Dr. Addams claimed at 62 because he “wanted the money while the government still had it.” Six months later he picked up locums shifts at $200 an hour. Before full retirement age, Social Security withholds $1 for every $2 you earn above $24,480, so his own paycheck ate his benefit. (Social Security credits some of that back at full retirement age, but the cash-flow plan he built was toast.) Semi-retired physicians are exactly the people who keep earning after they file.

Two other quirks hit doctors harder. The formula averages your 35 highest-earning years, and residency plus a late start can leave early retirees with zeros in that average; the bend points in the formula soften the blow for high earners, but pull your record at ssa.gov before assuming anything.

If you’re married, the higher earner’s claiming age also sets the survivor benefit, so delaying to 70 works like inflation-adjusted life insurance for your spouse at a price no insurer will match.

A serious diagnosis or a family tree with short branches can justify claiming early. For a healthy 62-year-old internist with a seven-figure portfolio, it’s usually the wrong call.

Capital protection and double-digit monthly cash flow, without becoming a landlord.

Tue, Oct 13  ·  10:00 am PT  ·  11:00 am MT  ·  1:00 pm ET

The textbook move as retirement approaches is to dial down risk. Physicians who take that advice too far end up with a portfolio that can’t outrun their withdrawals.

Run the timeline. Retire at 57 and your money may need to last 35 years or longer. A bond-heavy portfolio feels safe in year one and starts losing ground to inflation and withdrawals by year ten, which is why stocks still have to do some of the lifting deep into retirement.

High earners face a sneakier version of this mistake, and it lives in asset location. Taxable bond interest gets hit at ordinary rates. At 37% plus the 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax (which applies above $250,000 of modified AGI for married couples and has never been indexed for inflation), you hand close to 41 cents of every interest dollar to Washington before your state takes its cut.

Park bonds inside the 401(k) or 403(b), hold broad stock index funds in taxable, and look at municipal bonds if you need fixed income outside retirement accounts.

How much stock is enough? That depends on your spending, your other income, and how well you sleep through a 25% drawdown. “As little as possible” is not an allocation.

Landmark Wealth Management puts the S&P 500’s annualized return from 1926 through 2024 at about 10.3%. It’s a lovely number, and nobody in history has received it in a straight line.

Sequence-of-returns risk turns a reasonable plan into a slasher film.

Two physicians retire with the same $4 million and the same 10-year average return. Dr. Smart retires into three good years and coasts. Dr. Lucky (who, it turns out, was not) retires into a bear market, sells shares near the bottom to fund two years of travel, and never gets those shares back when prices recover. Same average, very different endings.

The 4% rule tries to account for that. William Bengen published it in 1994: withdraw 4% in year one, then adjust that dollar amount for inflation every year after. Bengen has since revised his own number upward to about 4.7%.

The real mistake is treating any single figure as permanent. Retirees who trim spending after bad years (guardrail strategies) or who keep two to three years of withdrawals in cash and short-term bonds (the bucket approach) give their stocks room to recover instead of selling them on the way down.

Pick a method, stress-test it against a crash in year one, and expect to adjust it.

Read: Is the 4% Rule Too Frugal for Doctors?

Maxing your 401(k), 403(b), and 457(b) during peak earning years at 37% is a good move. The trouble starts when it’s the only move for 25 years.

Dr. Smart retires at 60 with $5 million, nearly all of it pre-tax. Required minimum distributions begin at 73 (75 if you were born in 1960 or later) and stack on top of Social Security, up to 85% of which is taxable.

Suddenly, a retired doctor is back in a high bracket, paying tax on money she deferred at a high bracket. Then Medicare notices.

Medicare’s IRMAA surcharges for 2026 begin at a modified AGI of $218,000 for couples ($109,000 single).

At the top tier, Part B jumps from the standard $202.90 a month to $689.90, plus a $91 Part D surcharge, which adds up to roughly $6,900 a year per person in surcharges alone. Medicare also uses a two-year look-back, so the income you report at 63 sets your premiums at 65.

The fix lives in the gap years. Retire at 58, delay Social Security, and you may get a decade where taxable income is the lowest it’s been since residency. Converting chunks of pre-tax money to Roth in that window, filling the lower brackets on purpose, shrinks future RMDs before they become a problem.

During your working years, fund backdoor Roth IRAs ($7,500 limit in 2026) and send part of your savings to the Roth side of your employer plan.

If you’re 50 or older and earned more than $150,000 in FICA wages last year, the IRS already made that choice for you: your 2026 catch-up contributions have to go in as Roth.

Rental income, a part-time medical director role, or expert witness work can also give you an income stream that doesn’t depend on draining one enormous tax-deferred account.

Physicians tend to underestimate retirement spending for a simple reason: they’ve never tracked it. The paycheck covered everything, so nobody looked.

Pull 12 months of actual spending from your cards and accounts, then adjust for what changes after medicine. Disability insurance, licensing fees, CME, and the commute fall away. Travel tends to swell and front-load into the first decade.

Healthcare before Medicare can run five figures a year for a couple buying their own coverage. Long-term care waits at the back of the line: Genworth figures cited in Fisher Investments’ healthcare guide put a semi-private nursing home room at roughly $111,000 a year in 2024, and federal estimates say almost 70% of people will need some form of long-term care, for about three years on average.

Errors cut in two directions. Underestimate spending, and you drain the portfolio early. Overestimate it, and you work three extra years you didn’t need, a loss that never shows up on any statement.

Anyone who practiced through 2022 watched CPI peak at 9.1% that June. Inflation cooled afterward, but prices never went back down.

The damage compounds quietly. A $200,000 annual retirement budget becomes about $361,000 in 20 years at 3% inflation. Any income stream that doesn’t adjust (a fixed annuity, a pension without a cost-of-living rider, a practice buyout paid in level installments) loses purchasing power every year you hold it.

You already know this feeling from the reimbursement side. The AMA estimates Medicare physician payment has fallen by roughly a third since 2001 once you adjust for inflation in practice costs. Give your retirement plan the same respect for erosion you’ve watched happen to your fee schedule, and build in an inflation assumption a bit above whatever the current forecast says.

The urge to leave is real, and it’s showing up earlier. In Doximity’s physician polling, the share of doctors aged 45 to 49 considering early retirement rose between 2023 and 2026, from 30% to 46%. Among emergency physicians, the figure climbed from 30% to 52%.

Burnout is a legitimate reason to change your life and a poor reason to skip the math. Retiring at 52 instead of 60 means eight fewer years of contributions, eight extra years of withdrawals, and a longer stretch buying your own health insurance before Medicare.

Several costs belong to medicine alone. If your malpractice policy is claims-made, leaving can trigger a tail coverage bill, often priced at a multiple of your annual premium, unless your employer covers it or your carrier offers a free tail at retirement age.

A few years away can complicate credentialing if you want back in, and some boards will ask for a formal re-entry program.

On the brighter side, physicians have unusual access to early withdrawals: governmental 457(b) plans carry no 10% penalty once you separate from service, at any age, and the rule of 55 lets you tap the 401(k) or 403(b) of the employer you leave in or after the year you turn 55.

A middle path often beats a hard stop. Dropping to 0.6 FTE, picking up locums, or moving into a nonclinical role keeps income flowing and lets the portfolio grow a few more years untouched.

Medicine breeds a specific condition. You hit your number, decide you need a bigger number, and a market dip convinces you to stay another year, until you’re 68 with $9 million and a partner gently asking whether you’ve thought about slowing down.

Dr. Addams (yes, him again) planned to retire at 62, then 64, then “once the kids finish school.” His youngest graduated in 2019. Money saved after you’ve crossed the finish line buys very little extra safety, and the years spent earning it come out of your healthiest stretch of life.

Hospitals are changing the math as well. Some now require cognitive and physical screening for late-career physicians past a set age, so the decision to keep practicing may not stay entirely yours.

Pick a number and a date, and write down what you’ll do the Monday after. In my experience, physicians who retire toward something stick the landing far more often than those who are simply running from the pager.

Learn what Class A, B, and C really mean, how building quality affects distributions and resale, and why some passive investors prefer properties outside the top tier.

This is the first of three entries that replace the generic advice, and it’s the one high earners ask me about most.

Long-term rentals generate depreciation, but for a full-time physician those losses usually land in the passive bucket, where they can’t touch clinical income.

Short-term rentals play by different rules. If the average guest stay is seven days or less, the property isn’t treated as a rental activity under the regulations. Materially participate (most commonly by logging more than 100 hours a year and more hours than any other individual) and the losses become non-passive, free to offset your W-2 or 1099 income.

Pair that with a cost segregation study and 100% bonus depreciation, permanently restored by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act for property acquired after January 19, 2025, and the first-year numbers get large.

A $500,000 short-term rental might produce $150,000 to $200,000 of year-one depreciation, depending on the property and the study. In the 37% bracket, that’s roughly $55,000 to $74,000 of federal tax that stays in your pocket.

The fine print, which the Instagram gurus skip, matters as much as the pitch:

If any of your income arrives on a 1099 (locums, telehealth, medical director stipends, expert witness work, consulting), you have access to retirement accounts your W-2 colleagues can only envy.

Plenty of contractors open a SEP-IRA and stop there, which is an expensive default.

A Solo 401(k) usually beats it. For 2026, you can defer up to $24,500 as the “employee” (a limit shared with any W-2 401(k) or 403(b) you also contribute to), plus an employer contribution of roughly 20% of net self-employment earnings as a sole proprietor, or 25% of W-2 salary through an S corporation, up to a combined $72,000.

Add $8,000 in catch-up contributions at 50, or $11,250 between ages 60 and 63. The employer side stands apart from your hospital plan, so an employed doc with meaningful side income can layer it on top of what they already contribute at work. The SEP has one more flaw for high earners: its balance counts under the pro-rata rule and sabotages the backdoor Roth.

Older 1099 physicians with steady income should price out a cash balance plan. It’s a defined benefit plan layered on top of the Solo 401(k), and allowable contributions rise with age, often into six figures a year for physicians in their 50s.

You’ll need an actuary and a funding commitment you can’t skip in a lean year, so it suits consistent earners.

Those deductions do double duty because of the QBI cliff. Physicians run a “specified service trade or business,” so the 20% qualified business income deduction phases out as taxable income rises.

For 2026, married couples get the full deduction at or below $403,500 of taxable income, and it vanishes entirely at $553,500 (the single thresholds are $201,750 and $276,750).

Dr. Lucky, married with roughly $500,000 of taxable 1099 income, sits deep in the phase-out. Fund the Solo 401(k) and a cash balance plan, drop taxable income below $403,500, and the QBI deduction rises from the dead on top of the retirement deduction itself.

Self-employment tax deserves a sentence of its own. Contractors pay the employee and employer shares of Social Security (12.4% combined) up to the $184,500 wage base and 2.9% Medicare on everything, plus another 0.9% above $250,000 for married couples.

An S corporation paying you a reasonable salary can trim part of that, though it adds payroll, a separate return, and a salary figure the IRS will scrutinize.

Physicians start saving late. Residency ends somewhere around 30 or 32, often with six-figure student debt, so the compounding years most savers get in their 20s went to call rooms and loan servicers. A year-end cram session can’t make that up.

The calendar matters more than usual this fall. These items won’t wait for the week between Christmas and New Year’s:

Pick one item from this list before you hand out the first fun-size Snickers, and make your CPA earn their fee in November instead of on a panicked phone call in March.

As a hospice physician, Jordan Gurmet discusses a familiar tragedy beyond the emotional weight of medical illness: the sudden, overwhelming chaos that unfolds when aging intersects with a lack of intergenerational financial planning.

Aren’t inheritances supposed to be a big deal? All dollars should be treated equally regardless of their source or use, but human brains aren’t wholly rational, and inherited money feels like it should be different from rents, dividends, gains, or earned income. It should be special.

Should we consider claiming Social Security earlier to squeeze more life out of it? Or, put another way, is there a subjective reason why $2000 per month at age 62 is more valuable than $3500 per month at age 70? And is that subjective reason so powerful that it’s worth locking in those lower payments for life?

Stop deluding yourself with the notion that only money will protect and guarantee a great retirement. Building muscle is the cheapest insurance you will ever purchase. It lowers your risk of falls and injuries. Sarcopenia, the loss of muscle mass, is a leading cause of frailty in older people.

Most physicians own at least one investment sitting below its purchase price this year. Selling it before December 31 can offset capital gains, trim up to $3,000 from ordinary income, and carry any leftover loss into future years. At a 37% marginal rate, that adds up fast. Trip the wash-sale rule, though, and the IRS wipes out the benefit.

Join me and Carson Henderson, CPA/PFS, Senior Wealth & Tax Advisor at Earned, on Tuesday, October 27 at 2:30 PM ET / 11:30 AM PT. Carson will show which holdings to harvest, how to dodge wash-sale trouble, and what to ask your CPA before the year runs out.

Nine weeks sounds like plenty. Holiday call schedules disagree.

#8702. Year-End Tax Planning for Physicians. What To Do Before 2026 Is Over

Taxes may be the last thing on your mind right now. The kids are studying for mid-terms and the holidays are almost upon us. But with less than 3 months left in 2026, you have a small window to implement strategies to minimize your tax bill for 2027.

According to Medscape’s 2026 compensation report, physicians earn, on average, $386,000 a year. Primary care physicians earn $298,000 and specialists make, on average, $417,000.

In 2026, a single filer’s taxable income of $256,225 puts them in the 35% bracket. Same for an income of $512,450 MFJ (married filing jointly). The 37% bracket starts above $640,600 for singles and $768,700 for couples.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) made permanent many provisions that had been scheduled to expire after 2025. It also added limits and phaseouts that affect higher earners specifically. In this guide, I’ll cover the changes that matter to physicians and what you can do before the year is up.

You can’t always choose when you receive income but some form of income like bonuses, self-employment income, Treasury bill income, and voluntary retirement distributions can be timed to reduce your tax bill for 2026.

Deferring income means you receive it in 2027 instead of 2026, and thus pay the tax a year later. Accelerating work in the opposite way. You can also defer or accelerate deductions to either lower this year’s bill or leave it on the table for next year.

If your employer pays a $20,000 bonus on Dec. 20, it counts as 2026 income. If your employer pays it on Jan. 5, it counts as 2027 income. At a 35% rate, that single date change delays $7,000 of federal tax by a full year.

If you expect to be in the same bracket with lower rates next year, you can defer the bonus. If you think you’ll be in a higher bracket next year, go ahead and take it in 2026.

According to this comprehensive guide by Plante Moran, pushing income into 2027 and pulling deductible expenses into 2026 delays tax, which usually helps. A higher bracket next year means you should take the opposite approach because you pay tax on 2026 income at your lower current rate.

If you’re starting as an attending in 2027, you fit the second group. Taking taxable gains or converting pre-tax IRA money to Roth this year will cost you less than doing it after your pay jumps.

Learn more: The Best Time for Roth Conversions May Be Now

Learn what Class A, B, and C really mean, how building quality affects distributions and resale, and why some passive investors prefer properties outside the top tier.

Employed physicians don’t have much control but ask your group whether it can pay a year-end bonus in January. Locums and 1099 physicians can, however, control invoicing and equipment purchases.

Check your Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT) exposure before you defer anything. AMT works like a second tax calculation.

First, you calculate your regular tax, then, you recalculate with certain deductions added back, including your SALT deduction. Then you subtract an AMT exemption, which in 2026, is $90,100 for single filers and $140,200 for joint filers. You then must pay whichever tax is higher.

The OBBBA shrank that exemption for high earners in 2026. It starts the reduction at $500,000 of AMTI for singles and $1,000,000 for couples. It then cuts the exemption by 50 cents for every dollar above those thresholds.

The exemption disappears at $680,200 for singles and $1,280,400 for couples.

All that is to say that each extra $1,000 of income inside the phaseout range costs you $500 of exemption, so $1,500 becomes taxable at 28%. That equals a 42% marginal rate, which beats the 37% top regular rate.

Once the exemption disappears, your marginal AMT rate drops to 28%. Estimate your marginal rate for 2026 and 2027, then move income toward the lower-rate year.

Your employer withholds the additional 0.9% Medicare tax only on wages above $200,000, regardless of your filing status or your spouse’s pay. The tax itself applies above $250,000 for joint filers.

Two married physicians who each earn $300,000 have an employer who starts withholding the extra 0.9% Medicare tax once that physician’s pay passes $200,000. Each physician has $100,000 above that line, so each employer withholds $900. Together, the couple has $1,800 withheld.

With a combined wages of $600,000 the joint cutoff is $250,000, so the couple owes 0.9% of the rest of the $350,000. That’s $3,150. After subtracting the $1,800 withheld by the employers, the  couple owes $1,350 more when they file.

You can raise your W-4 withholding before Dec. 31 to cover it. This will require you to submit a new W-4 to your employer and enter the extra amount per paycheck in Step 4(c).

Withholding counts as paid evenly across the year so it beats a late estimated payment. Penalty protection requires payments of at least 90% of your 2026 tax or 110% of your 2025 tax. The 100% safe harbor covers only taxpayers with 2025 AGI of $150,000 or less, which rules out most attendings.

The annualized income installment method helps when income skews toward year-end, as locums and bonus income often do.

The 3.8% net investment income tax (NIIT) starts at $200,000 of MAGI for single filers and $250,000 for joint filers.

Those thresholds have stayed the same since 2013, so every raise adds more of your investment income into the tax. Anything that lowers MAGI, including retirement contributions and HSA deposits, lowers your NIIT too.

The IRS raised the 2026 employee limit for 401(k), 403(b) and governmental 457 plans to $24,500. Catch-up contributions add $8,000 at age 50 or older, for a total of $32,500.

There’s also a bonus catch-up of $11,250 for ages 60 to 63, which brings the total to $35,750. If your hospital also offers a governmental 457(b), that plan carries its own limit of $24,500.

SECURE 2.0 now requires employees who earned more than $150,000 in 2025 wages to direct catch-up contributions to Roth accounts. That’s all attendings. If your plan offers no Roth option, you can’t make 2026 catch-up contributions at all.

Direct Roth IRA contributions phase out between $153,000 and $168,000 for single filers and between $242,000 and $252,000 for joint filers.

Employed physicians can contribute $7,500 to a nondeductible traditional IRA and convert it. This works best when neither spouse has funds in a traditional IRA, and you owe tax only on growth between the contribution and the conversion.

A pre-tax IRA balance makes part of the conversion taxable, so roll it into your 401(k) before Dec. 31 if your plan accepts rollovers.

Practice owners have bigger options. A profit-sharing plan allows total contributions of $72,000, or $80,000 with catch-up, or $83,250 at ages 60 to 63.

A SEP allows $72,000 and requires at least $360,000 of self-employment income before the deduction.

A defined benefit plan can allow larger deductible contributions than either, depending on your age and target benefit. The 2026 maximum is $290,000 or 100% of your highest 3-year average earned income, whichever is lower.

Self-employed physicians can set up a plan and make 2026 contributions as late as the tax return due date, including extensions. If you have employees, you likely must let them participate.

Also read: Backdoor Roth IRA 2026: A Step by Step Guide with Vanguard

For 2026, the HSA limits are $4,400 for self-only coverage and $8,750 for family coverage, plus $1,000 at age 55 or older. Contributions reduce AGI and qualified withdrawals come out tax-free. A family contribution of $8,750 can save you about $3,063 in federal tax at a 35% rate.

A health FSA is limited to $3,400 and you can carry over up to $680 of unused funds to 2027. The dependent care FSA limit rose to $7,500 from $5,000, which saves you $2,625 at a 35% rate. Those contributions reduce the expenses you can claim for the child and dependent care credit.

Today’s relatively low rates raise the odds that your retirement rate will be higher.

Permanent rates have no expiration date but Congress can still raise them. Converting in chunks over several years keeps each year’s income from jumping into a higher bracket. But a Roth conversion adds to your taxable income in the year you convert so confirm you can pay the tax from outside the IRA.

Early-retired and part-time physicians must now deal with expiration of the enhanced premium tax credit. This means that the ACA cliff now applies to them.

If you earn $1 above 400% of the poverty line, you lose all marketplace subsidies. The threshold is $62,600 for a single person and $129,000 for a family of 4 in 2026.

Tommy Lucas, a CFP at Moisand Fitzgerald Tamayo recommends pairing a high-deductible plan with HSA contributions, which lower your AGI.

Two new rules have reduced the value of itemized gifts.

A 0.5% of AGI floor is now in effect which means a physician with $500,000 of AGI can’t deduct the first $2,500 of donations.

The OBBBA also caps the tax benefit at 35 cents per dollar for filers in the 37% bracket.

Bunching charitable giving can fix most of the floor issue. The floor applies once per year, so 5 years of $10,000 gifts at $500,000 of AGI forfeit $2,500 each year and leave $37,500 deductible.

One $50,000 gift forfeits $2,500 once and leaves $47,500 deductible. The extra $10,000 saves $3,500 at a 35% rate.

Charissa Anderson, a CFP at Ferguson Wellman Capital Management, says that bunching works best when you pair a donor-advised fund with appreciated stock. A donor-advised fund lets you make 1 large gift now and send grants to charities over time.

Plante Moran warns that you should get written acknowledgment that the sponsoring organization holds exclusive legal control of the assets.

If you itemize, shares held for more than 1 year before donating let you deduct full market value and skip the capital gains tax you’d pay otherwise. Most physicians pay 15% on long-term gains plus the 3.8% NIIT, which totals 18.8%.

Physicians with taxable income above $545,500 (single) or $613,700 (joint) pay 20% plus the NIIT, which totals 23.8%. If you donate $50,000 of shares with a $20,000 basis, you can avoid up to $5,640 at 18.8% or $7,140 at 23.8% of the $30,000 gain.

The deduction is capped at 30% of AGI for public charities and you can carry the excess forward 5 years.

Donors can use tax lot selection, as in choosing which specific shares to give. Lots with the largest gains usually make the best candidates. Never donate shares that trade below your basis. Sell them, claim the loss and donate the cash.

Physicians who take the standard deduction ($16,100 single, $32,200 joint) can now deduct up to $1,000 of cash gifts or $2,000 for couples. A couple in the 35% bracket can save $700.

Physicians aged 70 1⁄2 or older can send up to $111,000 from an IRA directly to charity in 2026. That transfer counts toward required minimum distributions and steers clear of taxable income.

For 2026, the SALT cap is $40,400. As your MAGI exceeds $505,000, the cap drops by 30 cents for every extra dollar.

A couple with $550,000 of MAGI have an excess of $45,000. The cap drops by 30% of $45,000, which is $13,500. Their cap falls from $40,400 to $26,900. As your MAGI approaches $606,333, the cap reaches its $10,000 minimum. Above that, it stays at $10,000.

If your 2026 state and local taxes will fall short of the cap, prepay your 2027 property tax bill by Dec. 31. Your county needs to have assessed the bill already.

Plante Moran estimates a single filer in the 35% bracket saves $14,140 by deducting the full $40,400. Check your AMT first, though. A large SALT deduction can trigger it. You also need enough total itemized deductions to beat your standard deduction.

The Section 199A deduction is permanent and equals up to 20% of qualified business income.

Medicine counts as a specified service business, so as your income increases, the deduction gets smaller before eventually disappearing.

The 2026 phase ranges from $201,750 to $276,750 for single filers, with double those amounts for joint filers. Part-time physicians, lower-earning specialties and couples with taxable income below $553,500 can still claim some deduction. Retirement contributions that lower your taxable income can pull you back into the range.

S corporation owners can take part of their income as distributions instead of salary, which avoids payroll taxes and the 0.9% Medicare tax. The IRS scrutinizes this closely, so make sure your salary is reasonable.

The OBBBA also lowered the cap on business losses that offset other income to $256,000 for single filers and $512,000 for joint filers in 2026. Rental income and losses count as passive unless you qualify as a real estate professional.

That status requires more than half of your personal services and more than 750 hours in property businesses. Special rules can help spouses meet material participation.

Equipment buyers can deduct 100% of the cost of qualifying property in the first year through bonus depreciation. This applies to property you acquire after Jan. 19, 2025. Section 179 expensing reached $2.56 million in 2026 and phases out above $4.09 million of purchases.

The equipment must be placed in service by Dec. 31.

Dec. 31 for most moves, including charitable gifts, payroll retirement deferrals and property tax prepayments. Self-employed physicians can set up and fund a retirement plan until the 2026 return due date, including extensions.

Add up your deductions and pick the larger amount. The standard deduction is $16,100 for single filers and $32,200 for joint filers. Itemize when your SALT, mortgage interest and charitable gifts exceed it.

Defer if you expect the same or a lower tax rate next year. Accelerate if you expect a higher one. A fellow who starts as an attending in 2027 fits the second group.

It is 0.9% of wages above $200,000 for single filers and above $250,000 for joint filers. Employers start withholding at $200,000 regardless of your filing status, so couples often owe extra when they file.

Pay at least 90% of your 2026 tax or 110% of your 2025 tax. Raise your W-4 withholding before Dec. 31 to cover any shortfall.

You can contribute $24,500 to a 401(k), 403(b) or governmental 457 plan. Add $8,000 at age 50 or older. Ages 60 to 63 can add $11,250 instead.

Employees who earned more than $150,000 in 2025 wages must make catch-up contributions to Roth accounts. If your plan has no Roth option, you can’t make 2026 catch-up contributions.

Direct contributions phase out between $153,000 and $168,000 for single filers and between $242,000 and $252,000 for joint filers. Most physicians use a backdoor Roth, which converts a nondeductible traditional IRA contribution of up to $7,500.

It affects early-retired and part-time physicians who buy marketplace coverage. Earn $1 above 400% of the poverty line and you lose all subsidies. CNBC reports the 2026 threshold at about $63,000 for a single person.

The cap is $40,400. It drops by 30 cents for every dollar of MAGI above $505,000 and bottoms out at $10,000 at about $606,333.

Often only in part. Medicine counts as a specified service business, so the deduction phases out between $201,750 and $276,750 of taxable income for single filers and disappears above that. Joint filers get double those amounts.

The 0.5% of AGI floor applies once per year, so one large gift loses less than several small ones. At $500,000 of AGI, a $50,000 gift saves $3,500 more than 5 yearly gifts of $10,000 at a 35% rate.

Yes. If you itemize and held the shares for more than 1 year, you deduct full market value and avoid the capital gains tax you’d owe on a sale. Donate publicly traded shares directly to the charity or donor-advised fund.

Yes. A CPA who knows your state and practice structure can model your return for you before you act.

The bonus-timing example is concrete: a $20,000 bonus paid Dec. 20 lands in 2026 wages, while a Jan. 5 pay date pushes the same dollars into 2027 and, at a 35% marginal rate, delays about $7,000 of federal tax for a year. Pairing that with the 2026 HSA ceilings ($4,400 self-only / $8,750 family, plus $1,000 catch-up at 55+) and the checklist on accelerating or deferring deductions gives employed physicians a short year-end punch list even when W-2 wages themselves are inflexible.

The S&P 500 is an index that tracks the 500 largest publicly traded companies in the United States, weighted by market capitalization. It includes Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Nvidia, Alphabet (Google), Meta, Berkshire Hathaway, and approximately 493 other companies that collectively represent about 80% of the total U.S. stock market value.

The index is maintained by S&P Dow Jones Indices, which periodically adds and removes companies based on criteria including market cap (must exceed ~$18 billion), profitability, liquidity, and domicile. When a company is added to the S&P 500, every index fund tracking it automatically buys shares — and vice versa when companies are removed.

An S&P 500 index fund is a mutual fund or exchange-traded fund (ETF) that holds all 500 stocks in the same proportions as the index. Instead of picking individual stocks, you buy one fund and instantly own a piece of every major U.S. company. The fund mechanically replicates the index — no stock picking, no market timing, no overpaid fund managers.

The data is overwhelming. Over any 15-year period, approximately 92% of actively managed large-cap funds underperform the S&P 500 after fees, according to the SPIVA scorecard. Over 20 years, that number exceeds 95%. The reasons are simple: active fund managers charge 0.50% to 1.50% in annual fees, they generate taxable trading activity, and they cannot consistently pick winners.

Warren Buffett bet $1 million that an S&P 500 index fund would beat a selection of hedge funds over 10 years. He won decisively — the index fund returned 125.8% vs 36.0% for the hedge fund basket. As Buffett has said: "By periodically investing in an index fund, the know-nothing investor can actually outperform most investment professionals."

The top S&P 500 index funds deliver nearly identical performance because they all track the same index. The differences come down to expense ratio, minimum investment, fund structure (ETF vs mutual fund), and tax efficiency. Here is a detailed comparison of the five most popular options.

The most popular S&P 500 ETF and the default recommendation for most FI seekers. At 0.03% expense ratio, a $500,000 investment costs just $150 per year in fees. VOO is tax-efficient due to the ETF structure and Vanguard's patented heartbeat trade process, which minimizes capital gains distributions. Fractional shares are available at most brokerages.

The lowest-cost S&P 500 fund available at 0.015% — half the cost of VOO. No minimum investment requirement makes it ideal for beginners. As a mutual fund, you can set up automatic investments in exact dollar amounts (e.g., $500/month). FXAIX is an excellent choice if your brokerage is Fidelity.

BlackRock's S&P 500 ETF with a 0.03% expense ratio, matching VOO. Functionally identical performance. Slightly different creation/redemption mechanics than VOO but the practical difference for individual investors is negligible. A strong alternative if you prefer iShares or trade through a brokerage that offers commission-free iShares ETFs.

The oldest and most heavily traded S&P 500 ETF, launched in 1993. SPY is the most liquid ETF in the world, making it the preferred choice for active traders. However, its 0.0945% expense ratio is over three times higher than VOO or IVV. For long-term FI investors, VOO or IVV are better choices. SPY's structure as a unit investment trust also makes it slightly less tax-efficient than VOO.

Schwab's mutual fund offering at 0.02% expense ratio with no minimum investment. Like FXAIX, the mutual fund structure allows automatic dollar-amount investing. An excellent choice for Schwab customers building automated investment plans.

Investing in an S&P 500 fund takes less than 15 minutes:

For retirement accounts (401k, IRA), look for the S&P 500 index fund option within your plan. It may have a different name (e.g., "Large Cap Index Fund" or "Institutional S&P 500") but will track the same index.

The total stock market index (tracked by VTI/VTSAX/FSKAX) holds approximately 3,600 stocks compared to the S&P 500's 500. The additional 3,100 stocks are mid-cap and small-cap companies. Here is how they compare:

Historically, the performance difference between the two is minimal — typically within 0.1-0.3% per year in either direction. The S&P 500 has outperformed in periods when large-cap growth stocks dominate. The total market has outperformed when small and mid-cap stocks lead. Over 20+ year periods, the returns converge closely.

The FI community's honest answer: it does not matter much which you choose. Investing $24,500 per year in VOO or VTI will produce nearly identical outcomes over 20 years. Consistency and contribution amount matter far more than the choice between S&P 500 and total market.

S&P 500 index funds typically yield 1.2% to 1.6% in annual dividends. In a tax-advantaged account (401k, IRA, Roth), dividends compound tax-free. In a taxable account, qualified dividends from S&P 500 funds are taxed at the favorable long-term capital gains rate (0%, 15%, or 20% depending on income).

ETFs (VOO, IVV) are generally more tax-efficient than mutual funds (FXAIX, SWPPX) in taxable accounts because ETFs rarely distribute capital gains. Vanguard's mutual funds are an exception — their patented ETF share class structure gives Vanguard mutual funds ETF-like tax efficiency. For taxable brokerage accounts, VOO or VFIAX (Vanguard's mutual fund version) are the most tax-efficient choices.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The most common mistake with S&P 500 index funds is waiting for the "right time" to invest. Research from Vanguard shows that investing a lump sum immediately outperforms dollar-cost averaging about two-thirds of the time, because markets go up more often than they go down. Missing just the 10 best trading days over a 20-year period can cut your returns nearly in half. If you have money to invest, the data overwhelmingly says to invest it now — not next week, not after the next pullback, not when it "feels right."

Open an account at Vanguard (for VOO/VFIAX), Fidelity (for FXAIX), or Schwab (for SWPPX). All three offer commission-free trading on their own index funds, excellent customer service, and robust retirement account options. You can also buy any of these funds at most brokerages.

ETFs (VOO, IVV) trade like stocks at real-time prices and are more tax-efficient in taxable accounts. Mutual funds (FXAIX, SWPPX) allow automatic dollar-amount investing and are better for set-it-and-forget-it contribution schedules. For retirement accounts, either works equally well.

Transfer cash to your brokerage account and buy your chosen fund. Start with whatever you have — there is no minimum too small. FXAIX and SWPPX have $0 minimums, and VOO can be purchased in fractional shares at most brokerages for as little as $1.

Automate monthly or per-paycheck contributions. This removes emotion from the process and ensures consistent dollar-cost averaging. Most brokerages let you schedule recurring purchases of mutual funds. For ETFs, some brokerages offer automatic ETF purchases as well.

If you hold other asset classes (bonds, international), rebalance once per year to maintain your target allocation. Otherwise, do nothing — do not check daily prices, do not sell during downturns, and do not chase performance. The S&P 500 has recovered from every crash in history. Time in the market beats timing the market.

Fidelity 500 Index Fund (FXAIX) has the lowest expense ratio at 0.015%. Schwab S&P 500 Index Fund (SWPPX) is next at 0.02%. VOO and IVV tie at 0.03%. All four are excellent — the fee difference between FXAIX (0.015%) and VOO (0.03%) on a $500,000 portfolio is just $75 per year. Choose the fund offered by your preferred brokerage.

VOO is better for long-term investors. It charges 0.03% vs SPY's 0.0945%, saving you about $325 per year on a $500,000 portfolio. VOO is also more tax-efficient due to its ETF share class structure. SPY's advantage is liquidity for active trading, which long-term index investors do not need. For buy-and-hold FI investing, VOO is the clear winner.

Either is an excellent choice. The S&P 500 covers approximately 80% of the U.S. stock market by value. A total market fund adds mid-cap and small-cap stocks for fuller diversification. Over long periods, performance is nearly identical — typically within 0.1-0.3% per year. The FI community consensus is that the best fund is the one you will consistently invest in without overthinking the decision.

As little as $1. FXAIX and SWPPX have zero minimum investments. VOO and IVV can be purchased as fractional shares at most brokerages. There is no minimum too small — starting with $50 or $100 per month and increasing contributions as your income grows is exactly how most people on the FI path begin.

The S&P 500 has returned approximately 10.3% per year on average since 1957 (including dividends). Adjusted for inflation, the real return is approximately 7.0% per year. These are long-term averages — individual years range from -38% (2008) to +38% (1995). The key is staying invested through the down years to capture the recovery gains that follow.

S&P 500 index funds carry market risk — they can lose significant value in the short term (the index dropped 34% in early 2020 and 38% in 2008). However, the S&P 500 has recovered from every decline in its history and has never lost money over any 20-year period. For investors with a 10+ year time horizon, the risk of not investing (missing out on 10% average annual returns) is far greater than the risk of temporary market declines.

S&P 500 index funds are the single most important building block for long-term wealth. With expense ratios as low as 0.015%, you keep virtually all of your returns while owning a piece of the 500 largest U.S. companies. VOO, FXAIX, IVV, and SWPPX all deliver near-identical performance — choose the fund offered by your preferred brokerage and automate your contributions. The FI community has proven through thousands of real-world examples that consistent investing in a low-cost S&P 500 index fund, held for decades without panic selling, is the most reliable path to building wealth and reaching financial independence.
