#8696. Six Dumb Misconceptions About The Economy (that the Politicians Want You To Believe)

Well, it looks like we’re here in another US election year already.

As Advanced Mustachians, we already know that the ongoing battle of Harris vs. Trump should not be consuming much of our time.  Sure, we do our research and cast our votes but after that we move right on to focus on other things within our own circle of control.

But out of all the things the politicians like to bicker about, there’s one area where MMM does need to set the record straight, and that area is of course money. Your money, the economy in general, and the overall wealth of the nation.

Politicians are already not known for being the sharpest tools in the shed when it comes to technical stuff like science, technology, or economics. But this year the discourse has become particularly dumb, as our candidates try to manipulate undecided voters in swing states with ideas that are based on irrational emotions rather than sound economic sense.

For one particularly funny example, you may have noticed that the competing party (Trump in this case) is attacking the incumbents (Biden/Harris) over the “bad economy.” When in fact the US economy is stronger than it has ever been, with the lowest unemployment we’ve ever seen as well.

It’s hard to imagine a better situation than we have right now, and in fact the recent bout of higher inflation is a sign that things have been going too well, and we needed to step on the brakes with the help of higher interest rates.

But somehow the people still seem to believe that we have a “bad” economy. Take a look at this Gallup poll showing that while most people (85%) are doing really well right now, they assume that it’s just their own good fortune – only 17% believe the economy is doing well.

This is mathematically impossible, because if most people are doing well, that’s the definition of a good economy! And suspiciously enough, this widespread wrongness correlates quite nicely with the rise of social media misinformation.

So the politicians and the news have been doing the opposite of what they should be doing in an ideal situation (sharing accurate information). And sure, we can always just ignore their speeches and go on with our lives. But when it comes to economics, knowledge is power (and money). The more accurately we understand how things really work, the wealthier we will all become.

So with all that in mind, I hereby present you with my list of the…

Top Dumb Things Politicians Want You To Believe About The Economy

If there’s a recession, the opposition party likes to blame it on the current president. If the economy is booming, the current president likes to give himself (or possibly soon herself) credit for all of that success. But really, the US economy is way too big – and thankfully way too free – for the president to control or really even influence all that strongly.

In reality, our economy is a gigantic machine which converts labor and materials into things like iPhones, hospitals and pumpkin pies. And although we’re the biggest economy at 26% of the planet, we are still heavily influenced by that much bigger 74% of economic activity that the other 7.6 billion people on Earth are busy producing everywhere else.

When we have our inevitable little boom and bust cycles, they are mostly caused by the normal cycle of irrational exuberance (and greed) like the 2007 housing boom, followed by brief periods of extreme fear and pessimism like the 2008-2012 financial and housing crash.

The government does play a role too, by setting tax rates and other rules. But the effects of these policies are usually so delayed and unpredictable, that you can’t draw a straight line between today’s president and today’s economy. In other words, the government does its best to adjust the rudder on our giant ship, but in the short term our economy lurches around on the waves and storms of the ocean.

This one is especially funny to me, as our candidates feign sympathy for the hard life of middle class Americans, who now face higher borrowing costs on their credit cards and car loans and mortgages. They claim they will fight to bring the interest rates down. Trump even goes as far as bullying our Federal Reserve board members (who can only do their jobs if we allow them to function as independent experts) and suggesting that he would take over the whole department, if elected.

The real story is that while monetary policy would be a terrible tool to leave in the hands of a sitting president (see Argentina), it does function as an excellent set of gas and brake pedals for the economy if used properly. When things slow down and unemployment gets too high, a cut to the interest rates will produce a boost in everything from new jobs to stock prices. But if things get too hot, you get rapid inflation which can mess up the system.

3: Inflation has Made Life Harder for Americans (and the President Can Magically Reverse it)

This line of reasoning is even dumber than the last one. For a couple of years after the Covid era, we had rapid inflation. It was caused by a rare combination of a goods shortage caused by things like factory closures and remote work, plentiful demand from government stimulus spending and low interest rates. These factors have since ironed themselves out, and inflation is back down to an ultra-low 2.4%.

But most significantly, wages have still risen faster than inflation so we are all better off than before! Since 2019, overall prices are up 19% and our wages are up 21%. So even after all that inflation, we are still doing just fine. But the candidates are still bickering over inflation as if it’s an actual problem, and even worse promising to “bring prices back down”. And they’ve managed to convince the electorate that “higher wages and prices” is the same thing as “a bad economy”. Which is just plain wrong.

Bonus dumbness: politicians also occasionally blame “greedy corporations” for increasing prices to hoard profits. While price increases are totally acceptable in a market system (as a business owner you are free to set prices wherever you like), in reality it doesn’t usually happen because our markets are too competitive. For example, a recent deep analysis from NPR showed that no, grocery stores haven’t made any windfall profit at all off of this recent bout of Covid-fueled inflation.

One important thing that has changed over the past ten years is that US house prices and rents have both risen much faster than general inflation and even wages. On the positive side, interest rates have also risen which tends to make houses feel more expensive and is supposed to help bring house prices down. But it hasn’t happened yet which means we have the double whammy of higher prices and higher interest costs for mortgage borrowers.

The dumb part is that our candidates are proposing things that would make the problem even worse, like subsidies for first-time homebuyers or schemes to reduce the interest rates. When really the solution is to increase the supply of housing, which I personally think will happen if we stop putting up roadblocks for homebuilders (myself included) to build housing.

Things like faster and cheaper permits, less onerous and expensive building codes, eliminating suburban-style zoning and setback and car parking rules, and changing laws so that NIMBYs no longer get any say over what other people do with their own land could all help reduce the cost of building a house by about 50%, quickly and permanently.

5: The President Controls Gas Prices, and They Are Currently “High” and We Want Them Lower

Ahh, gasoline! The most ridiculous of things to worry about and the fuel for many of MMM’s rants since 2011.

First of all, on an inflation-adjusted basis, gasoline is still about the same price as it was in 1950: in the $3-4 range per gallon, in today’s dollars.

Secondly, it is so cheap that even with our huge inefficient American vehicles, the average household is still only spending 2.5% of their disposable income on the stuff! (The funny part is that they spend many times more on the rest of the car ownership experience while thinking gas is the part that is expensive)

Third, gasoline has been obsolete for almost a decade now. You can get a used electric car for less than the price of a comparable used gas car, or if you’re a fancypants money waster like me, new EVs are also cheaper than their gas counterparts. You get a faster, nicer car that almost never needs maintenance OR gasoline, and save money.

So why are we even still talking about this antique fuel of a previous era? Why aren’t the candidates also arguing over the price of Kodak film or typewriters or fax machines?

6: The Economy is Something We Should Even Worry About

The funniest part about all this economic talk is that we’re focusing on the wrong thing. While hard work and business and advancing the frontiers of human knowledge are all fun things, the reality is that we passed the point of having “Enough” decades ago. When the American middle class complains about how hard we have it these days, it’s like a bunch of overfed people at a buffet wishing they could just have one more flavor of donuts stacked onto the table.

Yes, we have income and wealth inequality so that the rich tend to get richer more quickly. And yes, we should keep that in check with a somewhat progressive tax system because a more equal society tends to be a more peaceful and happy one.

But have you noticed that as the rich people get richer, they don’t get any happier? It’s because after you pass the point of “Enough”, adding more money doesn’t really help much.

And “Enough” is much more defined by your mindset (and your collection of life skills) than your paycheck. So if the politicians really cared about improving our happiness and wellbeing, they’d be preaching the Principles of Mustachianism rather than pandering to the specific requests of coal miners or billionaires.

But alas, winning an election is a very different thing than proposing stuff that is actually best for the country. And for that reason, we cast our votes for the best party and then tune back out until the next election.

Autarky is the end goal of all these tariffs, and it has negative economic consequences that seem to be missing from what the politicans say. Without the ability to trade, countries lose the benefits of specialization and comparative advantage. This leads to higher prices for in country consumers and a lack of diversity in available goods. Autarky stifles innovation and technological progress by isolating a country from global competition and advancements. An autarkic system is also more vulnerable to domestic economic shocks, such as natural disasters or supply disruptions, because it cannot rely on imports to balance shortfalls. Autarky reduces a country’s economic growth potential by cutting off access to international markets, foreign investment, and trade-driven employment opportunities. Finally, it risks diplomatic isolation, as trade restrictions often result in retaliatory measures from other nations, further limiting a country’s global economic and political influence. While autarky may appeal in terms of self-reliance, the downsides—higher costs, reduced growth, and vulnerability—make it unsustainable in the modern country.

1. “Government deficits don’t necessarily cause inflation. They are funded by the sale of T-bills and bonds.”

Yes, but if demand for those bonds is weak, the central bank steps in as the lender of last resort, printing money to purchase them, which can lead to inflation.

2. “Even an expanding money supply does not dictate the inflation rate. As we saw last year, we can have inflation even when the money supply shrinks, and this year we have much lower inflation even with a growing money supply.”

Yes, but inflation often lags behind changes in the money supply—it can take time for new money to fully circulate and impact prices.

3. “Moderate inflation is NOT bad and does not destroy purchasing power (unless you keep your wealth all in cash).”

Inflation does destroy purchasing power. Investing in assets that grow faster than inflation, like stocks or real estate, can keep you ahead of it. They don’t avoid inflation, they just try to beat it.

Mr. Money Mustache October 30, 2024, 7:23 pm

I think hybrids were great as a transition technology, because they helped our gas cars become more efficient back when batteries were too expensive to make an affordable all-electric car.

For example, in 2013, electric car battery packs cost about $780 per kWh to build, meaning my Tesla Model Y’s 80 kWh pack alone would have cost $62,000!

Today (2024 as I write this) that battery pack number is about $100, so my battery is only $8k of the car’s price. And since an electric car no longer needs an engine, transmission, exhaust system or all the other junk that comes with combustion, we now see electric cars have become LESS expensive than gas cars of equivalent quality/performance (the model Y is in the low $40s brand new, and under $30k used)

With the combination of easy+cheap home charging plus a bunch of nationwide fast charging networks (Tesla’s is still the best by far), there is no reason to have to settle for a hybrid – unless you’re shopping in the cheaper end of the used market. An under $10k used Prius with low miles is still a great frugal car if you can find one!

Avoid Nissan Leafs since their charging standard is no longer used and their batteries are air cooled, leading to far more degradation than other EVs that have active cooling. If you’re looking at Chevy Bolt’s make sure the battery modules were repaired per the recall. One of the best things about them is that your house is your “fuel” station. If you don’t have at home charging available it can be more of a challenge (unless your work has chargers).

Our 2014 Leaf that we bought used for a song in 2019 is still doing exactly what we need it to do – around town car, usually under 10 miles per day (eBike would be even more economical, but I kinda like my climate control here in the very hot, very humid southeast). If you’re needing to do a lot of long-distance driving, then yeah – Leaf’s, particularly older ones aren’t a great choice.

Agreed on at-home charging still the best way – public charging is expanding, but paid public charging is often as expensive as gasoline.

I’m a city dweller with a desk job, so take this analysis for what its worth. Also, a farm or ranch is a business, so a approaching it from a personal finance perspective may not be the right way to look at it.

From what I understand most small farms and ranches in the US aren’t profitable. Based on my parents’ neighbors and many of the sources I’ve read, I think this is because farming and ranching is often a cultural identity and a lifestyle choice, and these properties aren’t being run as an efficient business. They’re hobby farms run by rich dentists, or their owners identify as “cattle ranchers” whether or not the market supports that identity and without a diversified, efficient business plan to maximize the profitability of the entire enterprise.

Here are some Mustachian principles I think apply to farms, ranches, and people who live in rural areas.

Trade the pickup truck for a smaller, less expensive, and preferably used vehicle that does the job better and drive it as little as possible. For everything else, buy a bike or small (used) sedan. There are shades of rural, but a lot of transportation needs can still be met by bike or electric bike. I rode my ebike about 40 miles yesterday to run errands in the city. I grew up in the sticks, and I’d have had a lot more freedom if I’d had an ebike. An electric cargo bike may able to be substituted for a four-wheeler or pickup truck for a lot of on farm transportation. The bike I have can basically carry the weight of two people. If you’re moving a dozen 40lb bags of feed around, that’s a max of four trips by electric cargo bike. Bikes are low, so loading one is faster and easier than throwing bags up into a pickup truck bed.

When it comes to farm equipment and purchases of all kinds, ask if you really need the equipment or if its just a status symbol. Can the job be done with muscle power. If you need the equipment, can you buy it used or substitute a less flashy alternative. Financing for farm equipment is similar to financing for a new car. Probably a money hole.

Every single farm input needs scrutiny and optimization. Fertilizer that washes into the river is money going down the sewer. This includes water, fertilizer, pesticides, etc. Spraying money at the problem isn’t solving it.

Cut your Cash-Leaking Umbilical Cord. If you moved to the country to enjoy the country, why do you need 500 channels of entertainment?

Focus on your Circle of Control, not your Circle of Interest. You can’t change the global cattle market, but you can decide whether to add sheep and goats, get paid by a land conservancy, host duck hunters, market your beef to yuppies at farmers markets, or do any number of other things to increase the profitability of your property.

Reduce grocery trips and expenses by growing your own food and trading with neighbors. Put in some fruit trees and a kitchen garden. Raise some chickens. Trade for milk. This should be one of the big advantages of living in the countryside in farm country.

That’s just a quick look, but I think a lot of the Mustachian principles apply in rural areas too.

#8692. You’re Not Rich — And Neither Am I

Warren Buffett has spent decades telling anyone who’ll listen that he lives simply. Same house in Omaha he bought in 1958 for $31,500. No mansion, no car collection, nothing flashy.

He eats at McDonald’s, drinks Coke by the case and has said more than once that a person could live like him on a fraction of his fortune and lose nothing that actually matters.

A physician two decades into a cardiology career already has a six-bedroom house on two acres with a three-car garage. Something that would put Buffett’s Omaha home to shame.

But Buffett flies private. On his personal jet. Which he owns. (He also owns the company that made his plane just FYI).

That cardiologist couldn’t touch a private jet with a ten-foot pole. Not on a $600,000 salary carrying a jumbo mortgage, two kids in private school and a home equity line he opened for the kitchen renovation.

Buffett could write a check for that physician’s entire house and still have money left for the furniture.

My point is, quantifying wealth is not a black and white endeavor. McMansions don’t lead to private jets. And “modest” lifestyles don’t rule them out.

It’s a strange world we live in. One where most people are blindly chasing perception rather than what actually matters.

Capital protection and double-digit monthly cash flow, without becoming a landlord.

Tue, Oct 13  ·  10:00 am PT  ·  11:00 am MT  ·  1:00 pm ET

Also read: Why Most Doctors Retire With Too Much Money (And What to Do About It)

The Federal Reserve’s Survey of Consumer Finances states that the median American household net worth is $192,084. The average is more than 5x that at $1.06 million due to a relatively small number of extremely wealthy households that pull the average up.

Physicians, as a group, are ahead of that median and the gap keeps widening.

Medscape’s 2026 Physician Wealth & Debt Report found that 24% of physicians now report a family net worth of $5 million or more — largely thanks to stock market gains and rising home values.

However, the same report makes it clear this wealth isn’t evenly spread. The physicians in the $5 million group are mostly in procedure-based specialties which have the highest earning ceilings to begin with.

Plenty of physicians in lower-paying specialties spend most of a career well short of that mark despite carrying the same title, the same debt load at the start, and the same years of deferred income during training.

All physicians start with some sort of student debt — small or big — regardless of specialty. The median medical school debt for the class of 2025 is $215,000, not counting undergraduate loans.

Or any non-education debt, credit cards and car loans that tend to accumulate during residency for that matter.

A newly minted attending earning six figures can still have a negative net worth. It takes years to pay down debt and bring it up to zero.

Years more to enter the black. Those early years are the reason for the gap between a $5-million-net-worth radiologist and a physician twenty years into practice who still hasn’t crossed seven figures.

Let’s talk about two doctors who have the same degree and the same starting debt but two very different philosophies on spending money.

For this example we’ll play into the most common stereotypes doctors have faced — and fought hard to shed — for years.

Dr. Flashy “invests” in a new Range Rover every three years. He’s got a lake house two hours outside the city, a boat he uses maybe four weekends a summer — if the weather cooperates.

And surprisingly to some, he’s not broke. He makes real money and a part of his lifestyle is funded from that same income.

Almost every single one of these major purchases generates its own follow-on bill which continues to recur exponentially.

The Range Rover’s routine maintenance costs more than a lot of people’s monthly car payment. The lake house needs a new roof eventually, landscaping every season, comes with a property tax bill that rises every time the county reassesses and someone to physically check on it every time a storm rolls through three states away.

The boat comes with marina fees, winterizing and a marine mechanic who bills by the hour. Buying something nice is the equivalent of signing up for a subscription with an indefinite term and a rising rate.

This is called the hedonic treadmill. Once someone upgrades something in their life, the old version stops being satisfying, permanently. And the new version only delivers that same satisfaction for as long as the novelty lasts.

Eventually the purchase itself becomes pointless. It was the feeling of upgrading that felt good but that feeling fades fast enough that the next upgrade becomes necessary just to get back to the baseline.

Luxury goods are sneakily good at triggering this because so much of what they deliver is the status attached to the price tag. Any functional improvement or value they bring is usually beside the point.

Dr. Flashy’s income may be large. He might even be a neurosurgeon earning $829,161. But at some point his lifestyle needs additional funding to keep up. That’s when he turns to financing.

Eventually, the bank becomes something he is increasingly dependent on.

To be clear, I’m not speculating on his character. Forbes reports that the highest-income American households, those above the 90th percentile, carry the largest average credit card balances of any income group (over $11,000 on average) despite being the group least likely to carry a balance at all.

So data shows us that the people who look the most financially comfortable are disproportionately dependent on revolving debt to stay there. Not all high earners are predisposed to open lines of credit, but when they do, they tend to rack up more of it because the lifestyle they’re financing costs more to maintain than anyone else’s.

The thing is, money is finite even with a large income. Spending more of it means you need more just to sustain the spending at its current level. And that treadmill doesn’t slow down as the years go by.

Dr. Net-Worth has the same income as Dr. Flashy. Same specialty, even, same call schedule, same patient panel.

But Dr. Net-Worth drives a Honda he’s had since fellowship. It’s got a cracked bumper he keeps meaning to fix. He lives in a house that’s nice but completely unremarkable from the street — not something you’ll see featured in Architectural Digest.

Still, his investment accounts feature a sum that would make your eyes water. No one except him and his accountant know what it is.

We have come to perceive net worth as some concrete evaluation of a person’s wealth. But it really isn’t. In fact, the more zeroes it has, the less real it is.

I mean, this year we saw Elon Musk become (briefly) the first ever trillionaire. But does that mean he’s got a Scrooge McDuck vault full of gold coins stacked to the ceiling?  Well, he might — but he won’t have an actual trillion in there to dive into and swim around in.

Capital protection and double-digit monthly cash flow, without becoming a landlord.

Tue, Oct 13  ·  10:00 am PT  ·  11:00 am MT  ·  1:00 pm ET

That number is mostly the market’s opinion of his equity stakes on a given day. An opinion that can — and does — swing by tens of billions of dollars before lunch and back again by dinner. All without a single dollar changing hands or a single decision on his part.

Dr. Net-Worth’s number works the same way just on a smaller scale. Most of it lives in a house he’s still making payments on every month, a retirement account he can’t touch before a certain age lest he trigger a penalty, and an ever-growing brokerage account he could never imagine drawing from.

All of it is his. Yet, he doesn’t use a dollar of it beyond the mortgage payment and the grocery bill. He’s rich! Technically. Psychologically, it might as well be someone else’s money.

You can’t fault him for being this way. Sometimes it’s just temperament. Plenty of high earners are simply frugal by nature, genuinely uninterested in the lake house and actually happier to keep the Honda running for another hundred thousand miles. Nothing wrong with that. At least Dr. Net-Worth doesn’t need rescuing from the life he has chosen.

But sometimes the hesitation to spend stems from fear. Constant worry that the money could vanish overnight, that one bad market year or one malpractice suit could erase everything you’ve built.

That spending on anything beyond the bare essentials is an invitation for disaster to strike. Dr. Net-Worth worked his butt off to build a financial fortress that classifies him as financially free. Yet the day may never come when he actually gets to taste that freedom.

Dr. Flashy is one bad year/one slow season at the practice/one unexpected repair bill on the boat away from a very uncomfortable conversation with a lender.

Dr. Net-Worth has already won the game by any objective measure but refuses to enjoy it.

Financial planner Derek Hagen says that money that isn’t pointed at anything in particular just accumulates, and accumulation without a purpose behind it isn’t freedom. Dr. Net-Worth has plenty of money with no real purpose for it.

Dr.  Flashy has an answer: status and visible proof that he has “made it”. But his answer costs more to maintain with every passing year, never quite delivering the sense of arrival he’s chasing.

There’s no handbook that outlines exactly where the divide between enjoying the money and hoarding it is. And anyone who claims there is one wants to sell you something.

You, the physician reading this, are probably nothing like Dr. Flashy or Dr. Net-Worth. And asking which one is better or worse isn’t the point either.

Your money, no matter how it is accumulated or spent on, deserves to be used to fund a life you chose on purpose. Not one assembled by accident out of habit, fear or…what the neighbors might notice.

Buffett kept the house and bought the plane because both of those choices added up to a life he actually wanted. That is rich (of course being worth $144.6 billion doesn’t hurt).

Everything else is just perception in a strange world that will never stop raising the bar.

Good, thoughtful article, Thanks! I have to agree about the ongoing obligations that the treadmill gets us into. I have to identify with Dr Net-Worth, but rather than having no purpose, I would say that one real, tangible benefit he has is security. Knowing he or his spouse can incur some life altering accident or illness and not affect the well being of the rest of the family. As an example my mother in law has dementia and has been in memory care for a decade. Her current bill is 200k per year. She and her husband planned very well and regardless of how long she lives she will be taken care of. The kids have not needed to contribute at all. My household has planned in a similar way. Thank you for separating a headline net worth figure from a life actually funded by it. The contrast between Dr Flashy and Dr Net-Worth is useful precisely because neither extreme answers the question of what the money is for. I found the follow-on costs point especially practical: a purchase is rarely a one-off price, and marina fees, maintenance and rising property taxes can quietly turn a status purchase into a continuing obligation. On the other side, treating a net worth statement as a market snapshot, rather than spendable security, helps explain why accumulating without a purpose can still feel anxious. A more useful middle path might be to define, in advance, what ‘enough’ looks like in cash-flow terms — housing, time, work flexibility and family priorities — and then judge each upgrade against that, rather than against another physician’s lifestyle or another year’s market valuation.

Of course, $5 million in a West or East Coast city means something entirely different than $5 million in a medium sized town in the Midwest or South. By way of information, if anyone is interested in how their assets compare relative to the U.S. net worth figures (by age, education or region).

Also, in another 6-8 weeks, the Federal Reserve Bank will issue the results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finance (SCF), which presents its own set of (updated) net worth and income figures.

The lingering question is – how do you determine the net present value of future social security payments or a pension, if eligible for one? Do you include that in a net worth statement or not?

The takeaway I have this article is to be neither a hoarder nor a ‘flashy’. Be comfortable in your spending style. And, in spite of the stress of the medical profession, it is good to practice gratitude for the opportunities to serve and have a roof over our heads.

Btw, I think the US government is going to face financial headwinds over the next 10 years. Social security and Medicare are going to run out of money (2032, 2033). In 2027, a large number of long-term bonds are going to mature and need re-financing. The real details can be found on the web, but you have to go digging for them. Carpe Diem.

Thanks for reading, and for adding so much to the discussion.

You’re right about geography. Five million in Manhattan or the Bay Area buys a smaller house and a longer commute than the same number buys in Omaha, which might explain why Buffett never bothered leaving. (Your link to the net worth comparison looks like it got eaten by the comment system, by the way. Feel free to repost it.)

On Social Security and pensions: I leave them off the net worth statement. You can’t sell them or borrow against them, and most of their value dies with you, so folding them in puffs up a number that’s already mostly opinion. Where they earn their keep is the retirement income plan. A pension paying $40,000 a year does roughly the work of a $1 million portfolio at a 4% withdrawal rate, which means the nest egg you need to build shrinks accordingly. I’d count them in that spreadsheet and keep them out of the other one.

On the trust funds, one detail tends to get lost in the headlines. When the reserves run dry in the early 2030s, benefits don’t drop to zero. Under current projections, incoming payroll taxes would still cover something like three quarters to four fifths of scheduled payments. Painful, sure, but a haircut is a very different problem than a guillotine. For younger docs, penciling in about 75% of your statement estimate seems like reasonable caution without veering into doom.

And I’m with you on gratitude. Most of this job’s stress comes with a roof, meaningful work and the chance to retire on our own terms, which is more than a lot of people ever get to complain about.

Carpe diem right back at you. -Jorge Sanchez, MD

It’s almost Halloween, and much like everyone else, I have been sucked into the tradition of watching horror movies with my wife before we take our daughter trick-or-treating. One of the movies I’m still thinking about from last week is Backrooms. It is the highest-grossing film A24 has ever released, and most of it takes place in rooms that look like a hospital at 3 a.m.

Yellowed walls. Fluorescent tubes that buzz loud enough to notice. Carpet that has absorbed something you would rather not identify. Corridors that turn left, then left again, until you’re somehow back where you started. If you trained at a big academic center, you have walked these halls, and probably still dream about them.

The film grew out of Kane Parsons’s YouTube series about a dimension of endless, empty rooms. Instead of the creature feature I expected, I got a picture of the doctor who is close to financial independence and can’t bring themselves to leave.

Full disclaimer: only read ahead if you’ve watched the film because there will be spoilers!

Clark is a failed architect running a struggling furniture store in San Jose. He drinks too much, his marriage is over, and he has started sleeping at the store. One night he goes down to check the breaker box, notices a glowing slit in the wall, and falls through it.

On the other side is a copy of the world that is slightly wrong. Rooms that almost look like rooms. Furniture that seems to have melted at the edges. Hallways longer than the building could possibly hold. Later in the film it gets described as a faulty, misremembered version of reality.

That description fits medical training better than anything I’ve heard in a wellness lecture. Residency is a copy of adult life with the proportions off. You have a title and real responsibility for people’s lives, but you’re 31 with a negative net worth, and you haven’t made it to a friend’s wedding without checking your phone in years.

Capital protection and double-digit monthly cash flow, without becoming a landlord.

Tue, Oct 13  ·  10:00 am PT  ·  11:00 am MT  ·  1:00 pm ET

Real life is always one room ahead: after boards, after fellowship, after the loans, after partnership. So you keep walking.

After a few trips in and out, Clark leaves his therapist a message. He’s staying in the Backrooms, and he won’t be coming back. He has found a way out of the failing store, the drinking, the empty house. The place he picked is worse than the one he’s leaving, but it’s familiar, and it doesn’t ask him to deal with anything.

The FIRE crowd has a name for this: one more year. You hit your number, or get close enough to see it, and you sign another contract anyway. The reasons all sound sensible. The market is choppy. The kids start college in four years. The group is short two partners.

Besides, what else would you do on a Wednesday morning?

Plenty of physicians keep working after financial independence because they love the work, and that’s a good outcome. The question worth asking is whether you’re staying because you chose to, or because the hallway is the only place you know how to stand.

Early in the film, Clark shoots a cheap TV commercial for the store dressed as its pirate mascot. It’s a little embarrassing and a little sweet. It is the version of himself he has to perform to keep the business alive.

By the end of the film, the costume becomes a towering, distorted Clark in the pirate outfit, peg leg and all, is waiting for him in the Backrooms. Clark tries to calm it down the way you’d talk to a dog you raised from a puppy. It kills him.

The Backrooms in this film make monsters from what people carry in, their memories and their feelings, and build with it.

Doctors have a costume too. The white coat, the title, the steady voice you use to tell a family the scan came back bad. You need it, and your patients need you to have it. The trouble starts when it stops coming off after the shift. You introduce yourself as Dr. at your kid’s soccer game. The hobbies lapse one at a time. Every close friend works in your department. Your income, your marriage, and your sense of being a decent person all run through one job.

Then the job goes sideways. A lawsuit, a patient death you can’t stop replaying, an RVU target that climbs every year, a private equity buyout that changes everything except your title.

What turns on you in those moments is the professional self you spent fifteen years building, now bigger than the person wearing it.

The second half belongs to Clark’s therapist, Dr. Mary Kline (Renate Reinsve). Worried about her patient, she goes to the store and walks into the Backrooms after him.

She doesn’t walk in clean. Mary is still working through the demolition of her childhood home and her mother’s institutionalization. A professional helper carrying a stack of her own unprocessed losses into someone else’s crisis is a fair description of a lot of people in medicine.

Inside, Clark ties her to a chair in a fake dining room. Three human-shaped figures sit around the table with them. They don’t move or react to anything. Clark shows her they’re made of an edible white substance, and it becomes clear the Backrooms feed on them.

It might sound odd, but I couldn’t watch that scene without thinking about the Maslach Burnout Inventory. It measures three things: emotional exhaustion, a fading sense of accomplishment, and depersonalization.

Doctors are familiar with depersonalization. Patients start to feel like tasks, and after a while you feel like one too. You’re at the table every day, and you look fine from across the room, while the place slowly takes what it needs from you.

The pirate gets rid of Clark comes for Mary next. Her survival is noteworthy.

Cornered in a lopsided replica of the furniture store, she snaps the monster’s peg leg with a hat rack, then hits it in the face with a chunk of concrete from her childhood home. The thing she has been grieving the whole movie turns out to be the thing she fights with.

For a physician, that chunk of concrete is whoever you were before medicine. The kid who played bass in a garage band. The person who built bookshelves, or ran trails, or cooked for twelve friends on a Saturday. Those parts didn’t vanish when you matched. They got buried under a decade of training.

The doctors I’ve seen leave clinical work well, or drop to part-time without falling apart, usually started digging some of that back up long before they needed it. They had a corner of life the job wasn’t allowed into, and they’d been living in it for years by the time they gave notice.

This is where the analogy gets uncomfortable.

Mary’s fight with the pirate sets off a gas trap. Researchers in hazmat suits haul her out to a facility run by Async, a company that used to make MRI machines before it found the Backrooms and made them its main business.

Whether or not the filmmakers meant anything by it, a medical imaging company ending up in charge of the maze is a hard detail to ignore if you work in a hospital.

In the last scene, Mary sits in an interrogation room across from Phil, one of Async’s scientists. She asks whether they’re going to let her go. He tells her the decision isn’t his.

Learn what Class A, B, and C really mean, how building quality affects distributions and resale, and why some passive investors prefer properties outside the top tier.

A lot of doctors make it through the burnout, the bad years, the cases that almost broke them, and end up in that room. They’re ready to leave, and they find out the exit belongs to someone else:

None of these are sinister on their own. Each one just moves the decision a little further from you and a little closer to a contract, a lender, or an employer.

For a physician, that’s what financial independence is really for. It’s less about retiring at 45 and more about who gets to answer the question Mary asks.

The film’s final shot is a copy of Mary, deformed and silent, sitting in a rough replica of that interrogation room somewhere deep in the Backrooms. The place has learned her. Whatever happens to the real Mary, a version of her stays behind.

Medicine leaves a copy of you behind too, and that isn’t all bad. The judgment, the pattern recognition, the calm you have in a code are yours for life. The goal isn’t to get out with nothing of the doctor left. It’s to make sure the doctor isn’t the only thing left.

A few things that help, roughly in order of effort:

Clark stayed because the maze was easier than his life. Most doctors who stay too long do it for a version of the same reason. Staying in medicine can be a great choice, as long as you’re the one making it.

The Pro Forma Never Paid Anyone’s Mortgage

If you bought into a multifamily syndication around 2021, you remember the deck. Glossy photos, a tidy IRR, a confident exit year. Then rates climbed, valuations slid, and plenty of investors watched distributions pause while their capital sat locked inside a deal that no longer penciled out.

Private real estate lending puts you in a different seat. The lender gets paid ahead of equity, holds a lien on the property, and collects interest from monthly loan payments rather than waiting on a sale that may never hit its number. You give up the home-run upside. In exchange, nobody calls you about a broken water heater at 2 a.m., a perk I’ve come to value after enough overnight shifts.

In a recent webinar, I joined Dr. Christy Burakovsky and Chris Lopez of Property Llama to discuss how private real estate loans are underwritten, where the actual risks lie, and what investors should ask any fund before wiring a dollar.

We also covered the importance of looking beyond projected returns and understanding the fundamentals behind a lending strategy.

The takeaway? Before investing, know how the loan is structured, what protects your capital, and what happens when a deal doesn’t go according to plan.

“I’m sick of the scaring, the terror, the fright. I’m tired of being something that goes bump in the night. I’m bored with leering my horrible glances, And my feet hurt from dancing those skeleton dances. I don’t like graveyards, and I need something new. There must be more to life than just yelling, ‘Boo!'”

—Tim Burton, The Nightmare Before Christmas

Dr. Wednesday Addams sat alone in her office at 11 PM, glaring at her retirement calculator the way you’d glare at a pathology report you already suspect is bad.

Twenty years of serious income, the kind that makes the neighbors assume you’re rich, and the screen looked like a crime scene.

Projected retirement age: 79. Probability of success: 23%. Her portfolio had roughly the life expectancy of a jack-o’-lantern left on the porch until Thanksgiving.

She was 58. She wanted out at 61, and blocking the exit stood a tangle of whole life policies her cousin had sold her, a 401(k) ignored for a decade, a pre-tax balance quietly wiring itself into a tax bomb, and a household burning $35,000 a month like a furnace nobody remembered to turn down.

Her story isn’t rare. It isn’t even interesting.

Physicians stumble into the same open graves with the reliability of a zombie shuffling toward the nearest brain, and the tax code waiting at the bottom helps itself to 37 cents of every married dollar above $768,700. Some of these graves are fresh. A few were dug by Congress.

The AMA’s latest national data has 41.9% of physicians reporting at least one symptom of burnout in 2025, down from 48.2% in 2023. Progress, technically. Emergency medicine and hematology-oncology still sit near 50%, coin-flip odds that the physician running tonight’s code is cooked.

Burnout steals your joy first and your retirement date second. You plan to work until 68, the call schedule wins at 61, and the seven years of full income your plan quietly assumed shrink to a few years of part-time pay, or nothing at all.

The itch is arriving earlier, too. In Doximity’s polling, the share of physicians aged 45 to 49 considering early retirement nearly doubled between 2023 and 2026, from 23% to 44%.

Dr. Smart and Dr. Addams both started at 35 earning $300,000. Smart saved 25%, or $75,000 a year. Addams saved 10%.

Run that $45,000 annual gap through 25 years at a 5% real return and it grows to about $2.15 million by age 60, a fortune separating two doctors with the same income at the same hospital, parked in the same doctors’ lot, one of them driving home to a plan and the other to a calculator that reads like a death certificate.

Learn what Class A, B, and C really mean, how building quality affects distributions and resale, and why some passive investors prefer properties outside the top tier.

Addams spent every productivity bonus. You’ve already met her at 11 PM.

You go from a resident making $65,000 to an attending earning $350,000, and the word “deserve” moves into your vocabulary. A bigger house. Then tens of thousands sunk into renovating it, followed by the new car, the au pair, private school, and first class to Maui.

Nobody warns you how hard it is to downshift once you’ve gotten used to the view. Your brain resets “normal” to match your paycheck and refuses to reset it back, so the spending tags along into retirement like a party guest who showed up uninvited and also brought luggage.

I watched an Arizona cardiologist discover at 66 that he needed $400,000 a year to keep living the way he lived. His portfolio could safely throw off maybe $180,000. He’s 71 now. Still full-time.

Simple, boring solution: live like a resident for two to five years after training, bank the gap, kill the student loans, and upgrade slowly enough that your brain never registers the drift.

Nearly every physician gets pitched whole life insurance, usually by a friend or relative whose licensing exam ink is still wet. The illustration promises cash value, tax-free growth, and a death benefit, all in one tidy package.

For most physicians who need life insurance, it’s mostly garbage. Premiums run many times higher than term. Commissions feed on the early years, and the cash value grows like it’s been bled.

Run an illustrative comparison: one physician pays $3,000 a month into whole life, while her colleague buys 20-year term for around $150 a month and invests the other $2,850, and at a 7% return that side account sits near $1.5 million after 20 years, with the policy’s cash value usually trailing by hundreds of thousands, still waiting for the illustration to come true.

Sold by family, illustrated in optimistic colors, and funded for 15 years by a doctor too busy to read past page two, Dr. Addams’s three policies carried combined premiums of $8,400 a month and a total cash value of $780,000.

Term plus investing would likely have left her near $1.9 million. She surrendered all three at 58. Ate the surrender charges. Started catching up.

In plenty of physician households, one person earns the money and the same person manages it.

Then the doctor dies, divorces, or has a stroke at 63, and the spouse inherits decades of decisions made behind a closed door, written in a language nobody bothered to teach them.

I’ve sat with widows who found out their physician husband had:

A spouse at the table pulls decisions toward the conservative side, a handy counterweight when the 2 AM version of you thinks genius has struck.

Build the plan simple enough that they could run it alone. Keep the account list and passwords somewhere they can actually find, which rules out your head.

Business school professors have a phrase for the bad investments that circulate in medical circles: deals that can only be sold to doctors.

Time poverty and overconfidence do the damage. Researching an investment takes hours you don’t have, so you trust people, and you assume that mastering the coagulation cascade somehow qualifies you to underwrite private equity. It doesn’t.

Physicians I know have poured money into restaurant groups that folded within 18 months, real estate “opportunities” that smelled faintly of Ponzi, and crypto tokens launched by a nephew’s roommate’s brother.

Index funds are boring. They work. Put $50,000 a year into low-cost index funds for 30 years at a 5% real return and you end up with about $3.32 million.

Lose 2% a year to fees and the same contributions grow to about $2.38 million, close to a million dollars handed to people in nicer suits than yours. If your portfolio needs a 40-page binder to explain, you’re the mark.

Most physicians blow past the taxable wage base ($184,500 in 2026) months before December, which puts you among the few groups who routinely qualify for the maximum benefit. Claiming age is a bigger lever for you than for almost anyone.

According to AARP, a worker at the 2026 maximum who files at 62 collects about $2,969 a month. Wait until full retirement age and that rises to $4,152. Hold out to 70 and it’s roughly $5,181.

Dr. Lucky filed at 62 because he “wanted the money while the government still had it.” Six months later he picked up locums at $200 an hour, and because Social Security withholds $1 for every $2 you earn above $24,480 before full retirement age, his own paycheck ate his benefit, which the SSA hands back after full retirement age in small monthly crumbs.

If you’re married, the higher earner’s claiming age also sets the survivor benefit, so delaying to 70 works like inflation-adjusted life insurance for your spouse at a premium no insurer will match. A serious diagnosis can justify claiming early.

For a healthy 62-year-old with a seven-figure portfolio, it’s usually the wrong call. You’ve delivered enough prognoses to know which patient you are.

Most physicians stuff nearly everything into pre-tax accounts during peak years, which makes sense at 37%. Trouble arrives when that’s the only move for 25 years, because a $4 million pre-tax portfolio is a smaller number dressed up for the party.

If you need $180,000 a year to live and pull it entirely from pre-tax accounts, you might withdraw $240,000 to get there. Your 4.5% withdrawal plan just became a 6% plan.

Required minimum distributions start at 73 (75 if you were born in 1960 or later) and stack on top of Social Security. Then Medicare notices.

IRMAA surcharges for 2026 begin at modified AGI of $218,000 for married couples, and at the top tier Part B jumps from $202.90 a month to $689.90, plus a $91 Part D surcharge, roughly $6,900 a year per person, a fine levied for the crime of saving diligently in the wrong bucket.

Medicare looks back two years, so the income you report at 63 sets your premiums at 65.

But if you retire at 58, delay Social Security, and you may get a decade of taxable income lower than anything since residency, a window for converting chunks of pre-tax money to Roth on purpose, in measured doses, the way you’d titrate a drip rather than push a bolus.

While you’re still working, fund a backdoor Roth IRA ($7,500 limit in 2026) and send part of your savings to the Roth side of your employer plan. If you’re 50 or older and earned more than $150,000 in FICA wages last year, the IRS already decided for you: your 2026 catch-up contributions go in as Roth.

Asset location matters too, and municipal bonds can help outside retirement accounts.

At 37% plus the 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax, close to 41 cents of every taxable bond interest dollar goes to Washington. Keep bonds inside the 401(k) or 403(b). Hold broad stock index funds in taxable.

Two physicians can retire with identical portfolios and identical withdrawal rates and still get completely different endings. Timing decides which. Finance calls it sequence of returns risk, and you’ll call it something less printable.

Retire in February 2020 and you watched the Dow fall from about 29,550 to under 19,000 in roughly six weeks. Retire into 2022 and the S&P 500 dropped about 19% as inflation spiked.

Even 2025 had teeth: the S&P 500 fell almost 19% between its February high and early April as tariff headlines rattled markets.

Dr. Smart retires into three good years and coasts. Dr. Lucky (whose name keeps aging badly) retires into a bear market, sells near the bottom to fund two years of travel, and never gets those shares back.

William Bengen’s 4% rule, published in 1994, tries to account for that, and Bengen has since nudged his own number up to about 4.7%. The real mistake is treating any figure as carved on a tombstone.

Retirees who trim spending after bad years, or who keep two to five years of withdrawals in cash and short-term bonds, give their stocks room to recover instead of selling them on the way down.

Dr. Addams checked her allocation at 59 and found 95% stocks, 5% cash, and no plan for a crash. She moved to 60/30/10 stocks, bonds, and cash and started building a three-year buffer. Her mix won’t fit everyone, but “I’ll figure it out when it happens” fits nobody.

Don’t overcorrect into a bond basement either. Retire at 57 and your money may need to last 35 years, so stocks still have work to do.

CPI peaked at 9.1% in June 2022. Inflation cooled. Prices didn’t.

A $200,000 retirement budget becomes about $361,000 in 20 years at 3% inflation, and any income stream that doesn’t adjust, whether a fixed annuity, a pension without a cost-of-living rider, or a practice buyout paid in level installments, shrinks every year you hold it, rotting quietly from the inside the way pumpkins do.

You already know this feeling from the reimbursement side. The AMA estimates Medicare physician pay has fallen by roughly a third since 2001 after adjusting for practice-cost inflation.

Capital protection and double-digit monthly cash flow, without becoming a landlord.

Tue, Oct 13  ·  10:00 am PT  ·  11:00 am MT  ·  1:00 pm ET

Give your retirement plan the same respect for erosion you’ve watched eat your fee schedule.

Your brother needs $50,000 for a business. Your sister needs $30,000 to stop a foreclosure.

A few years later your kid asks for $80,000 toward a house, because you’re the rich doctor, and the rich doctor is who people call, and nobody in the history of families has ever called the rich doctor to pay him back.

Treat money to family as a gift with no strings, sized to what you can afford to never see again. Dr. Addams lent her brother $120,000 for a restaurant. It failed. He filed for bankruptcy, and they haven’t spoken in six years.

Long-term rental losses usually land in the passive bucket, where they can’t touch clinical income. Short-term rentals play by different rules.

If the average guest stay runs seven days or less and you materially participate, most commonly by logging more than 100 hours a year and more than any other individual, the losses turn non-passive and can offset W-2 or 1099 income (a separate route from Real Estate Professional Status), the closest thing the tax code offers to a garlic necklace for your paycheck.

Pair that with a cost segregation study and 100% bonus depreciation, which the One Big Beautiful Bill Act permanently restored for property acquired after January 19, 2025.

A $500,000 short-term rental might produce $150,000 to $200,000 of year-one depreciation, worth roughly $55,000 to $74,000 in federal tax at 37%.

Locums, telehealth, medical director stipends, expert witness work: if any of it lands on a 1099, a Solo 401(k) usually beats the SEP-IRA most contractors open by default. For 2026 you can defer up to $24,500 as the “employee” (shared with any W-2 plan you also use), plus an employer contribution of roughly 20% of net self-employment earnings, up to $72,000 combined, with $8,000 in catch-up at 50 or $11,250 between 60 and 63. The SEP also poisons your backdoor Roth through the pro-rata rule.

Older 1099 physicians with steady income should price out a cash balance plan on top, where contributions often reach six figures for doctors in their 50s. Those deductions pull double duty because of the QBI cliff.

For 2026, married couples get the full 20% qualified business income deduction at or below $403,500 of taxable income, and it disappears at $553,500. A married 1099 doc with $500,000 of taxable income who funds both plans can slide below $403,500 and watch the deduction rise from the dead.

Medicine breeds a specific condition. You hit your number, decide you need a bigger one, and a market dip talks you into another year, then another, until you’re 68 with $9 million and a partner gently asking whether you’ve considered slowing down.

Every year worked past enough gets paid for with a year you’ll never get back at that age, a year of knees that still handle a trail and a back that still lifts a grandkid, traded for a margin of safety your spreadsheet stopped needing long ago, which makes one more year the only prescription in medicine with no ceiling dose.

Physicians who bolt without a plan for Monday get haunted by the opposite problem. You were Dr. Johnson, the cardiologist. Now you’re Bob, with 50 empty hours a week and no idea what to put in them.

Some Bobs end up unretiring just to have somewhere to be.

Easing out tends to go better than slamming the door. Dropping to 0.6 FTE, picking up locums, or teaching keeps income flowing and lets the portfolio grow untouched a few more years.

Watch for a malpractice tail bill on a claims-made policy, and remember that governmental 457(b) plans carry no 10% penalty once you separate from service, at any age.

In my experience, physicians who retire toward something stick the landing far more often than those simply running from the pager.

Dr. Addams caught her mistakes at 58 instead of 68, and that gave her room to work. She hired a fee-only fiduciary advisor, wrote a plan, surrendered the bad policies, sold the vacation home, and maxed every account she had.

She retired at 64 on about $18,000 a month instead of $35,000. Plenty, it turned out.

Several year-end moves for 2026 can’t wait for the week between Christmas and New Year’s:

For the rest of the year, check every beneficiary form, add up 12 months of actual spending, swap whole life for adequate term and disability coverage where it makes sense, and bring your spouse into the conversation. Then raise your savings rate 1 to 2 points every year until you hit 25% to 30% of gross.

You’ll make mistakes. Everyone does. What matters is catching them at 58, the way Dr. Addams did, while the options are still standing in the room, instead of at 70, when most of them have left the building and switched off the porch light behind them.

Pick one item from this list before the first trick-or-treater rings your doorbell. Make your CPA earn their fee in November instead of on a panicked phone call in March.

This article is for educational purposes and isn’t individualized tax, legal, or investment advice. Run any strategy past a CPA or fee-only advisor who knows your full situation.

Thanks for this informative and entertaining article. should be required reading for all docs. Made me realize that I am fortunate to have avoided the worst of bad decisions. I’m 78 now and comfortably retired with close family. Life is good.

I’ve made some of these mistakes in my 30s by falling into the luxury trap when decent salaries first hit the accounts. Living in Los Angeles it would be VERY easy to burn 35k per month without luxury cars or private schools. In fact we’re not too far off and we drive older EV cars that are paid off and the kids go to great public schools. The costs of living have increased to the point of needing to pay very close attention to all expenses and max out investment and retirement accounts even when it hurts. We’ve started catching rounding 40, traveling a bit less, no new cars, only making required fixes to the house. After reading this I’m more confident that we’ve made the right decisions to get smart and aggressive about this now.

Interesting article focused on finances with a smattering of other issues. Importantly, what are your support systems upon retirement, like spouse, friends, etc.? Sometimes friends are not there because they choose to move closer to their children or they are deceased. What are your interests in medicine and outside medicine? What are your hobbies? Do you want to volunteer? You have been going 90 miles mph and then slow down to 10 mph. Without some kind of plan to fill your time, with and without your spouse/significant other, this is a recipe for depression and disaster. Do you want to stay connected to medicine in some way? Maybe you can observe trainees doing an H&P and counseling. Maybe you can offer advice as to how to set up an office practice for senior residents. In another ote, how is your health and do you take care of yourself? Going into retirement with significant health issues can influence how your retirement goes and when you retire, perhaps restricting travel and other activities. We have written an article on retirement that might compliment the informative blog here. Whereas it is focused on academic physicians, there are many points applicable to those in practice (Greenberg L, Fischel JE, Siegel B. Academic clinician educators: Confronting the challenges to successful retirement. Educ Health (Abingdon). 2023 Jan-Apr;36(1):24-32. doi: 10.4103/efh.efh_192_22. PMID: 38047344.). Planning ahead is the key, applying principles mentioned in this blog and our paper. We all have worked so hard…..we deserve a great retirement.

great article…great advice. As the offspring of depression era parents, I was taught (by example) early to be thrifty and save. When burnout came at age 62, I was ready and haven’t looked back. My only regret is being too conservative with my investments, but then again being more aggressive would have forced me to hang on some extra years after the 2008 market crash.

I am so sorry, you lost me at the fact that you actually were burning 35k per month!!! how is that even possible!!! you are exactly where you chose to be, its consequences. Most of us, and I honestly believe I speak for the majority of physicians, do not even get remotely close to such an exaggerated figure. Most of us have limited our spending as our reimbursement has declined. Many of us have actually struggled even keeping a low profile and living with economic restraints. I stopped reading at that figure because it is just absurd.

I appreciate you taking the time to comment, even if you stopped reading at the $35K figure. Let me address your skepticism directly, because you’re right to be shocked—and that’s exactly the point. When I wrote this article, I had a word count limit on how much I could disclose on the background of Doctor Addams (who is really a he). What I did not go into detail about is how he arrived at where he is today. It’s not one absurd decision. It’s twenty years of reasonable-sounding decisions that compound like interest you can’t afford.

Dr. Addams didn’t wake up one day and decide to burn through $420K annually. He made decisions that seemed perfectly justified at each step. I would not have discovered what my friend was going through had I not asked him to invest in my startup back then. He then confided how illiquid he was and how much in a hole he was in.

The reality is that our monthly expenses are not the usual discussion physicians talk about in the physicians’ lounge. It’s really very personal, so I get it that this sounds absurd, but the reality is that there is a lot of shame ascribed to our salaries when we really aren’t visibly successful. So why would we share it? Which may explain why it sounds so absurd to you. Sadly, he is not the first person in such a financial hole since its more common than you think. So what happened?

His surgical group was thriving pre-COVID. She was making $400K+ and felt secure in budgeting for this lifestyle. Then the floor dropped:

Insurance reimbursements got slashed Hospital-based specialty groups ate their market share

His income dropped to $280K, then $240K (he was already burned out from trying to get bigger dividends he had to do more call, which was not sustainable. Yeah, many private groups make these kind of dead-end deals)

What happened next? He did not scale back his lifestyle because he was optimistic about his future. I don’t have the space here to list his expenses but what I remember after a very emotional and stressful session was that his parents were aging and he had to help financially. His sister-in-law had a business that he helped with some capital, which became a recurring theme. All these decisions are made with good intentions, but they add up. He leased a really nice car and could not figure out how to back out of that deal.

The real lesson: This story isn’t about judgment. It’s about prevention. Every physician should see this and think: “Could this happen to me with just 3-4 different decisions?”

Because here’s the truth: The distance between financial security and financial disaster for a high-earning physician is about five bad decisions over twenty years. That’s it.

Your restraint is admirable. But I wrote this article for the physicians who haven’t shown that restraint yet—and who still have time to fix it before they’re staring at a retirement calculator at age 58.

The $35K isn’t absurd. It’s terrifyingly more common (than you think) among physicians who started making big money without a financial plan. If this article makes even one physician audit their spending before it’s too late, it was worth writing—and worth your discomfort reading it.

As someone who spends at 30k per month, let me help with this: $2500 per month goes to an aging parent on one side, $2000 to an aging parent on the other. 3.5k per month goes to a vacation home mortgage and expenses, although it has appreciated enough over time that that will be eventually recovered. Travel is a big one as our 6 children and 6 grandchildren live all over the place, and flights, airport parking etc are $5000 per month. Life insurance is a big one, at 2k per month, health for myself is only $600 per month but it’s $1500 for my wife. I’ll stop there, but we are not driving fancy cars and our primary residence is only worth 330k, hardly a mansion. I retired with over 6 million NW and 60k in pension/ss, which will probably cover it: once the elderly parents have passed it should work out, but we might have to sell the vacation house when we are older.

This should be required reading for every resident – and required re-reading every year of residency and beyond! I appreciate the comments about spouses being involved in all finances – that goes for us, too! Many of us are married to high-earners who manage their own (and sometimes our) finances and find out too late that they were terrible at it.

Thank you! You’re absolutely right—this should be mandatory reading starting in residency, before the income jump happens and the mistakes become expensive.

Your point about spouses needing to be involved cuts both ways, and it’s critical. I’ve sat with too many people who discovered their high-earning spouse was: – Flying blind with no actual plan – Paying 2% in fees to an advisor who was just collecting checks – Invested in their buddy’s restaurant/startup/crypto scheme – Carrying three whole life insurance policies they didn’t understand – Making $400K but somehow living paycheck to paycheck

Financial competence doesn’t correlate with income or intelligence. A physician making $500K can be just as clueless as anyone else—sometimes more so, because the high income masks the problems until it’s too late.

Being involved doesn’t mean you need to manage everything. It means you know where the accounts are, understand the plan, can access everything if needed, and serve as that crucial second set of eyes. Your spouse’s overconfidence plus your informed questions might prevent a catastrophic mistake.

Money is a team sport. Whether you’re the earner or the spouse, staying informed and involved isn’t optional—it’s survival.

They left out the annuity with a 5% rate guaranteed growth with step ups if the market does better than 5% minus fees. You can attach an ins package for your spouse. take a 4% W/D on your money. dont increase your standard of living to just be like everyone else. avoid the race to nowhere and stay away from out of state tuition. your kids will do well anywhere they go if they apply themselves: they got the intellect and drive from their parents not private school or private universities. Cars get you to and from work – where is the luxury? in the car dealerships pocket. Bigger houses dont mean happy homes and what do you do with the extra bedrooms when the adults start their own lives? Money left over after you max a 401k with a profit sharing plan (employ your spouse after the kids are gone), time to put extra into index funds with a downside sharing of risk. might not make the 14-19% that other are making but none of the panic when covid 2.0 comes to the shore. I went through 3 financial planners (all with vacation homes on my money) before I found Andrew. I was sold when he asked me a simple question. How much do you spend per month? Let’s see how much you have to have saved to make that per year with inflation. Its amazing how much you can love medicine when you can retire whenever the fancy hits you once you have attained the above goal!

Thanks for sharing your journey! You’ve clearly learned the hard lessons that most physicians skip—keeping lifestyle inflation in check, avoiding the luxury trap, and finding a real fiduciary advisor after getting burned by commission-chasing “planners” (those vacation homes weren’t free!).

Your point about annuities is worth noting for the right situation, though they’re not for everyone. The real gold in your comment is this: “How much do you spend per month?” Most physicians never ask themselves this question until it’s too late. They assume their income means they’re wealthy, then discover their spending ate everything.

The freedom you describe—loving medicine because you can retire whenever you want—that’s what happens when you get the math right early. You avoided the nightmare by doing exactly what Dr. Addams eventually learned: live below your means, ignore the Joneses, and make the boring financial moves that actually work.

This was an informative and entertaining article: creatively written with the Halloween metaphors!

it all makes so much sense!!! thank you!!!

#8685. Trick or Treatment: The Spookiest Things Physicians Learn About Being Human
