#8671. Hyatt Category 4 Free Night Certificate — Card Perk Sweet Spot

Savings rate, FI number, and the path to freedom.

Withdrawal plans, Roth ladders, and early access.

Index funds, asset allocation, and real estate.

Roth conversions, capital gains, and FI tax planning.

Career growth, side hustles, and entrepreneurship.

Beliefs, purpose, and financial psychology.

Exercise, nutrition, and mental wellness.

The simplest high-value card perk in travel rewards — no points math required

Picture this: you walk into a stunning hotel lobby — maybe it's the Hyatt Regency Kyoto, maybe it's the Andaz Maui at Wailea, maybe it's a chic Hyatt Centric in the heart of a city you've always wanted to explore. You hand over your World of Hyatt card at check-in, and the night is on the house. Not because you're a high roller. Not because you spent $50,000 on a credit card. Because you crossed a spending threshold you were hitting anyway, and Hyatt rewarded you with a free night certificate that covers any Category 1–4 property in the entire portfolio. This is what the ChooseFI community means when we talk about travel rewards done right: identifying the moments where a credit card benefit perfectly intersects with your normal life, and extracting maximum value with minimum complexity. ## The Math That Makes This a No-Brainer Here's the value proposition in plain numbers. Category 4 Hyatt properties — places like the Thompson Nashville, the Hyatt Regency Maui, or the Andaz San Diego — regularly command **$200 to $400 per night** in cash. On peak dates, holiday weekends, or in premium markets, that number climbs even higher. Your free night certificate covers any of these properties at no additional points cost. None. Zero. This isn't a discount. It's a full, unrestricted free night at properties that charge real-world luxury rates. Why does this represent a genuine pricing inefficiency? Because Hyatt's Category 1–4 certificates are earned through a flat spending threshold — $15,000 on the World of Hyatt Credit Card in a calendar year — and can be redeemed at properties whose nightly rates vary enormously. A Category 4 certificate costs the same to earn whether you use it at a $150 roadside property or a $400 resort. The system rewards you for targeting the high end of the range every single time. For a household already putting everyday spending on a rewards card, $15,000 across a full calendar year is often an achievable benchmark. Groceries, utilities, insurance premiums, quarterly tax payments — it adds up faster than you think. And when it does, Hyatt drops a certificate in your account that can deliver **$300–$400 in hotel value** without spending a single additional point. In the World of Hyatt program — consistently rated the **best hotel loyalty program for value per point** — this certificate is one of the most quietly powerful perks on any hotel card in the market.

The core mechanism here isn't a transfer partnership exploit or a routing rule loophole. It's simpler and more durable than that: Hyatt's Category system creates a ceiling, not a floor. When you earn a Category 1–4 free night certificate, you're not locked into a $150-a-night budget motel. You're handed a key that opens any door in that range — and some of those doors lead to genuinely spectacular properties.

Hyatt operates on a fixed award chart, ranging from 3,500 points for a Category 1 night all the way up to 45,000 points for a Category 8 night. Unlike programs that use dynamic pricing (where award costs swing with cash demand), Hyatt's chart is static. A Category 4 property costs the same 15,000 points whether it's a Tuesday in February or New Year's Eve.

Your free night certificate functions exactly like those 15,000 points — but you earned it through card spending, not through a points balance. This means the certificate has a defined and predictable value: whatever a Category 4 property charges in cash on the night you use it is exactly what you're getting for free.

The pricing inefficiency exists because Hyatt assigns categories based on average nightly rates across the year — but peak-season rates at desirable Category 4 properties can blow well past that average. A Hyatt Regency in a major city might be Category 4 because its average annual rate qualifies, but on a conference weekend or holiday weekend, that same room might cost $350–$400. Your certificate captures that peak-season value without any upcharge.

While this sweet spot is certificate-based (no points required), World of Hyatt integrates beautifully with two major transferable currency programs:

This matters for your broader strategy. If you want to stack a certificate with a separate points redemption — say, booking multiple nights where the first is covered by the certificate and subsequent nights use transferred points — you have two strong, flexible on-ramps into the Hyatt ecosystem. Chase Ultimate Rewards is the workhorse of the FI community's travel rewards stack, and having Hyatt as an instant 1:1 partner makes it one of the most actionable transfer relationships in the game.

Hyatt charges no fuel surcharges on award redemptions — a meaningful distinction compared to some airline programs where surcharges can swallow most of your savings. Your certificate redemption is clean: one certificate, one free night, no surprise fees at checkout beyond standard resort fees (which, to be fair, do apply at some properties — more on that in Pro Tips).

World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. As a World of Hyatt Credit Card holder, your card activity will naturally keep your account active, so expiry is rarely a concern for cardholders. But if you ever cancel the card, make sure you use your points and certificates before they age out.

Booking a World of Hyatt free night certificate is genuinely one of the easiest processes in all of travel rewards. Here's the complete walkthrough from certificate to check-in.

Log in to your World of Hyatt account at hyatt.com and navigate to your account dashboard. Under the "My Certificates & Awards" section, confirm your Category 1–4 free night certificate is present and note its expiration date. Certificates are typically valid for 12 months from issuance, so don't let it sit unused. If you don't see it and you've crossed the $15,000 annual spend threshold on your World of Hyatt Credit Card, allow a few days for it to post after your statement closes, or call Chase to confirm.

Go to hyatt.com and use the hotel search function. You can filter by World of Hyatt category — specifically, search for Category 4 properties in any destination you're targeting. Don't shortchange yourself by defaulting to a Category 1 or 2 property out of habit. The certificate works at any Category 1–4 property, so always target the top of the range. Look for properties with high nightly cash rates — this is where your certificate delivers the most value.

Once you've identified a target property, search your dates on hyatt.com and switch the search to "Use Points." Category 4 properties will show award availability for 15,000 points per night. If award availability shows for that date, your certificate will cover it. Hyatt's booking window opens 395 days in advance, so for peak travel dates — holidays, major events, popular travel seasons — you can and should book the maximum window out.

Proceed through the booking process. At the payment step, you'll see an option to "Apply Free Night Award" or select your certificate from your account. Select the Category 1–4 certificate. The system will apply it and your total cash charge drops to $0 for the room rate (plus taxes and any applicable resort fees).

Hyatt award availability at popular properties can be limited during peak periods. Your tactical options:

Hyatt operates on a fixed category system where each property is assigned a category from 1 to 8 based on the brand and location, not the current market rate. This creates a structural pricing inefficiency: a Category 4 property in a high-demand market like Maui or Kyoto charges the same certificate cost as a Category 4 in a mid-tier city. Your free night certificate works at all of them equally. Unlike hotel programs with dynamic pricing where the cost of a free night fluctuates with demand, Hyatt's fixed chart means you can target the highest-value Category 4 properties without paying more. The card's $95 annual fee is one of the lowest in the premium hotel card category, yet the certificate alone delivers $250 to $400 or more in value — a return that makes the math trivially easy for any FI-minded household.

Card links may earn ChooseFI a commission. See our advertiser disclosure.

Let's make this concrete with a real example that represents exactly how this certificate shines.

The Andaz San Diego is a boutique lifestyle hotel in the Gaslamp Quarter — rooftop pool, stylish rooms, walking distance to everything downtown. It's the kind of hotel that signals a real trip, not just a place to sleep. On a standard weekend night, cash rates run $250–$350 per night. During Comic-Con, a Padres playoff weekend, or a major convention, rates push past $400.

Cash cost: $300 (conservative weekend estimate) Certificate cost: 0 points, 1 Category 1–4 free night certificate Your out-of-pocket: $0 for the room rate

You earned this certificate by crossing $15,000 in annual spending on the World of Hyatt Credit Card — a threshold many households reach through regular everyday spending over 12 months. The certificate posts automatically, you search availability on hyatt.com, and you apply it at checkout in about five minutes.

You're not redeeming into a budget experience. The Andaz brand sits at the upper-upscale tier of the Hyatt portfolio. You check in through a host model (no formal front desk), settle into a room with thoughtful design, and wake up knowing that $300 night cost you nothing extra beyond your normal spending.

If you hold World of Hyatt elite status — Discoverist, Explorist, or Globalist — that status applies to certificate bookings exactly like paid stays. Room upgrade requests, early check-in, late check-out: all the same benefits apply.

In every case, your one certificate delivers more value than most points redemptions in any hotel program. And you earned it without touching your points balance.

Your certificate works identically at a $150/night Category 4 property and a $400/night Category 4 property. Always search for the properties with the highest cash rates in your target destination. Use hyatt.com's rate display to compare award availability against current cash pricing — this directly shows you the value you're capturing.

Hyatt's booking window opens 395 days in advance. For properties in high-demand markets — Maui, New York, Chicago during peak season — award inventory gets claimed fast. Set a calendar alert to search exactly 395 days before your target dates and book the moment the window opens.

Your certificate covers one night. If you're staying multiple nights, stack it strategically: apply the certificate to the highest-cost night (often a Saturday) and book the remaining nights with World of Hyatt points transferred instantly from Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt Rewards at a 1:1 ratio. This hybrid approach maximizes the value of every currency you're using.

World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of inactivity. As a cardholder, your spending activity resets this clock automatically. But if you ever pause card use, make a small Hyatt purchase — even a $1 on-property charge — to reset the timer and protect your balance.

Hyatt does not waive resort fees on award and certificate bookings at all properties. Before booking, check whether your target property charges a daily resort fee — these can run $25–$50/night and will appear on your final bill. Factor this into your value calculation, especially at resort properties in Hawaii or Las Vegas.

The $15,000 spend threshold should come from natural household spending, not manufactured purchases. In the FI community, we optimize around spending you're doing anyway — insurance premiums, tax payments, groceries, utilities. If you're buying things you don't need to hit the threshold, you're eroding the value of the certificate.

Certificates issued by Hyatt are typically valid for 12 months. Mark the expiration date in your calendar the moment the certificate posts. An expired certificate is $300+ in value that simply disappears — one of the most painful mistakes in travel rewards.

This sweet spot is built for the everyday FI household that's already spending $15,000 or more annually on a single credit card and wants to redirect that activity toward a meaningful travel benefit. You don't need a large points balance. You don't need to understand transfer partners or award chart math. You earn the certificate by spending, you apply it at checkout, and you get a free night at a genuinely nice hotel.

You need: the World of Hyatt Credit Card, $15,000 in annual card spending, and a World of Hyatt account. No minimum points balance required — this is a card perk, not a points redemption.

If your annual spending is significantly below $15,000 on a single card, this particular mechanism won't trigger. In that case, the World of Hyatt Credit Card still earns Hyatt points on spending and delivers a Category 1–4 certificate on each card anniversary — so it retains value, just through a different path. Also, if you're deeply committed to a non-Hyatt hotel program, the benefit is obviously less useful without a library of Hyatt properties in your regular rotation.

## Rated: Easy (4/5 Beginner Friendly) This is one of the most accessible sweet spots in the entire travel rewards ecosystem, and that's by design. The certificate mechanism removes the two biggest friction points in traditional points redemptions: **finding the right number of points** and **navigating complex transfer timing**. You earn the certificate passively through spending, it posts to your account automatically, and the booking process on hyatt.com is as intuitive as booking any other hotel stay. ## What Makes It Easy - **No transfer required** — the certificate lives in your World of Hyatt account, ready to apply at checkout - **Fixed pricing** — Category 4 is Category 4 everywhere in the world; no dynamic pricing surprises - **Simple availability search** — hyatt.com's award search is clean and straightforward ## The One Genuine Challenge: Availability at Popular Properties The only real friction point is award inventory at high-demand Category 4 properties on desirable dates. Hyatt limits how many award rooms it releases per night, and popular properties in destinations like Hawaii or New York fill quickly. **Three ways to beat this:** 1. Search 395 days in advance when fresh inventory releases 2. Build a shortlist of 3–5 Category 4 properties in your target region so you have backup options 3. Stay flexible on dates — midweek nights almost always have more award availability than weekends If you can approach this with even modest date flexibility, you will find great options. The Hyatt portfolio at Category 4 is large and geographically diverse, and there is almost always a compelling property available somewhere you'd actually want to go. For anyone new to travel rewards, this certificate is the perfect first redemption — low complexity, high reward, and a genuinely memorable hotel stay to show your household what this strategy can deliver.

Log in to hyatt.com and check My Certificates and Awards after your card anniversary. Note the expiration date — certificates are typically valid for 12 months. If it does not appear within a few weeks of your anniversary, contact Chase.

Search hyatt.com for Category 4 hotels in your target destinations. Compare the cash rate against the free certificate value. Target properties where cash rates exceed $300 per night — these deliver the highest return on your $95 annual fee.

Hyatt opens its booking window 395 days in advance. For popular Category 4 properties in Maui, New York, or Kyoto, set a calendar reminder and book the day the window opens. Apply your certificate during the booking process on hyatt.com.

Use the free night certificate for the most expensive night of your stay (typically weekends or peak dates), then book remaining nights with World of Hyatt points at 15,000 points per Category 4 night. This combination stretches your overall lodging value significantly.

Category 4 includes well-known properties like the Andaz Maui at Wailea, Hyatt Regency Kyoto, Andaz San Diego, Hyatt Centric locations in major cities, and many Thompson hotels. The full list is available on hyatt.com by filtering the award chart. Category 4 is the sweet spot tier where property quality is high but the award cost remains accessible.

The World of Hyatt credit card automatically issues a Category 1-4 free night certificate each year on your card anniversary. A second certificate is earned after you spend $15,000 on the card in a calendar year. No special action is required beyond holding the card and meeting the spending threshold for the bonus certificate.

Yes. The free night certificate is valid for any available standard room at a Category 1-4 property, including weekends and holidays. There are no blackout dates. However, standard room availability may be limited during peak periods, so booking early is recommended.

The certificate expires 12 months after issuance and cannot be extended or refunded. If you know you will not use it, consider booking a refundable reservation at a Category 4 property to hold the value, then cancel and rebook if your plans change. Do not let it expire unused — the value easily exceeds the annual fee.

The Hyatt Category 4 free night certificate is the most accessible sweet spot in travel rewards. You do not need to understand transfer partners, award charts, or complex booking strategies. You hold the World of Hyatt credit card, the certificate arrives on your anniversary, and you redeem it at a hotel where cash rates run $250 to $400 or more per night. The $95 annual fee pays for itself three to four times over with a single use. For FI-minded households that consolidate $15,000 or more in annual spending on one card, the second certificate doubles the value. This is the card perk that turns skeptics into believers — simple math, real savings, no tricks required.

One of the biggest problems for rich smart people is overconfidence and herding when it comes to listening to other rich smart people. Intelligent people have no problem making irrational choices with their money. Everyone wants an affordable America. Good luck agreeing on what that means. On the growing sense that our financial futures are out of our control, why it’s changing how we vote, and what happens when people stop believing they can get ahead.

If it feels like there are more millionaires in the U.S. than ever before, you’re right. However, most millionaires don’t have $1 million in their checking or brokerage accounts. The bulk of their wealth is tied up in their home equity and retirement accounts. If we excluded both, the number of millionaire households in the U.S. would drop by over 50%.

It takes time to build wealth. Young people have time. In general, they will use that time to earn income, save for the future, and benefit from compounding. That time is an opportunity, although people differ in their ability to use it. As we get older, we can accumulate more financial wealth. But we also have less time left. Most older people would gladly trade some of their wealth for more time.

Retirement is increasingly becoming a touchy topic for many, especially those of us who are used to a certain level of stability. A New York Life survey of more than 2,000 adults found that 34% had already delayed retirement or planned to, and 46% of them expected to push it back 5 years or more. Their top reasons were a lack of savings (46%) and inflation (45%).

Here are some common and dangerous assumptions that individuals make when planning for retirement: stock and bond market returns will be robust, inflation will be benign, you’ll be able to work past age 65, and you will receive an inheritance. Here are some ways to avoid them.

In the financial independence community, people often struggle to identify their true purpose. The bull case for housing is the fact that we simply aren’t building enough houses. There’s also a strong possibility we will experience a surge in housing activity if and when mortgage rates fall to a more reasonable level.

Health flexible spending accounts, or FSAs, are tax-advantaged accounts that let workers set aside pretax money to cover eligible health expenses. However, they’re often use it or lose it, with unspent balances forfeited at the end of the plan year.

Every January, a physician somewhere learns about a tax strategy that would have saved them $40,000. Would have. The deadline was December 31, and nobody mentioned it until the W-2 landed.

That’s the whole trap of earning a high salary with no business attached. The money shows up, the withholding leaves, and you assume the gap between gross and net is simply the cost of being a doctor. You max the 401(k). You do the backdoor Roth. You feel responsible. Then you write a six-figure check to the Treasury and wonder why the radiologist down the hall seems so relaxed.

When I became an accredited investor, I found myself among an elite group with the financial means and regulatory clearance to access investments that many couldn’t. This opened doors to exclusive realms like hedge funds, venture capital firms, specific investment funds, private equity funds, and more.

Even though I had this “exclusive access” it took me a while to start investing in alternative asset classes.

The Securities and Exchange Commission states that as an accredited investor, I possess a level of sophistication that equips me to craft a riskier investment portfolio than a non-accredited investor. While this might not be universally true for everyone, in my case, I had demonstrated the financial resilience to bear more risk (see barbell investing), especially if my investments took an unforeseen downturn.

One of the intriguing aspects I discovered was that investment opportunities for accredited investors aren’t mandated to register with financial authorities. This means they often come with fewer disclosures and might not be as transparent as the registered securities available to the general public.

The underlying belief is that my status as a sophisticated investor implies a deeper understanding of financial risks, a need for less disclosure of unregistered securities, and a conviction that these exclusive investment opportunities are apt for my funds.

On a personal note, as a practicing CFP®, I haven’t always worked with accredited investors. Early in my career, I didn’t quite grasp the allure. However, as time went on, I began to see the broader spectrum of investment options available to accredited investors.

As I learned more the clearer it became why this realm was so sought after. The variety and potential of these exclusive opportunities were truly eye-opening, reshaping my perspective on the world of investing.

An accredited investor is an individual or a business entity that is allowed to trade securities that may not be registered with financial authorities. They are entitled to this privileged access because they satisfy one or more requirements regarding income, net worth, asset size, governance status, or professional experience.

The concept of an accredited investor originated from the idea that individuals or entities with a higher financial acumen or more resources are better equipped to understand and bear the risks of certain investment opportunities.

Historically, the distinction between accredited and non-accredited investors was established to protect less experienced investors from potentially risky or less transparent investment opportunities.

Regulatory bodies, such as the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), have set criteria to determine who qualifies as an accredited investor, ensuring that they have the financial stability and sophistication to engage in more complex investment ventures.

To be classified as an accredited investor, one must meet specific criteria set by regulatory bodies:

Here’s a rundown of some of the top investments for accredited investors…

Fundrise has revolutionized the real estate investment landscape. By democratizing access to real estate portfolios, it allows individuals to invest without the complexities of property management or the need for vast capital. The platform’s innovative approach provides exposure to a traditionally lucrative, yet often inaccessible, sector of the market

Through Fundrise, investors can access a diversified range of properties, from commercial ventures to residential units. The platform’s expert team curates these portfolios, ensuring a balance of risk and reward. With its user-friendly interface and transparent reporting, Fundrise has become a top choice for many venturing into real estate investments.

Investors start by choosing a suitable investment plan on Fundrise. Once invested, the platform pools the funds with other investors and allocates them across various real estate projects. As these properties generate rental income or appreciation in value, investors receive returns in the form of dividends or appreciation.

Equitybee offers a unique platform that bridges the gap between private companies on the cusp of going public and potential investors. This innovative approach provides a golden opportunity for investors to tap into the potential of startups and other private firms before they make their public debut.

The platform’s primary focus is on employee stock options. By allowing investors to invest in these options, they can potentially benefit from their appreciation as the company grows. With a vast array of companies, from emerging startups to established giants, Equitybee presents a diverse range of investment opportunities.

Investors browse available stock options from various companies on Equitybee. Once they choose an option, they invest their funds, which are then used to purchase the stock options from the employees. If the company goes public or gets acquired, the investor stands to gain from the increased value of these stocks.

Percent stands as a beacon in the vast sea of the private credit market, illuminating a sector often overshadowed by traditional investments. This burgeoning market, valued at over $7 trillion, consists of companies borrowing from non-bank lenders. Percent offers a unique vantage point into this market, allowing investors to diversify their portfolios beyond typical stocks and bonds.

The allure of Percent lies in its ability to offer shorter terms and higher yields, combined with investments that are largely uncorrelated with public markets. This makes it an attractive proposition for those looking to step away from the volatility of traditional markets.

Upon joining Percent, investors are presented with a plethora of private credit opportunities. After selecting an investment, funds are pooled with other investors and lent out to companies seeking credit. As these companies repay their loans, investors earn interest, providing a steady income stream.

Masterworks paints a vivid picture of art investment, blending the worlds of finance and fine art. Traditionally, investing in art was a luxury reserved for the elite. However, Masterworks has democratized this, allowing individuals to buy shares in artworks from world-renowned artists.

The platform’s strength lies in its expertise. From authentication to storage, every facet of art investment is handled meticulously. This ensures that investors can appreciate both the beauty of their investments and the potential financial returns.

After registering on Masterworks, investors can browse a curated selection of artworks. They can then purchase shares, representing a fraction of the artwork’s value. Masterworks take care of storage, insurance, and eventual sale. When the artwork is sold, investors share the profits based on their ownership.

Yieldstreet stands at the intersection of innovation and alternative investments. It offers a smorgasbord of unique investment opportunities, ranging from art to marine finance. For those looking to venture beyond the beaten path of traditional stocks and bonds, Yieldstreet presents a tantalizing array of options.

The platform’s allure lies in its curated selection of alternative investments, each vetted by experts. This ensures that while investors are treading unconventional grounds, they’re not stepping into the unknown blindly.

Investors begin by browsing through the diverse investment opportunities on Yieldstreet. After selecting their preferred asset class, their funds are pooled with other investors and allocated to the chosen venture. Returns are generated based on the performance of these assets, be it through interest, dividends, or asset appreciation.

AcreTrader, as its name suggests, brings the vast expanses of farmland to the investment table. It offers a unique opportunity to invest in agricultural land, combining the stability of real estate with the evergreen nature of agriculture. With the global population on the rise, the value of fertile land is only set to increase.

The platform meticulously vets each piece of land, ensuring only the most promising plots are available for investment. This rigorous process ensures that investors are planting their funds in fertile ground, poised for growth.

Investors peruse available farmland listings on AcreTrader. After selecting a plot, they can invest, effectively owning a portion of that land. AcreTrader manages all aspects, from liaising with farmers to ensuring optimal land use. Investors earn from the appreciation of land value and potential rental income.

EquityMultiple is a testament to the power of collective investment in the real estate sector. By leveraging the principles of crowdfunding, it offers a platform where multiple investors can pool their resources to finance high-quality real estate projects. The platform’s strength lies in its curated selection of real estate opportunities, ranging from commercial spaces to residential properties. With a team of seasoned real estate professionals at the helm, EquityMultiple ensures that each project is vetted for maximum potential and minimal risk.

Upon joining, investors can explore a variety of real estate projects. After committing to a project, their funds are pooled with other investors to finance the venture. Returns are generated through rental incomes, property appreciation, or the successful completion of development projects.

CrowdStreet stands as a pillar in the commercial real estate investment domain. With its vast experience and industry connections, it offers a platform where investors can tap into prime real estate projects across the nation. The platform’s expertise ensures that each project is meticulously vetted, offering a blend of potential returns and stability. For investors looking to delve into commercial real estate without the hassles of property management, CrowdStreet is an ideal choice.

After registration, investors can browse a myriad of commercial real estate offerings. Upon investing in a project, CrowdStreet manages the investment, providing regular updates and ensuring optimal project execution. Investors earn returns based on the project’s performance, be it through rentals, sales, or project completions.

Mainvest offers a refreshing twist in the investment landscape, focusing on the heart and soul of the American economy: local businesses. The platform’s community-centric approach ensures that investments are not just about returns but also about fostering local economies. For those looking to make a difference while earning, Mainvest presents a unique opportunity.

Vinovest uncorks the world of wine investment, offering a blend of luxury, history, and financial growth. Fine wines have been a symbol of opulence for centuries, and Vinovest provides a platform where this luxury becomes an accessible investment.

With a team of wine experts guiding the way, the platform ensures that each wine is not just a drink but an investment poised for appreciation. From sourcing to storage, Vinovest handles every facet, ensuring the wine’s value grows over time.

Arrived Homes offers a fresh perspective on real estate investment, focusing on the charm of single-family homes. While skyscrapers and commercial complexes often dominate real estate discussions, single-family homes offer stability, consistent returns, and a touch of nostalgia.

The platform’s strength lies in its focus. By concentrating on single-family homes, it offers investors a chance to tap into a stable real estate segment, benefiting from both rental income and property appreciation.

Investors browse available properties on Arrived Homes. After selecting a property, they can invest in shares, representing a portion of the home’s value. RealtyMogul stands tall in the commercial real estate investment landscape. It offers a platform where diversification meets opportunity, presenting a range of commercial properties for investment. From bustling office spaces to serene residential complexes, RealtyMogul provides a plethora of options for investors to expand their portfolios.

The platform’s prowess lies in its dual approach. Investors can either dive into non-traded REITs or make direct investments in specific properties. This flexibility ensures that both novice and experienced investors find opportunities that align with their investment goals.

Upon joining RealtyMogul, investors can choose between REITs or direct property investments. Their funds are then channeled into these real estate ventures. Returns are generated through rental incomes, property sales, or successful project completions.

The world of accredited investing is dynamic and ever-evolving. Emerging trends suggest a shift towards democratizing investment opportunities, with regulatory bodies considering more inclusive criteria for accredited investor status. This shift aims to balance the need for investor protection with the recognition that financial acumen can come from experience and education, not just wealth.

Furthermore, technological advancements are playing a pivotal role. The rise of blockchain and tokenized assets, for instance, is creating new avenues for investment and might reshape the landscape of opportunities available to accredited investors.

As the line between traditional and alternative investments blurs, the future promises a more integrated, inclusive, and innovative environment for accredited investors.

Understanding the role and opportunities of accredited investors is crucial in the modern financial landscape. While the distinction offers privileged access to unique investment opportunities, it also comes with increased risks and responsibilities.

As the world of investing continues to evolve, potential accredited investors are encouraged to stay informed, conduct thorough research, and seek professional advice. The realm of accredited investing, with its blend of challenges and opportunities, promises exciting prospects for those ready to navigate its complexities.

#8668. Why The 401(k) Still Dominates (Even Its Inventor Has Doubts)

In 1980, a benefits consultant named Ted Benna figured out how to use Section 401(k), a little-known provision Congress added to the tax code in 1978, to build the first 401(k) plan. It quickly became a favorite among companies looking to offer employees more retirement benefits.

Today, it is still the cornerstone of retirement planning in America. Even physicians who often have a 403(b), 457(b), or defined benefit plan available too, usually max out their 401(k) first.

Recently, Benna has made headlines for calling out his invention, the 401(k), for disproportionately rewarding the wealthy. He may have a point. But I still think the 401(k) is the best retirement account most workers can get, and that it’s still worth it for doctors.

Also read: Beyond the 401(k): Why Physicians Are Turning to Defined Benefit Plans

In a recent Bloomberg interview, Benna argued that the modern 401(k) has grown too complicated and too costly, and that it benefits wealthier savers more than middle- and lower-income workers, the people who arguably need it most.

Affluent employees can afford to max out an account and reap the tax break on top. Benna believes low-income workers either lack access to a plan or can’t afford to contribute if they do.

Research seems to agree. Researchers at Vanguard, Yale and MIT found that about 44% of employer matching dollars go to the top 20% of earners at their companies.

And the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics has reported that while 70% of private-sector workers have access to a defined contribution (DC) plan such as a 401(k), only 49% participate. That means roughly 3 in 10 workers who could use a plan but don’t.

Source: BLS. Alt text: BLS chart showing 70% of private-sector workers have access to a defined contribution plan and 49% participate, March 2026

Discover legitimate, IRS-recognized tax strategies physicians can use to potentially reduce their tax bills, which options high earners qualify for, and which aggressive approaches could attract IRS scrutiny.

Ideal for: Physicians and high-income professionals looking to understand their tax-saving options before speaking with their CPA.

Sat, Nov 14  ·  1:00 pm ET  ·  10:00 am PT

Most physicians sit on the other side of this. Every specialty earns well above the national average. Doximity’s latest compensation report names pediatric infectious disease as the lowest-paying specialty, at $217,819. By comparison, the average American salary is $69,770.

The reason I bring this up here is so that physicians who run practices can make sure their employee 401(k) structures do not reflect these statistics. More on that below.

The 401(k) has been one of the most effective tools for building middle-class wealth the U.S. has ever had.

Household stock ownership went up from 32% in 1989, right before one of the best multi-decade stretches for stock returns on record, to 58% by 2022. Almost one-fifth of American households now hold a net worth above a million dollars— much of it held in home equity and retirement accounts like the 401(k)..

So even if the account rewards people who already earn enough to contribute, it still enables actual wealth-building for millions of ordinary workers who’d otherwise have little beyond Social Security waiting for them at retirement.

Access and participation are both on the rise largely thanks to policy changes. Many states now require employers without a retirement plan to enroll workers in a state-run IRA program. Employers can usually opt out by setting up their own plan, which is pushing more of them to offer a 401(k).

Small businesses, which employ close to half the American workforce, have historically skipped retirement benefits altogether. Tax credits and cheaper providers are changing that. Cerulli Associates projects that the number of 401(k) plans will grow 36% over the next five years, passing one million by the end of the decade.

Auto-enrollment deserves a lot of the credit for the jump in participation.

Under SECURE 2.0, 401(k) and 403(b) plans set up after December 29, 2022 must automatically enroll employees, starting with plan years that began in 2025. Older plans, businesses less than three years old and employers with 10 or fewer workers are exempt.

The effect is large. Vanguard found that plans with auto-enrollment had a 94% participation rate, compared with 64% for plans where employees sign up on their own.

Learn more: Year-End Tax Planning for Physicians. What To Do Before 2026 Is Over

For 2026, the IRS raised the 401(k) employee contribution limit to $24,500, up from $23,500 in 2025. Workers 50 and older can add a catch-up contribution of $8,000 on top of that, up from $7,500, bringing the total to $32,500 for savers in that age bracket.

A newer “super” catch-up of $11,250 lets savers ages 60 to 63 put away even more. It replaces the regular $8,000 catch-up for those years rather than stacking on top of it, bringing their total to $35,750.

re limited to 72,000for2026(80,000 with the age-50 catch-up, or $83,250 for ages 60 to 63), or 100% of eligible pay, whichever is lower. If your plan allows after-tax contributions, the room between your own contributions and that cap is what makes a mega backdoor Roth possible.

Important: starting in 2026, if your wages from the employer sponsoring your plan topped $150,000 in 2025, any catch-up contributions you make must go in as Roth (after-tax) instead of pretax. Two details matter for physicians:

If you’re weighing Roth against pretax for the rest of your contributions, here’s how to choose between a Roth and traditional 401(k). Full details are on the IRS catch-up contributions page.

Many employed physicians don’t have a 401(k) at all. Hospitals and academic centers usually offer a 403(b), which works almost the same way, with the same $24,500 limit and the same catch-ups.

Many also offer a 457(b), which has its own separate $24,500 limit. If you have both, you can defer up to $49,000 in 2026 before counting any catch-ups.

One caution: in a non-governmental 457(b), the money technically belongs to your employer until it’s paid out, so it’s exposed if the hospital runs into financial trouble. Here’s our full guide to 457(b) contributions.

If you own a practice with staff, plan design decides who actually benefits. A safe harbor 401(k) is the common choice. You make a required contribution for employees, either 3% of pay or a match of up to 4%, which vests right away.

In return, the plan skips the annual nondiscrimination tests that can otherwise cap what owners contribute. Under SECURE 2.0, small practices can also claim tax credits of up to $5,000 a year for three years toward startup costs, plus $500 a year for adding auto-enrollment.

Owners who want to save more than the 401(k) allows often pair it with a cash balance plan. And if you’re a solo practitioner with no staff, a solo 401(k) or SEP-IRA is usually simpler.

More than 80% of employers who sponsor a 401(k) offer some form of match, usually tied to how much the employee contributes. Some employers match dollar for dollar up to a set percentage of salary.

Others match 50 cents on the dollar up to a higher contribution threshold. The formula changes how much match each dollar you contribute actually earns, and that’s where dual-income households can come out ahead.

A brief published by the Center for Retirement Research (CRR) examined whether married couples coordinate contributions to capture both employer matches. Just over 40% of couples actively coordinate to maximize their combined match and roughly one in five couples leaves match money uncaptured.

In one example from the brief, a couple decides how to split $480 a month in savings between two accounts with different match formulas. Moving contributions toward the partner with the more generous 1-to-1 match, as opposed to splitting evenly, nets the household an extra $30 a month in employer money.

Stretched over 30 years at a 5% inflation-adjusted return, that $30 monthly difference compounds into roughly $25,000 in additional retirement savings, without either partner setting aside a single extra dollar of their own income.

Source: CRR. Alt text: CRR chart showing how couples split 401(k) contributions to capture employer matches.

Plenty of couples capture both matches without planning it, because each partner contributes enough on their own. That works fine.

Coordination matters when money is tight, like when one spouse is still in residency, working part-time or paying down loans hard. In those years, send your savings to the richer match first, then fill the other.

Say a resident earning $66,000 and her spouse earning $120,000 can save $600 a month between them. Her plan matches 50 cents per dollar on the first 6% of pay. His matches dollar for dollar on the first 4%, up to $400 a month.

Split evenly at $300 each, they collect $450 a month in match. If he puts in $400 and she puts in $200, they collect $500. That’s an extra $600 a year in employer money from the same $600 a month.

Compare match formulas with your spouse, figure out which account pays the better rate, and adjust the split.

Finally, if you’re wondering about how aggressively you should contribute, I’ll say that starting early beats chasing a better return.

In an example from Forbes, we see two 25-year-old savers earning identical salaries. One enrolls immediately at a 10% deferral rate with a 3% match. The other waits five years, then contributes 6% to capture the same 3% match.

The second saver’s fund even outperforms the first, returning roughly 8.9% annually versus 8.4%, partly from a private equity allocation meant to make up lost ground.

By 65, the early starter still ends up with roughly $3 million, compared with $2 million for the saver who waited. That $1 million gap comes from two things: five fewer years of compounding and a lower savings rate (9% of pay versus 13%). The higher return didn’t come close to closing it. If you’re still in training, here’s what to set up now.

As you can see, when it comes to retirement savings, your timing often matters more than any other variable.

A dollar contributed at 25 has decades to compound and no later contribution, however large, can fully make up for a late start. The 401(k) is also one of the few accounts you can start on day one without worrying much about what happens when you change jobs.

That’s because, as opposed to pensions and employer-funded bonus plans, the 401(k) is portable. Your own contributions are yours the moment they hit your account, and they go with you when you leave. Employer matches can be different. Many plans vest the match over time, either all at once after up to three years or gradually over up to six.

Leave before you’re vested and you lose the unvested part, so check your plan’s vesting schedule before you time a job change. You can roll it into a new employer’s plan or an IRA, and it will continue to compound without interruption.

Benna may not be happy with how his invention turned out, but for me, looking at how it has created a new class of millionaires, it is the one non-negotiable account in retirement planning for physicians and beyond.

Also read: One Big Beautiful Bill Act: What It Means for Physician Taxes in 2025 and 2026

The IRS caps employee contributions at $24,500 for 2026. Workers 50 and older can add an $8,000 catch-up, and those between 60 and 63 get a larger $11,250 “super” catch-up instead, bringing their total to $35,750.

No. More than 80% of employers who sponsor a 401(k) offer some form of match, but the formula varies. Some match dollar for dollar up to a set percentage of salary, others match 50 cents on the dollar to a higher threshold.

Yes. A 401(k) invests in the market through mutual funds or target-date funds, so balances can drop during downturns. Over decades, though, contributions and compounding have historically outpaced short-term losses for most savers.

It depends. A 401(k) is portable, so you keep the balance and can roll it into a new employer’s plan or an IRA when you switch jobs. A pension pays guaranteed income for life, but most of the benefit builds in your later years with one employer, so people who change jobs often come out behind.

Yes. Directing more of a couple’s combined savings toward whichever spouse has the richer employer match captures free money that even splits often miss, sometimes adding thousands to household retirement savings with no extra out-of-pocket cost.

Yes, if your 2025 wages from the employer sponsoring your plan topped $150,000. Your catch-up contributions must go in as Roth. Partners paid through K-1 income aren’t affected.

You keep everything you contributed yourself, plus any match that has already vested. The unvested part goes back to the plan.

Nearly. Both have the same $24,500 limit for 2026 and the same catch-up rules. A 403(b) is offered by nonprofits like hospitals and universities, and some have fewer investment options.

#8666. Gift Cards Below Face Value – A Discount on Spending You’d Do Anyway

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Buy discounted gift cards for the stores and restaurants you already use, and everything you buy with them costs less. Look for warehouse club multipacks, holiday bonus offers, and resale sites that guarantee the balance. Pay with a credit card that earns rewards on gift cards, and spend each one within a few months.

Paying $80 for $100 in restaurant gift cards takes 20% off meals you’d have eaten anyway. The catch is finding cards that cheap, then keeping the discount once you have them.

Start at a warehouse club. Costco says its restaurant gift cards typically sell at a 20% to 25% discount, as eGift cards or physical multipacks. Some restaurant chains add a bonus card over the holidays. The Cheesecake Factory’s annual holiday offer has given a $15 bonus card for every $50 in gift cards, usable only from Jan. 1 through Feb. 28.

Resale sites such as CardCash sell other people’s unwanted cards at discounts that vary by store. Kroger, the grocery chain, gives 2 loyalty points for every dollar spent on most gift cards, and every 100 points takes $1 off groceries, a 2% return.

Paying with a rewards credit card adds to the discount, but check its terms first. Cards that earn American Express Membership Rewards points, for one, earn none on gift cards. For online orders, start at a cash back shopping portal, which pays you back a percentage of the order, then pay with the gift card. Some stores pay no portal cash back on the part of an order paid by gift card, so read the store’s terms on the portal before you buy.

Then protect the discount. Check a resale card’s balance the day it arrives, since CardCash refunds a balance that comes up short only if you report it within 45 days of purchase. Don’t stockpile cards, either. A chain that closes unexpectedly can leave its cards useless, the Consumer Federation of America warns. And skip prepaid Visa and Mastercard gift cards, which add a purchase fee to the face value, such as $5 on a $50 card at Target.

Start with the store where you spend the most, and buy no more than about three months of your usual spending there at a time.

Rent out an unused garage, driveway, or lot on Neighbor if it would sit empty for months, since listing is free and the fee is 4.9% plus 30 cents a payout. Understanding the cost of a million-dollar life insurance policy can be pivotal in securing your family's financial future. But have you ever wondered just how accessible or costly such a policy might be?

Do you think a million-dollar term life insurance policy sounds like too much insurance?

As a Certified Financial Planner, I see underinsured people every day.

A million-dollar term life insurance policy might actually be the minimum coverage needed for the typical middle-class household, but it’s affordable.

That might sound like an exaggeration, but if you crunch the numbers – just as we’ll be doing a little bit – you’ll realize that a million-dollar policy might be just what you need.

The good news is term life insurance isn’t nearly as costly as most people think.

What makes term life insurance even better is that larger policies cost less on a per thousand basis than smaller policies do. You may find the premium on a $1 million policy is only a little bit higher than it is for $500,000.

Probably, but let’s find out. A general rule of thumb is that you should get 10x your income as baseline coverage for life insurance.

If you’re young, that may be low because you may want to provide your family with enough to replace your income for 15 years or more.

Today, $1 million has become the new baseline for life insurance by a primary breadwinner. Anything less could leave your family financially impaired.

Here’s a list of all the different obligations you may want to have life insurance cover in the unfortunate event you pass away early.

Now that you have an idea of these obligations, let’s punch them into this life insurance calculator to find out if you need a million-dollar policy.

According to Policy Genius, the average cost for a 20-year $1 million term life insurance policy for a 35-year-old male is $53 per month. However, your rate will vary according to the following factors.

The best, and easiest place to start is online. I recommend having two or three insurers compete for your business to make sure you get the best rate and coverage. To see how cheap term life can be, choose your state from the map above to be matched with top life insurance providers instantly.

Let’s look at the individual components that can quickly add up to over a million-dollar policy.

This is where things can get a bit intimidating. Even if you earn a modest income, you may need close to $1 million to replace that income after your death in order to provide for your family’s basic living expenses.

The conventional wisdom in the insurance industry is that you should maintain a life insurance policy equal to between 10 times and 20 times your annual income. So if you earn around $50K per year, that would mean policy coverage between $500K and $1 million.

The complication today is that with interest rates being as low as they are that might not be enough either.

For example, if you have a $1 million policy that could be invested at 5% per year, your family could live on the interest earned – which conveniently comes to $50,000 per year – for the next 20 years.

That would still leave the original $1 million intact to cover other expenses. But with today’s microscopic interest rates, there’s no way to get a guaranteed return of 5% on your money, certainly not for 15 or 20 years.

Also, keep in mind that most insurance companies have a maximum multiplier you can apply to your income for life insurance coverage. For example, it wouldn’t make much sense for a 22-year-old making $27,000 per year to get a $2 million life insurance. Or a 65-year-old that is retired to secure a $3 million dollar policy.

The table below is approximately how much you’re allowed to multiply your income based on your age and income:

Using the table above as a guide, a 35-year-old making $150,000 per year would be capped at taking out a $4.5 million term policy ($150,000 x 30 = $4,500,000).

Here we start with the basics – wrapping up your final affairs.

This will include funeral costs and any lingering medical costs. A reasonable estimate for a typical funeral is around $20,000.

Crazy, right? You can get burial insurance to cover only the most basic of final expenses.

Debt burdens are high in the US, and debt can be especially crushing on remaining family members. Many life insurance customers make sure they can pay off most of their debt with the policy.

Medical costs are a serious variable. Even if you have excellent health insurance, there are likely to be unpaid medical bills lingering after your death. This has to do with copayments, deductibles, and coinsurance provisions.

Collectively, they can add up to many thousands of dollars. But where things get really complicated is if you die of a terminal illness.

For example, if you are stricken by an illness that lasts for several years, you could incur a number of expenses that are not covered by insurance. This may include the cost of personal care and even experimental treatments.

A home may be a large asset, but it’s also often a homeowner’s largest debt. The average mortgage balance in the US is roughly $236,443 according to Experian data. So you could easily use a life insurance policy to pay off that debt and relieve your loved ones of a monthly mortgage payment.

Credit card debt and other personal debt are some of the most expensive obligations carrying rates upward of 20% in some cases. Make sure you have enough to cover this very expensive debt.

Below is a sampling of major expenses your family is likely to incur, either on an annual basis or at some point after your death.

Tuition costs continue to skyrocket. The Department of Education suggests that four-year public college tuition has been rising an average of 5% per year, far exceeding the rate of inflation. If you have one child who attends an in-state public school, a second at an out-of-state public school, and a third in a private university, the total expenditure will reach $416,560.

Vehicles and other forms of transportation represent another large sum. Unfortunately, with increasing electronics and safety features, the average cost of a new car continues to grow.

If your family relies on your work for healthcare, take notice. According to eHealth.com, the average health insurance premium for a family is $22,221. That’s a shade under $2,000 per month in additional cost. This cost will only rise, and the need could last for years.

So far, we’ve been describing the financial obligations likely to affect a typical household.But there may be certain situations that will produce obligations that are less obvious.

For example, if you’re a business owner, there may be debts or other financial obligations that will need to be paid upon your death.

Even though no one in your family may be qualified or interested in taking over your business, the payoff of those obligations may be completely necessary to enable the sale of the business.

Another possibility is that you’re a real estate investor.

If your properties are heavily indebted, extra insurance proceeds may be necessary either to carry the properties until they’re sold, or even to pay off existing indebtedness to free up cash flow for income.

You may even need additional funds if you are taking care of an extended family member, like an aging parent.

These are just some of the many possibilities of expenses that will need to be covered by insurance proceeds.

Before we move on to specific life insurance quotes, let’s first consider the factors that affect term life insurance premiums.

This is typically the single most important premium factor. The older you are, the more likely you are to die within the term of the policy.

This is a close second and why it’s so important to apply for a policy as early in life as possible. Premiums on life insurances rates literally increase by each year.

If you have any health conditions that may affect mortality, such as diabetes or hypertension, your premiums will be higher. This is another compelling reason to apply while you are young and in good health.

It’s not that policies are not available to people with health conditions, it’s just that they’re less expensive if you don’t have any.

A 10-year term policy will have a lower premium than a 20-year term policy, which will be lower than a 30-year term. The shorter the term, the less likely it is the insurance company will have to pay a claim before it expires.

Size of the policy matters, but not the way you might think. Yes, a $1 million policy will cost more than a $500,000 policy. But it won’t cost twice as much.

The larger the policy, the lower the per-thousand cost will be.

When the size of the death benefit is considered, the larger policy will always be more cost-effective.

For example, certain occupations are more hazardous than others (think policeman versus librarian). Deep-sea diving is higher risk than golf. And smoking is the one activity guaranteed to raise your premiums substantially.

With this information in mind, let’s take a look at whether you should consider a $1 million whole life policy instead.

Any discussion on life insurance should include a comparison of whole life and term life insurance coverage. After all, both products can be immensely valuable in the right situation, yet one product (whole life) costs considerably more than the other.

Most of the time, the debate is settled in favor of term life insurance based on cost alone.

A whole life insurance policy can easily cost 10x the same amount of coverage you can get with a term policy.

With that being said, whole life insurance and other investment-type life insurance coverage can be valuable in terms of the cash value you can build up over time. Whole life insurance also offers a fixed benefit amount for your heirs that will last for your entire life, yet the cost of your premiums are guaranteed to stay the same.

The cash value of a whole life insurance policy also grows on a tax-deferred basis, and you can borrow against this amount if you need a loan. Further, many whole life policies from reputable providers also pay out dividends during good years, which can be substantial.

The problem with whole life and other similar policies like universal life is the fact that premiums can be exorbitant for the amount of coverage you might need.

A couple with young children provides a good example since they might need a $1 million dollar policy or more to provide income protection for their working years and have money left for college tuition and other expenses.

With young families, expenses are already high.

This includes costs for food for a family, childcare, heavy use of health care, and the seemingly endless demand for clothing, furniture, and even entertainment as the children grow.

As you can see from the cost comparison below from State Farm, there’s not enough room in the typical family budget to afford the type of life insurance that’s needed.

A 40-year-old mother and breadwinner in excellent health would pay $80.09 per month for a term life policy that lasts 20 years, whereas a whole life policy in the same amount would cost $1,266.69 per month (or $14,560 annually).

This is a classic situation where term insurance rides to the rescue. The family can afford to buy the amount of coverage they need at an affordable price, whereas paying for permanent life insurance coverage in the same amount would be difficult to justify.

And just as important for people of any age and in any circumstance, the extra funds not being spent on insurance premiums can be invested to gradually improve your financial situation.

So absolutely, term insurance will work best for most people.

As you’ll notice, each table has a wide array of information. Knowing that everybody is in a different situation, I wanted to make sure that I offered term life quotes for almost every conceivable situation.

I’ve included life insurance rates for a 30-year term, 20-year term, and a 10-year term million dollar life policies. If you’re a tobacco user, I’ve also included some quotes from life insurance for smokers.

For those that think that a million-dollar term policy is expensive, you’ll quickly notice that a 25-year-old male in good health only costs $645 per year while a 35-year-old costs $795.

On a monthly basis that’s almost next to nothing!

There is a big drop-off in life insurance rates between a 20 year and a 30 year since underwriters do not have to worry as much about life expectancy.

For many people, a 20-year policy gets them exactly where they want to be in life when the policy term runs out.

Once again, you get a $200 drop in the annual premium by losing another 10 years on the term.

If your life insurance agent isn’t giving you all these term options and is only focused on the death benefit, then you need a different agent.

For all you smokers out there – beware! The cost of your life insurance balloons as you’ll see here. If you’re considering kicking the habit, now is as good time as any.

Some life insurance companies will give you a lower rate if you complete a recognized smoking cessation program, and go on without smoking for at least two years.

It won’t help your immediate situation, but when you see the premium on smoker life insurance rates below, you might agree that it’s something to work toward!

If you’ve made the decision that $1 million of life insurance is the right amount of coverage you need and you’re ready to purchase a policy, here are the steps you’ll need to follow.

1. Determine How Much Coverage You Need: This is the first and most important step in securing a million life insurance policies. You need to have a clear understanding of how much coverage you actually need.

2. Choose the Right Type of Policy: There are whole life, term life, and Universal life policies available. Choose the one that best suits your needs.

3. Shop Around: Don’t just go with the first life insurance company you come across. It’s important to compare life insurance rates and coverage from a few different companies before making a decision.

4. Consider Your Health: If you’re in good health, you’ll likely qualify for lower rates. However, if you have health issues, you may still be able to get coverage, but it will probably be more expensive.

5. Consider Your Lifestyle: If you have a risky job or hobby, that could affect your rates.

6. Get Quotes From Multiple Companies: This is the best way to compare rates and find the cheapest policy.

7. Read the Fine Print: Make sure you understand all the terms and conditions of the policy before buying it.

8. Buy Online: You can usually get cheaper rates by buying life insurance online.

9. Pay Attention to Your Payment Schedule: Most life insurance policies require monthly or annual payments. Be sure you can afford the payments before buying a policy.

10. Review Your Policy Regularly: Life changes, and so do life insurance needs. Be sure to review your policy regularly to make sure it still meets your needs.

Following these steps will help you get the best possible rate on a million-dollar life insurance policy.

Make sure you understand all the terms and conditions before signing on the dotted line. Also, make sure to shop around and compare rates from multiple companies before buying a policy.

Yes, I know I’ve said that a few times in this article, but it’s worth repeating. Many people go with the first life insurance company they call, and that isn’t kind to their checkbook. It pays to shop around.

Here’s what you need to know about choosing the best life insurance company for your $1 million policy:

When choosing the best life insurance company, it’s important to consider the overall financial health of the insurance company. You want to make sure the company you choose is stable and will be around for years to come. You also want to consider things like the company’s customer service rating and claims-paying ability.

There are a lot of different life insurance companies out there, so it can be difficult to know which one is the best. Each company is rated by different organizations, so it’s important to look at multiple ratings before making a decision.

Rating agencies are the “Report Card” for life insurance companies. Choose a company with straight A’s!

The companies that rate insurance companies are A.M. Best, Moody’s, and Standard & Poor’s.

A.M. Best is a credit rating agency that specializes in the insurance industry. They rate insurance companies on their financial stability.

Moody’s is another credit rating agency. They also rate insurance companies on their financial stability.

Standard & Poor’s is a credit rating agency that rates companies on their financial stability.

The following life insurance companies are all rated A+ (Superior) by A.M. Best and are considered to be financially stable and have a good claim-paying ability.

When choosing a life insurance company, it’s important to consider their financial stability, customer service rating, and claims-paying ability. The companies listed above are all rated A+ (Superior) by A.M. Best and are considered to be financially stable with a good claims-paying ability.

Northwestern Mutual, New York Life, MassMutual, Guardian Life, State Farm, Nationwide, USAA, MetLife, The Hartford, and Allstate are all good choices for life insurance companies.

You can’t put a price on peace of mind, and with a $1 million life insurance policy you can have the peace of mind knowing that your loved ones will be taken care of financially if something happens to you.

Getting a one-million-dollar term life insurance policy is not as expensive as most people believe. You can start getting quotes today from a variety of top life insurers by selecting your state from the map above.

Even those who opt for the more expensive permanent life insurance policy will many times be surprised at the price.

Either way, you can get these larger amounts of coverage and still not break the bank. But get your policy now, while you’re still young and in good health.

The cost of a $1,000,000 life insurance policy will vary based on factors like your age, health, and lifestyle. However, you can expect to pay around $250 per year for a healthy 30-year-old. According to Ladder Life, a $1 million term life policy for healthy 30-year-old males costs around $2.08 per day.

A $1 million term life insurance policy is a type of life insurance that provides coverage for a specific period of time, usually 10-20 years. If you die during the term of the policy, your beneficiaries will receive a death benefit of $1 million. If you live past the term of the policy, the policy will expire and you will not receive any death benefit. A $1 million term life insurance policy is a good choice for people who want to make sure their loved ones are taken care of financially if something happens to them. It can also be a good choice for people with a lot of debt, like a mortgage or student loans, that they want to make sure is paid off if they die.

For the most part, yes; but there are examples of people who cannot buy life insurance. For instance, people with a terminal illness or those who have been diagnosed with a life expectancy of fewer than two years are not able to purchase life insurance policies. The other factors are your income, affordability, and suitability. If you cannot afford the premiums, then you will not be able to purchase the policy. And if your income is say less than $50,000 then the insurance company may not think it’s suitable to purchase a $1 million life insurance policy.

A million-dollar life insurance policy may not be right for everyone, but it can be a good idea if you have a lot of debt or if you want to make sure your family is taken care of financially if something happens to you. No one likes to think about their death, but it’s important to have a life insurance policy in place in case something happens to you. A million-dollar life insurance policy can give you and your loved one’s peace of mind knowing that they will be taken care of financially if something happens to you.

There is no one-size-fits-all answer to this question, as the best policy for you will depend on your specific needs and preferences. However, some of the top providers of million-dollar life insurance policies include AIG, Banner Life, and Prudential. So be sure to explore your options and compare quotes from different providers before making a decision.

#8661. Family Meal Planning on a Budget – Let the Week’s Sales Set the Menu

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Before you shop, spend 20 minutes planning the week’s dinners from what’s on sale and what’s already in your kitchen. Pick five dinners that share ingredients, save a night for leftovers, keep a backup meal on hand, and write your grocery list from that plan. You’ll make fewer trips and order less takeout.

Without a plan, you pick dinner in the store, where whatever looks good goes in the cart. Then you pick it again at 5:30 on a busy night, when takeout is easier than turning those groceries into a meal.

A plan saves money because it settles what you’ll buy before you walk in. Start it from the week’s sales, and the cheapest meat and produce set the menu. Start it from the fridge and pantry, and you eat what you already paid for before it spoils.

Say your family orders takeout twice a week at about $40 an order. This week chicken thighs and ground beef are on sale, so the plan includes tacos, sheet-pan chicken, and a double pot of chili, with Thursday for the leftovers. If the leftovers night and the backup meal replace both orders, and the extra groceries for them cost about $20, you save about $60 a week.

To make it stick, keep a two-week rotation of 10 dinners your family already likes, and let the kids pick one night’s dinner from it. A meal planning app can save that rotation and turn each week’s dinners into a grocery list.

Put the 20 minutes on the calendar for the evening before your shopping day, and write nothing on the list until the five dinners are set.
