Let's build a real example so you can see exactly what this looks like on paper — and in the air.

The Route: Toronto (YYZ) → Istanbul (IST, 4-day stopover) → Bangkok (BKK) The Carrier: Turkish Airlines business class on both segments The Points Cost: 75,000 Aeroplan miles for the two segments + 5,000 miles for the stopover = 80,000 Aeroplan miles total Cash Equivalent: A comparable business class itinerary on this routing typically retails for $9,000–$12,000 in 2026, depending on when you search and how far in advance you book.

The CPP Calculation: At the midpoint cash value of $10,500 against 80,000 points, you're extracting 13.1 cents per Aeroplan mile — well inside the 8–20 cent range this sweet spot delivers, and roughly 10–13 times the value of redeeming Aeroplan miles for cash back.

The Turkish Airlines business class product on long-haul routes is consistently rated among the top business class experiences in the Star Alliance network. On the YYZ–IST segment — operated on a 787 or A330 — you'll have access to a lie-flat seat with direct aisle access, the Turkish Airlines Lounge in Istanbul (widely considered one of the best airport lounges in the world, full stop), and a meal service that reflects the airline's culinary reputation. The IST lounge alone — with its restaurant, spa, golf simulator, and sleeping areas — is worth lingering in even before your onward connection.

In Istanbul, your four days might include the Hagia Sophia at sunrise, a Bosphorus dinner cruise, and the Grand Bazaar before you head to the airport to continue your journey. You've paid nothing additional for this stay beyond the 5,000-mile stopover fee.

The IST–BKK segment puts you into Bangkok in the evening, ready for Thailand's extraordinary food, culture, and cost of living — which, for the FI-minded traveler, means your lodging and meals on the ground are remarkably affordable, stretching the value of your trip even further.

Total points cost for two lie-flat business class segments and a full European city stay: 80,000 miles, earned on everyday credit card spending. That's the entire proposition, and those numbers are real.

Book at exactly 355 days out. Aeroplan opens its booking window at 355 days before departure. The best business class availability on popular routes — especially Turkish Airlines long-haul — appears at this window and gets claimed quickly. Set a calendar reminder and be ready to search at the 355-day mark for your target travel dates.

Use Chase Ultimate Rewards as your primary earning currency for this redemption. The instant transfer speed to Aeroplan is genuinely differentiating. When you find award space and need to move quickly, Chase lets you transfer and book in the same session. Amex, Capital One, and Bilt all require 1–2 days, during which your availability can evaporate.

Search availability before you transfer points. Confirm space exists on every segment before a single point moves. There's no undo button on a transfer, and Aeroplan points sitting idle in your account are fine — points transferred to an account where you can't find availability are a headache.

Call Aeroplan for complex routings. The online multi-city tool is functional but can struggle with nuanced stopover configurations. Phone agents are experienced with these bookings and have the same access to inventory. The call is worth it for an $80,000-point booking.

Leverage the open-jaw rule too. Aeroplan also allows open-jaw routing — fly into one city, depart from another. Combined with the stopover, you can design a route that visits three geographic points on a single award: fly into Istanbul, take trains or ferries to Athens, and fly home from Athens. The award prices the same way.

Don't assume partner availability matches Aeroplan's search. Turkish Airlines and other Star Alliance partners don't always make every seat available through Aeroplan's online portal. If you see space on the carrier's own site but not on aeroplan.com, call — agents can often access inventory the website misses.

Don't book inflexible connecting flights. Long-haul itineraries with tight connections are a risk. Build in at least a 3-hour connection at hub airports to protect against irregular operations that could affect your award segments.

Don't earn Marriott Bonvoy points with this redemption in mind. The 3:1 transfer ratio to Aeroplan makes Marriott a poor choice for funding this specific award. Stick to Amex, Chase, Capital One, or Bilt at 1:1.

Don't book this for a time-sensitive trip. Award availability, transfer timelines, and multi-carrier coordination mean this requires planning runway. Build in at least 3–4 weeks of lead time beyond the actual booking date.

This redemption is purpose-built for the advanced travel rewards enthusiast in the ChooseFI community — someone who has already mastered the basics (earning transferable points, understanding award charts, booking straightforward partner awards) and is ready to unlock the next level of value.

The ideal profile: A couple or solo traveler planning a milestone trip — a significant anniversary, a sabbatical, a once-in-a-decade adventure — who wants to experience two destinations in business class without paying business class prices for either one. You're flexible on travel dates, comfortable spending time on the phone with an airline agent, and genuinely excited about the trip-planning process as part of the experience.

Minimum points balance: You'll need approximately 80,000 Aeroplan miles to complete this booking (75,000 for the award plus 5,000 for the stopover). That's achievable from a single premium credit card welcome bonus, a combination of two or three mid-tier welcome bonuses, or 12–18 months of everyday spending on a 2x transferable points card.

For the ChooseFI traveler who's been building transferable points for a year or two and wants to see what this system is truly capable of, this redemption is the answer.

This redemption is rated **Hard** — and that rating is honest. It earns that designation from three compounding challenges, not just one. **Challenge 1: Finding availability on multiple segments simultaneously.** Business class award space on popular long-haul routes is limited. Finding saver-level availability on one segment is manageable. Finding it on two connected segments, with dates that create a coherent stopover itinerary, requires persistence and flexibility. This is the primary barrier. **Challenge 2: Understanding Aeroplan's routing logic.** Aeroplan's stopover rules, multi-city booking interface, and the distinction between how partner awards are priced require more than surface-level familiarity with the program. A misunderstanding of how the stopover is added can result in a significantly higher points cost or a booking that doesn't reflect your intended itinerary. **Challenge 3: Coordinating the transfer timing.** With a 355-day booking window and fast-moving business class availability, the timing of your point transfers requires active management — particularly if you're not using Chase's instant transfer speed. ## Three Tips to Overcome These Challenges 1. **Start your availability research 60–90 days before the 355-day window opens.** Know your target route, your preferred stopover city, and your date range before you ever log into aeroplan.com. Preparation turns a chaotic search into a focused one. 2. **Use united.com as your availability research tool.** It searches the Star Alliance network and shows you realistic inventory without requiring you to commit points. 3. **Don't be discouraged by the learning curve.** Every hard redemption in the ChooseFI community gets easier the second time. Plenty of members who now book these routinely considered them impossible the first time they looked. The complexity is real — but so is the $10,000 of value sitting on the other side of it.

Pick a final destination and a stopover city on the same Star Alliance routing. Classic combos: Istanbul + Bangkok, Zurich + Tokyo, Vienna + Singapore. The stopover city must be a natural connection point on a Star Alliance route between your origin and destination.

Set a calendar alert for 355 days before your departure date. Search for business class availability on each segment separately using United.com or Aeroplan.com. Both legs need saver-level award space on the same booking.

Before transferring any points, verify that saver award space exists on both the outbound leg (origin to stopover city) and the continuation (stopover city to final destination). If either segment is unavailable, the booking will not work.

Transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards (instant) or Amex Membership Rewards (1-2 days) to your Aeroplan account at a 1:1 ratio. Only transfer once you have confirmed availability on both segments.

Call Aeroplan or use the multi-city search tool online. Specify your stopover city and duration (up to the maximum allowed). The system prices it as one round-trip award. Confirm total points match expectations before completing the booking.

Aeroplan allows stopovers of up to 45 days on round-trip awards. You can stay in your stopover city for a few days or several weeks, giving you genuine time to explore rather than just passing through.

No, stopovers are only available on round-trip awards through Aeroplan. One-way bookings do not qualify for the free stopover benefit. This is one reason round-trip awards can offer better value than two one-ways.

Aeroplan has improved its online multi-city search tool, and some stopover itineraries can now be booked online. However, complex routings may still require a phone call. When calling, clearly state you want a round-trip award with a stopover and specify your stopover city and dates.

The best stopover cities are Star Alliance hub cities with strong business class availability: Istanbul (Turkish Airlines hub), Zurich (SWISS hub), Vienna (Austrian hub), Singapore (Singapore Airlines hub), and Tokyo (ANA hub). These hubs offer the most consistent saver-level award space.

The Aeroplan stopover is one of the most powerful tools in the travel rewards playbook. By adding a free stopover to a round-trip business class award, you can explore two world-class cities for the points cost of visiting one. It requires planning, patience at the 355-day booking window, and comfort with Star Alliance routing rules, but the payoff is extraordinary: 10-15 cents per point in value on experiences that would cost thousands in cash. For the FI community member who has mastered basic award bookings and is ready to level up, this is the redemption that changes how you think about travel.

Systeme.io has burst onto the digital marketing scene, brandishing a bold claim as an all-in-one, free platform.

Let’s face it, when you hear something like that, your first thought is, “This has got to be too good to be true.”

That was my initial reaction too. A free, do-it-all software that doesn’t suck? Highly doubtful.

But here’s the shocker: Systeme.io isn’t just blowing smoke. It’s a game-changer. As someone who’s navigated the maze of digital marketing tools, I was prepared for disappointment. Yet, Systeme.io left me floored with its capabilities.

Take it from someone who’s been around the block with the likes of ConvertKit, AWeber, and MailChimp. These giants lure you in with free offerings, only to tighten the screws when your audience grows. Then there’s WordPress.org – great for setting up a blog, but it’s like climbing Everest if you’re a newbie.

Systeme.io, on the other hand, is a beast of a different nature. Offering highly effective landing pages and robust sales funnels with professional templates for free? That’s unheard of. It’s like stumbling upon a treasure chest in your backyard.

My first foray into landing page software was with ClickFunnels, an undeniably powerful tool. But once the 14-day trial evaporates, you’re staring down the barrel of a $100 monthly fee. Worth it if you’re a pro, but a gut punch for beginners.

Yes, you can test it out 100% completely FREE.

And when the time comes to open your wallet, it’s less than $30 a month – an absolute steal for the arsenal of tools you’re getting.

Absolutely. It’s a diamond in the rough, especially for those just starting their digital marketing journey. For the veterans, it might not have the same allure, but for the rookies, it’s a godsend. Forget the skepticism; Systeme.io is a disruptor that’s here to stay.

The platform serves a multifaceted purpose, aiming to simplify the digital marketing process. It’s designed for entrepreneurs and businesses seeking an integrated solution for email marketing, sales funnels, website building, and more.

The importance of such a tool lies in its ability to streamline various marketing tasks, which are often scattered across different platforms, into one cohesive system.

The user interface of Systeme.io? It’s okay, but let’s not sugarcoat it. For a newbie who’s never dabbled in sales funnels or email campaigns, it can feel like being thrown into the deep end. It’s not the sleek, intuitive experience that tech gurus might rave about. But, and this is a big but, Systeme.io doesn’t just leave you hanging.

The saving grace here is their tutorials. These are goldmines for beginners. They walk you through the process, breaking down what could be an overwhelming experience into manageable chunks. So, while the interface might not win any beauty contests, the support system in place is BIG help.

At the core of Systeme.io are several key features that make it a comprehensive digital marketing solution. These include email marketing capabilities, sales funnel creation tools, a website builder, options for hosting membership sites, and affiliate program management.

Each of these features is designed to work seamlessly with the others, providing a unified experience. For instance, the email marketing service is notably efficient, rivaling established providers like ConvertKit, AWeber, and MailChimp, especially with its free subscription model that remains functional up to a certain point.

Here’s a breakdown of all the features Systeme.io offers:

And if here’s a fancy table to help simplify it even more:

When we talk about the cost-effectiveness of Systeme.io, we’re looking at a platform that offers a substantial suite of features without the hefty price tag that usually accompanies such versatility.

For starters, Systeme.io’s freemium model is a standout in the digital marketing space (click here to open a free account today). You can manage up to 2,000 contacts and create three sales funnels without spending a penny. This is a significant advantage for entrepreneurs and small businesses where every dollar counts.

To put this into perspective, let’s compare it with some industry counterparts. Platforms like ClickFunnels and Kartra, while offering robust functionalities, start their pricing at around $97 to $99 per month after their trial periods. This can be a steep investment for those just starting out.

In contrast, Systeme.io not only allows you to test the waters for free but also keeps the costs low even when you upgrade. Their paid plans, offering a broader range of features, start at less than $30 a month.

This pricing strategy makes advanced digital marketing tools accessible to a wider audience, breaking down the financial barriers that often hinder small businesses and startups.

The all-in-one nature of Systeme.io is its hallmark. It consolidates various marketing tools into one cohesive platform. This integration means you can manage email campaigns, build sales funnels, create websites, and even run affiliate programs without having to switch between different software. For many users, this integration simplifies the digital marketing process significantly, allowing for a more streamlined workflow.

However, it’s important to recognize that while Systeme.io covers a broad spectrum of functionalities, it may not offer the same depth as specialized standalone tools in each specific area.

For instance, while its email marketing capabilities are robust, they might not have the advanced features of a dedicated email marketing service.

Similarly, its website builder is competent for basic to intermediate needs, but it might not satisfy users looking for highly advanced web design features.

Systeme.io aims to be user-friendly, and for the most part, it achieves this goal. The interface is designed to be intuitive, especially for those who have basic familiarity with digital marketing tools. However, for complete beginners, there can be a learning curve.

The platform offers a range of tutorials and support materials, which are invaluable for new users. I’ve watched (and rewatched) several of these tutorials to lean how to use their software.

These resources are designed to help users navigate through the initial complexity and make the most out of the platform’s features.

Let’s get real about customization in Systeme.io. It’s got a decent selection of templates and the interface won’t make you pull your hair out, but if you’re looking to really dive deep into customization, you might hit a wall.

For those who have grand visions of a highly unique and tailored digital presence, Systeme.io can feel a bit like playing with kid gloves. It’s great for getting you up and running, but for the more ambitious or specific design needs, it’s not quite the creative playground you might be looking for.

Now, onto scalability. Systeme.io is like that compact car that’s perfect for city driving but struggles a bit on the open highway. For small businesses or solo entrepreneurs just starting out, it’s a match made in heaven. But as your business grows and your needs become more complex, Systeme.io might start to feel a bit cramped.

This is especially true for larger businesses or those niche ventures that need more than just the basics. As you scale up, you might find yourself needing more sophisticated tools and features that Systeme.io doesn’t offer.

Plus, when it comes to playing nice with other tools or services you might be using, Systeme.io isn’t always the most cooperative. It works well within its own confines but doesn’t always reach out to others easily.

When compared to competitors, Systeme.io’s pricing is highly competitive. For instance, platforms like ClickFunnels offer powerful functionality but at a higher cost, typically starting at around $100 per month after a free trial. This can be a significant investment, especially for new entrepreneurs or small businesses.

In contrast, Systeme.io’s paid plans, which provide access to a broader range of features, are more affordable, starting at less than $30 a month.

User reviews and testimonials play a crucial role in understanding the real-world effectiveness of Systeme.io. Many users have shared success stories, highlighting how the platform has helped them streamline their marketing efforts and grow their businesses.

Mercari works best for casual sellers of clothes, electronics, toys, and everyday collectibles who’d rather ship than meet a buyer. Find local buyers for furniture and appliances instead, and put rare collectibles up for auction on eBay, where bidders compete on price.

#8624. A Latte Every Workday Costs Over $1,000 a Year – Brew Most Cups at Home

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

A coffee shop latte costs about $5, and buying one most workdays adds up to more than $1,000 a year. At home, the same drink costs about 70 cents. Make most cups yourself with a setup that pays for itself within two months, and keep a café visit or two a week as the treat.

That $5 is the typical price of a 12-ounce latte at independent coffee shops, according to the fall 2026 Coffee Price Index by Fresh Cup. Buy one five workdays a week for 50 weeks and that’s $1,250 a year, before tax and tip.

Making the latte yourself costs a fraction of that. Ground coffee averaged $9.25 a pound in October 2026, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. At the weakest strength the National Coffee Association suggests for a French press, a 12-ounce mug takes about 22 grams of coffee, roughly 45 cents’ worth. Brew those 22 grams with less water for a strong base, add 8 ounces of whole milk at the bureau’s average of $4.10 a gallon, and a latte costs about 70 cents.

Pricier beans don’t close the gap. At $15 a pound, that latte costs about $1, still about $4 less than the café’s $5. Plain drip has a gap too, $3.25 for 12 ounces in those shops against about 45 cents at home.

The switch lasts only if you like the home cup, so spend on beans you enjoy before you spend on gear. A drip coffee maker or French press handles plain coffee. For lattes, pair a handheld milk frother with a moka pot, a stovetop brewer that makes strong, espresso-style coffee. Add a travel mug for the commute, plus a grinder if you buy whole beans, and keep the total near $100. At about $4.30 saved per homemade latte, that setup pays for itself in about 23 cups, six to eight weeks at three or four homemade lattes a week.

Judge any upgrade the same way. A $500 espresso machine takes about 117 homemade lattes to break even.

Keep the café for the visits you’d miss most. Brew at home three or four days a week, buy a latte on the others, and the year’s coffee costs about $390 to $610 instead of $1,250.

#8623. How Unlimited Free Stuff from Amazon Almost Ruined My Retirement

It all started last winter when I innocently posted a review for a heated vest I had bought on Amazon. I was happy with this fun new way to beat the winter and wanted to share it with others, so I gave it five stars. But soon after I clicked “Submit”, I got an email from Amazon which said something like,

“Congratulations! You’ve been selected to join Amazon Vine for writing helpful reviews!”

I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.

“Hey, that’s cool”, I thought, “Who doesn’t like free stuff?

Especially since I’ve already been writing product reviews out of the goodness of my heart – why not be rewarded for it?”

So without giving it much further thought, I clicked “accept” on their terms and conditions and joined the program.

And so began a saga that has taken me on a surprising journey over the past nine months causing me to:

Okay, I’ll admit that there were also some upsides. My original idea was partly to save some money, by getting stuff I genuinely would have bought anyway, in a way that sounded fun. And that did happen – I saved at least a few thousand dollars on tools and materials for my construction business and the MMM-HQ Coworking space, for free. Plus, at least some of the motivation for signing up was to put myself through an experiment so I could write this blog article about it. And if you’re reading this, it looks like that happened too.

But I was still surprised at how powerful the combination of small nudges and incentives from Amazon was able to hijack my frugality instincts –  and get me to do a bunch of work that wasn’t really the best use of my time.

So I figured if we review my journey and break it down with a bit of Behavioral Science, we could all learn a few valuable things by laughing at Mr. Money Mustache’s folly.

Scarcity Brain and the Online Casino Effect

One of the most interesting books I’ve read in recent years is Michael Easter’s Scarcity Brain. It’s an exploration of the sneaky ways that modern gambling platforms, marketing and social media algorithms are all built upon two weaknesses in our evolutionary programming:

As I look back now, I realize that I fell straight into those same traps, because the Vine program has all the key properties of a casino or a TikTok feed:

Every time you log into the exclusive “reviewers only” Vine website, you’ll see different stuff available for the taking. Sometimes there is almost nothing worthwhile – you’ll search for “porcelain plates” and get endless pages of pink plastic disposable party plates instead. You look for a toaster for your kitchen but instead there will be just a toaster cover with a cat wearing a witch hat. WTF!?

But occasionally, there will be genuinely useful things like super nice light fixtures, tools and plumbing parts, an EV charger, and even some clothing. My favorite ridiculous Eagle shirt as featured in the Mustachianism music video was an Amazon Vine find.

As were a whole supply of super-realistic artificial plants, which while tacky in principle, have been amazing for hard-to-water courtyard garden areas at the MMM HQ.

I also had a lot of fun roping in friends and coworkers from HQ to help and share in the bounty. I let them help me request and review stuff that they wanted, and then they got to keep it. This seemed like a win/win because we shared the work and the fun of laughing at some of the ridiculous products available.

Still, as I went through this experiment this spring and summer and allowed the system to coax me into doing 80 reviews so I could upgrade my account from Vine Silver to Vine Gold*, I noticed something didn’t feel quite right.

I was checking the Vine page every day for scores, even when I didn’t actually need anything. It would usually be a bust, but just often enough, something I actually wanted would come up, and I’d order it before it was too late. Scarcity and unpredictable rewards at work.

Then the bounty would come, I’d unpack it and photograph it with assembly-line speed so I could batch-write all the reviews once per week or so. For every review I did, I was spending time I’d rather spend doing something else. And for every questionable item I got, I was creating pollution and trash from its manufacturing and packaging – directly contradicting the main values of my life and my reason for writing this blog. And I saw all of this, yet I kept doing it!

During the worst of this consumerism bender, things were dire. I was getting packages almost every day and my recycling bin was overflowing with cardboard. My son and my girlfriend started laughing at some of my more frivolous purchases, so I found myself discreetly tucking away the boxes when they were around to evade scrutiny.

But eventually, I moved into a recovery stage. I had been letting this habit continue out of laziness and as a form of procrastination: it’s very easy to order shit online and pretend I’m doing something useful, and much more difficult to get moving to do the things that really make my life enjoyable.

But I’m old enough to know that hitting the running trails and the gym for my daily workouts, and making progress on all my construction projects, and focusing on the computer as a creative tool rather than an entertainment device so I can get stuff done like this blog post, are the things that bring me the most joy.

Admittedly, some of the sucky factors of the Vine program helped make it easier to recover too. For every genuinely useful thing I found like a contractor-grade extension cord, I had to scan through endless screens of trinkets which not only wasted my time but actually pissed me off at their very existence.

I also noticed some of the deliberately reviewer-unfriendly features built into the program which reminded me that we reviewers are definitely just low-wage workers rather than any form of VIP. The search functionality is crap, and there is no way to filter or sort the results, because they want you to have to look through everything and they don’t care about the value of your time.

Then there is the hilariously bureaucratic AI-based evaluation system which would occasionally flag my totally tame, factual reviews as “Not meeting our Community Standards” without explaining what the problem was. So I’d have to go in and edit my review, randomly changing a couple of words and maybe some punctuation, and suddenly the AI would be pacified and accept my review. Just dumb.

It dawned on me that for many people, this is just what “work” looks like. You are given a bunch of tasks and a bunch of rules to follow, in a system you didn’t create and don’t get much say in changing. And then as long as you crank out your TPS Reports without rocking the boat too much, you get your paycheck.

It reminded me of the Uber Driving experiment I did way back in 2017: as soon as I started working as a driver, I could immediately see dozens of improvements that could be made to the system that would make it function better for both drivers and passengers. But since I wasn’t the boss, nobody wanted to hear my ideas.

Experiences like these remind me that while I love hard work and I love learning new things every day, I greatly prefer being the boss. And I’ve gotten pretty damned accustomed to it after 20 years of financial independence, so I see no need to give it up.

One interesting “gotcha” of the Vine program is that they do keep track of all the free stuff you get and send you a 1099 for its retail value at the end of the year. So it’s not really free, just discounted to whatever your marginal tax rate is (about 25% for me this year). If we peek into my account right now, this is how my 2025 is looking:

So I got about $7000 worth of stuff, and could owe up to $1750 of tax on it. In my case, about 75% of it was “sold” to my business for commercial use (construction supplies which I used on jobs or HQ renovations) so it was effectively converted into real income rather than just tax burden. Some of it was stuff I would have bought anyway for my own house which I’ll gladly pay the taxes on. But there is also probably about $1000 of pure nonsense in there as well, for which I’ll owe a tax bill of $250 as penance for my itchy trigger finger on that “Order” button.

Thanks to some advice from wise readers in the comments (below), I have since learned that in most cases you can mark down this estimated value by 80% before declaring it – because you have effectively eliminated most of the resale value by opening and reviewing the product. Thus my tax bill will be more like $50 rather than $250. More detail in this Reddit discussion here.

So here we are today. While I admit that I didn’t explicitly cancel my account, I used the “Keystone Habit” trick to override the temptation to view the Vine page – mapping that browser bookmark to my daily habits list instead, a little chart which I call my “Badassity Tracker”. The net result is that every time I click it, I’m taken straight to a reminder to get up from the computer and do a quick round of exercise, so I do that instead.

And of course my writing of this article may be a violation of the terms and conditions of the program (“the first rule of Vine is to not talk about Vine”), so it might even get canceled on me. (and if so I’ll let you know because that would be funny story as well)

But I learned a lot about habits and addiction, and realized that this same feeling might be what drives people into One More Year Syndrome, as they keep working even when they can afford to quit. I have now coached enough people through this situation to see it is way more common than I would have ever guessed.

As with all MMM articles, there’s a real life lesson in this story. It’s not really about Vine or me or my habits, it’s about you continuing to look at yourself and your life, and always questioning your own assumptions or patterns. And asking the people you trust most for feedback as well:

We will never be perfect, but the great news is we don’t have to be. All it takes is a little bit of self reflection and putting ourselves on a slightly better path, as often as we can as life goes on. We are all on a very long journey, so even a tiny course correction can make a huge difference in where we end up.

*(Vine Gold is not all that useful as it turns out as 99.9% of the available items seem to be the same trinkets you see in the Silver tier)

Reduce your tax liability with the 50-20-0% rule for FMV

Mr. Money Mustache October 9, 2025, 1:55 pm

Excellent! Thanks JB – this is so useful that I will have to edit the article to include a link to that discussion on Reddit. For anyone reading it here: https://www.reddit.com/r/AmazonVine/comments/1iq0gze/reduce_your_tax_liability_with_the_50200_rule_for/

After you review every product, it’s is now a USED product and the FMV is greatly reduced. Remember we are all opening and using the products to review them

The 50-20-0% rule for used products is something on the lines of:

50% FMV for name brand products 20% FMV for off brand/non branded name products 0% FMW for things you use for “business purposes for review, are broken or damaged, and are consumables that can’t be resold after opening

Using this rule, let’s say you bought $1000 worth of non branded stuff, you’d reduce FMV by $800. As the remaining resale value of the used products is now $200 using the 20% rule. You’d patties on $200, not $1000.

Edit: You are welcome to claim Amazon’s reported ETV as hobby income. Just remember:

To maintain access to vine, we are required to “do work” (aka review 60%+ of products) to get access to the products. The process of reviewing an item, results in an adjustment to the fair market value after doing so. After you review the item, the “remaining” value is not the inflated ETV.

If you don’t understand accounting, you need to be very detailed with your CPA. If you can’t be bothered with some simple accounting, you are welcome to pay your marginal tax rate for your ETV as hobby income.

From all my research and extreme warnings from my CPA, this “50-20-0%” method is not a legally recognized tax strategy and carries massive audit risk.

The products we receive are legally considered non-employee compensation given to us in exchange for the service of writing reviews.

The IRS strictly requires taxpayers to report the Fair Market Value (FMV) of this compensation at the exact moment of receipt (though in practice, Amazon’s FMV is set at tine of ordering, not receipt).

Because you take immediate ownership of the item at its full value, opening and using it to write the review is legally considered personal use. Therefore, you cannot claim business depreciation or arbitrarily lower your 1099-NEC gross income for the “wear and tear” of opening your own compensation.

My CPA explicitly stated he will not file our taxes using fabricated internet depreciation formulas to arbitrarily lower a 1099-NEC.

Here is another discussion on the TurboTax forums where someone explains exactly why you cannot use this 50-20-0 rule and that there is no accepted way to manipulate the FMV of what you receive: https://ttlc.intuit.com/community/business-taxes/discussion/amazon-vine-1099-nec-schedule-c-deductions/00/3715093

The Vine program can easily cause a significant financial impact come tax season. Because Amazon issues a 1099-NEC, the IRS system automatically assumes this is business income subject to an additional 15.3% self-employment tax. When added to a normal ~25% income tax bracket, that creates a massive tax burden. For me, even living in Texas with no state income tax, I am still looking at roughly a 40% tax burden by default, which is brutal.

You can try to claim it as a hobby to avoid that 15.3% FICA tax, but overriding a 1099-NEC, moving it from schedule C to schedule 1, requires preparation to defend since the discrepancy because it can trigger an automated CP2000 notice.

For context, last year Amazon sent me a 1099-NEC with a massive $38,000 FMV for all my 2025 Vine items. (yes, the curse of making gold which means much more allowance and expensive >$100 items, such as a $1500 Gigabyte laptop amd $1k mini split AC, and a lot of other expensive gold exclusive items)

My CPA does not want to use the hobby declaration for that $38k because the sheer volume and daily review time makes it very hard to defend, even though I have not sold anything.

Beyond the tax classification, you must be extremely careful about Amazon’s published FMVs because they are often wildly inflated. Sometimes if you wait a few months, you will find that you could have purchased the exact same product outright for less cash than you are paying in tax liability through Vine.

This is why I am giving the warning that you have to do your homework before choosing things, sivh as checking price history and comparing to similar products. Buying outright means you only buy what you actually need, the item can be returned if you don’t like it, has a real warranty when it breaks, and you do not have to waste 30-60 mins writing a detailed review.

For example, I ordered a cold press juicer, even though I already own about nine other juicers, assuming the FMV was fair. I figured getting it for 40 cents on the dollar was a good enough deal. A few months later, the retail price dropped by about 75%. I ended up paying more in taxes for an un-warrantied, non-returnable item that I wasted an hour reviewing than if I had just bought it outright down the road.

In another instance, I selected a frozen drink slushie machine with an almost $300 FMV, meaning $120 in taxes for me. I spent a lot of time reviewing it, put it away, and then pulled it out months later to actually use it and found it was not freezing properly. I attempted to contact the seller but Amazon simply stated there is no warranty on a “free” product, making my $120 tax cost completely irrelevant. I also found that they replaced that product with a near identical model at a much lower, more competitive price.

I do not believe you can safely claim depreciation the way others have said, and even claiming hobby status to avoid the extra 15.3% FICA means going directly against Amazon’s 1099-NEC filing, requiring you to be ready to defend it. That said, I am now a much wiser Vine participant. I only select items that either have a $0 FMV or a very good one that is actually at or below actual value, and only if they are items that I actually need.

Actually, you don’t take “ownership” of the item until the 6-month mark, when you get the right of disposition, (if you cannot sell it nor give it away, you don’t own it). Before that the non-consumable item is the property of Amazon that you have been contracted to use & review in return for the compensation of the item in question at that 6-month mark. The item carries no value to you until then and when it does become yours, it’s value is depreciated from whatever FMV Amazon may set for a “new” item by virtue of its being used.

Funny, I just watched a Masterclass on getting control of your dopamine. It ended up being an in-depth look at the addiction cycle, how vulnerable we all are in this world of plenty, and how to take 30 days to break the cycle (abstinence). How many days did it take for you to stop habitually trying to check the Vine? How many days did it take to stop thinking about it regularly? I love your Badassity tracker and need to print out a copy for myself. I highly recommend picking up Dopamine Nation by Anna Lembke if you don’t have access to Masterclass.

Budget for a whole year of gifts at once instead of paying for birthdays, weddings, showers, and the holidays as they come. Total what you spent on gifts last year from your card and bank statements, set a cap for each person and occasion, and save a twelfth of this year’s total every month in a separate account.

One at a time, each gift looks small enough to put on a credit card. Over a year, a shower in March, two weddings in June, a graduation, and the holidays add up to a card balance that takes months to pay off.

The fix starts with what gifts cost you last year. Birthdays and the holidays come around at the same time every year, and the people on your list rarely change, so last year’s total is the best starting point for this year’s. Once you know that number, a year of gifts becomes one cost you can spread across 12 months.

Go through last year’s calendar one occasion at a time, and find each gift on your card and bank statements. Count the wrapping and shipping too. Then list everyone you’ll buy for this year and every occasion, with a cap for each. Holiday food, travel, and decorations belong in a holiday budget of their own.

Decide how much you can set aside each month and multiply it by 12. That’s this year’s limit, so trim the caps until they total about 90% of it, and hold the other 10% for invitations nobody saw coming. Save the monthly amount in a sinking fund, money set aside a little at a time for a cost you know is coming. An automatic monthly transfer into a separate high-yield savings account keeps the fund apart from your spending money.

Say your statements show $2,400 in gifts last year, and your budget can spare $150 a month. Your limit is $1,800, split into $1,620 in caps and a $180 buffer. When a gift won’t fit under its cap, pick a cheaper one instead of putting the difference on a card.

Start the transfer this week, and pay for each gift out of the fund.

Choose the gift fund’s account from the best high-yield savings accounts.

When you can’t afford a present, give your time instead, matched to something the person needs, such as a night of babysitting, a home-cooked dinner, or a chore they keep putting off. Write it on a coupon with exactly what you’ll do and by when, and book the first session as you hand it over.

Your time is also the easy answer for a relative who says they don’t want anything, because help with a real job takes up no shelf space. A coupon that says only “good for one favor” is the time gift most likely to go unused.

That coupon leaves the person to pick the favor, find a time that suits you, and then ask for it. Asking can feel like imposing, especially for a parent or grandparent used to doing the helping, so the coupon stays in a drawer. A time gift gets used when you’ve already decided what it is and when it happens.

Start with a real need. A quick question to their spouse or sibling can turn up the job they keep putting off, from raking leaves to setting up a new phone. For parents of young kids, the need may be a night out, and for a relative who no longer drives, rides to the doctor or the grocery store.

Then write the coupon with what you’ll do, how many times, and the dates or a deadline. “Dinner for four on the first Sunday of each of the next three months” works, and so does “babysitting from 6 to 10 p.m. on any Saturday in the next six weeks.”

A grandson who gives his grandparents a coupon for four Saturday mornings of yard work, two hours each, is giving them eight hours of help. Gardeners hired through Taskrabbit average $45 to $60 an hour, so the same eight hours would cost them $360 to $480 to hire out.

Book the first session as you hand the coupon over, and put every date on your own calendar with a reminder the day before, so you show up when you said you would.

The charity has to be theirs. A gift to your own favorite cause, made in their name, says more about you than about them. Give where they already donate or volunteer, and check the charity first in the IRS’s Tax Exempt Organization Search, which shows whether it can take tax-deductible gifts.

How they hear about it matters too, so pick a way that tells them it came from you:

Picture this: you settle into a Lufthansa Boeing 747-8 business class seat on the upper deck, somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Champagne in hand, your fully flat bed already made up behind you. New York to Frankfurt — a route that commands $4,000 to $8,000 in cash for a business class ticket — and you're here for 63,000 Avianca LifeMiles. No fuel surcharges. No carrier-imposed fees eating into your redemption. Just the experience. That's the moment the FI community lives for. Not the luxury itself — though Lufthansa's business class product is genuinely exceptional — but the *math*. The realization that the loyalty system has a pricing gap so wide you could fly a 747 through it. Here's what the numbers actually mean. At the low end, a $4,000 business class ticket redeemed for 63,000 points works out to **6.3 cents per point (CPP)**. At the high end — peak travel season, last-minute pricing, transatlantic demand — that same seat hits $8,000 in cash, which means your LifeMiles are delivering **12.7 cents per point**. For context, most travel rewards experts consider 1–2 CPP a baseline for points value. You're achieving 6 to 12 times that baseline. The reason this feels like a genuine inefficiency rather than just a deal: Avianca LifeMiles prices Star Alliance awards on a **fixed award chart** that doesn't fluctuate with cash fare demand. When airlines raise transatlantic business class fares during summer holidays or major events, your points cost stays exactly the same. The gap between what the market charges and what LifeMiles charges simply grows wider. And then there's the no-fuel-surcharge policy — the detail that separates LifeMiles from competitors like British Airways Avios, which can pile $600+ in carrier surcharges onto a single redemption. With LifeMiles, you pay government taxes only, typically $50–$150 for a transatlantic itinerary. That's it. For the ChooseFI community, this redemption represents exactly the kind of asymmetric value that underpins a great travel rewards strategy: use points where cash prices are highest, eliminate fees wherever possible, and fly a product you'd never justify paying full price for — because you didn't have to.

The core insight here is understanding why Avianca LifeMiles prices Star Alliance awards so aggressively — and then understanding how to get points into the program quickly enough to actually use them.

Avianca is a Star Alliance member, which means it has reciprocal award booking agreements with every other Star Alliance carrier — United, Lufthansa, Swiss, ANA, EVA Air, Singapore Airlines, and more. Like all alliance programs, LifeMiles can sell award seats on partner airlines. The pricing is set by Avianca's own award chart, not by Lufthansa's chart or United's chart.

This is the pricing inefficiency. Lufthansa's own frequent flyer program (Miles & More) charges over 100,000 miles for the same transatlantic business class route and layers on fuel surcharges. United MileagePlus charges 70,000–88,000 miles for the same seat. Avianca LifeMiles charges 63,000 miles with zero carrier surcharges. Same seat. Same plane. Wildly different cost.

Avianca keeps rates competitive because they want their program to be attractive to non-Avianca flyers — it's a revenue play. And because their route network is South America-focused, they've built a powerful award program that earns loyalty from customers who may never set foot on an Avianca plane.

Many programs claim no surcharges, then quietly pass through "carrier-imposed fees" that look indistinguishable from surcharges. LifeMiles is one of the genuine exceptions. On partner award bookings — including Lufthansa, Swiss, and other carriers that traditionally levy heavy surcharges — LifeMiles charges only government taxes. For a JFK–FRA business class award, expect to pay roughly $50–$150 out of pocket. That's the full cash outlay.

This is where the transfer partner ecosystem matters. LifeMiles accepts transfers from:

The instant Citi transfer is particularly powerful: if you find available award space today, you can move points and call LifeMiles to book within the same session. Capital One and Bilt are nearly as fast. Marriott's 3:1 ratio makes it less efficient unless you have a large Bonvoy balance and no better option.

LifeMiles runs frequent purchased miles sales, often 100%+ bonus miles on purchases. This is a legitimate strategy for topping off your balance when you're a few thousand miles short of a redemption. Combined with transfer partners, it creates significant flexibility. Watch for promotions at lifemiles.com — they typically appear 6–8 times per year.

The golden rule of any points transfer: never transfer miles until you've confirmed award availability. LifeMiles miles are non-refundable once transferred, and award space can disappear in hours.

United MileagePlus has one of the best Star Alliance partner award search tools available to the public. Go to united.com, start a search as if you're booking an award ticket, and look for business class availability on Lufthansa or Swiss flights on your target route. United displays Lufthansa partner space accurately in most cases. You're looking for "saver" level availability — marked as "X" class on Lufthansa.

Lufthansa's own website (lufthansa.com) sometimes shows availability that United misses, and vice versa. Search both. You're not booking here — just confirming the seat exists.

An ExpertFlyer subscription ($10/month) lets you set availability alerts for specific routes and dates. For a high-value redemption like this, it's often worth one month of the service to monitor your target window.

LifeMiles opens its booking window 355 days in advance. For peak travel periods — summer transatlantic, major European events — set a calendar reminder to search at the 355-day mark. Business class award space on Lufthansa releases in small batches and fills quickly.

Once you've confirmed space, act fast. Log into your points program and initiate the transfer:

Transfer exactly what you need — 63,000 miles for a one-way business class transatlantic award — plus a small buffer of 2,000–3,000 miles for potential routing variations.

Go to lifemiles.com and search your award. The website has improved but can still be inconsistent with partner availability display. If the online search doesn't show the space you found on United.com, call LifeMiles directly at their customer service line. Have your flight numbers, dates, and cabin class ready. Phone agents can access and book partner availability that the website sometimes fails to display.

After booking, you'll receive a confirmation email with a PNR (record locator). Verify this on the operating carrier's website — go to lufthansa.com or swiss.com and look up your reservation using the PNR. If it pulls up correctly, your booking is solid. Save this confirmation and check it once more 72 hours before departure.

Avianca LifeMiles uses a distance-based award chart for Star Alliance partner flights, and their chart is consistently 15-40% cheaper than competing programs for the same seats. The reason is strategic: Avianca wants to attract members to its loyalty program, and aggressive pricing on aspirational redemptions is how they compete with larger alliances. For you, this means the exact same Lufthansa First Class seat or ANA business class seat costs significantly fewer points when booked through LifeMiles versus through United MileagePlus or the carrier directly. The catch is that LifeMiles availability depends on the operating carrier releasing award space to partners, so you still need to search on the carrier or United.com before transferring.

Card links may earn ChooseFI a commission. See our advertiser disclosure.

Let's walk through a real redemption so you can see exactly what this looks like in practice.

The Route: New York JFK → Frankfurt FRA, nonstop The Aircraft: Lufthansa Boeing 747-8, upper deck business class The Cash Price: $6,500 (a realistic peak-season transatlantic business class fare) The Points Cost: 63,000 Avianca LifeMiles Out-of-Pocket Fees: ~$85 in government taxes CPP Achieved: 10.3 cents per point

You've transferred 63,000 Citi ThankYou points to LifeMiles — instantly — spotted the award space on United.com the morning it opened, called LifeMiles to confirm, and had your booking locked in within 90 minutes of finding the seat.

Lufthansa's 747-8 upper deck business class is one of the most iconic products in commercial aviation. The upper deck seats — in a 2-2-2 configuration — sit quieter and smoother than the main deck, with fewer passengers and a more intimate cabin feel.

Your seat converts to a fully flat bed of approximately 6 feet. You'll have direct aisle access (depending on your seat selection), a large personal entertainment screen, and Lufthansa's catering, which consistently ranks among the top transatlantic carriers. The meal service on JFK–FRA is legitimate: a proper multi-course dinner, a breakfast service as you approach Germany, and a snack menu available throughout.

Before you board, you'll have access to Lufthansa's business class lounge at JFK — typically the Lufthansa Business Lounge or, depending on timing, the partner lounge. Hot food, showers, and a genuine departure experience that costs nothing beyond the taxes you've already paid.

The flight itself is roughly 7.5 hours. In a flat bed, that's a real night's sleep — or close enough. You arrive in Frankfurt rested, which matters whether you're connecting onward or starting your trip immediately.

For the ChooseFI community: this is the redemption that pays for the honeymoon, the milestone anniversary trip, or the family adventure you've been planning since you first discovered travel rewards. The $6,500 you didn't spend stays in your index funds.

Book at the 355-day mark for peak dates. Lufthansa releases a small number of partner award seats when the schedule opens. The travelers who get summer business class awards are almost always the ones who searched on day 355. Set a calendar alert. Be ready.

Use Citi ThankYou for time-sensitive bookings. Because Citi transfers to LifeMiles are instant, you can find award space and complete your booking in a single session. This matters when you're racing to secure a specific seat before someone else grabs it.

Watch for LifeMiles purchased miles promotions. If you're 10,000–15,000 miles short of a redemption, purchasing miles during a 100% bonus promotion can effectively cost you 0.5–0.7 cents per mile — still leaving you with excellent overall CPP on the redemption. Check lifemiles.com regularly or set a Google Alert for "LifeMiles promotion."

Verify your booking on the operating carrier's website. After booking through LifeMiles, always look up your PNR on lufthansa.com or swiss.com. If it appears correctly, your seat is real. If it doesn't, call LifeMiles immediately.

Search Swiss as an alternative to Lufthansa. Swiss International Air Lines is also a Star Alliance member, also bookable through LifeMiles at the same rates, and also operates excellent business class products on transatlantic routes. Swiss often has more partner award availability than Lufthansa on certain dates.

Never transfer points before confirming availability. This is the most common — and most expensive — mistake in travel rewards. LifeMiles does not allow re-transfers out of the program.

Don't ignore the miles expiry policy. LifeMiles expire 12 months from your last earning activity. Any account activity — earning miles, purchasing miles, even a credit card transaction — resets the clock on your entire balance. Set a recurring reminder every 10 months to run a small transaction if you're holding a balance without an imminent booking.

Don't book Lufthansa First Class expecting the same experience. Lufthansa's First Class is a separate product with separate availability and pricing. Business class is the sweet spot here — outstanding value, more seats, and significantly better availability.

Avoid mixing Marriott Bonvoy transfers with tight timelines. At 3:1 and 1–5 days transfer time, Bonvoy is the slowest and least efficient path into LifeMiles. Plan accordingly.

This redemption is built for the experienced FI traveler who has already earned their first free night or domestic flight and is ready to graduate to aspirational international business class. You don't need to fly business class constantly — but for a honeymoon, a milestone birthday, or a long-planned European trip, this is the redemption that makes the experience extraordinary without derailing your savings rate.

You need 63,000 LifeMiles per person, per direction. A couple flying one-way needs 126,000 miles. Most people will get there through a combination of one or two travel credit card welcome bonuses and organic spending — entirely achievable within the FI community's existing card strategy.

## Rated: Hard — Here's Why This redemption earns its **hard** rating from three compounding challenges, none of which is insurmountable but all of which require deliberate effort. **Challenge 1: Award Availability Is Limited.** Lufthansa releases partner award seats conservatively. You may search for weeks before finding space on your preferred route and dates. This isn't a redemption where you decide Tuesday you want to go and book Thursday. You need a booking window of weeks to months, and flexibility in your travel dates helps enormously. **Challenge 2: The Booking Process Has Friction.** LifeMiles' website doesn't always surface partner award availability accurately. You'll likely need to search on United.com to find the space, then call LifeMiles to actually book it. That phone call requires patience — hold times vary, and you'll need to clearly communicate flight numbers, dates, and cabin class to the agent. **Challenge 3: Timing the Transfer Is High-Stakes.** Because you can't transfer points *out* of LifeMiles, you're committing your points the moment you initiate a transfer. Finding the seat, moving the miles, and completing the booking requires confidence and speed. ## How to Overcome the Challenges 1. **Start searching early** — 300+ days out for peak travel. Use ExpertFlyer alerts to monitor availability passively. 2. **Use Citi ThankYou for instant transfers** so you can act immediately when you find a seat. 3. **Practice the phone booking process** once before your high-stakes redemption — call LifeMiles with a simple question to understand their system. If you've successfully booked one or two simpler awards before, you can absolutely do this. The ChooseFI community has members completing this redemption every year — and every single one says the boarding moment made the effort completely worth it.

United shows Star Alliance partner availability that LifeMiles can book. Search for Saver-level awards in business or first class on your target route. Note the exact carrier, flight number, and date.

Log into LifeMiles.com and run the same search. Confirm the flight appears and note the exact mileage required. Some partner space visible on United may not be available through LifeMiles, so always double-check.

Amex MR, Chase UR, Citi ThankYou, and Capital One miles all transfer to LifeMiles. Amex transfers are often fastest (same day). Transfer only after confirming availability in Step 2.

Premium cabin award space is limited and competitive. Once your transferred miles appear in your LifeMiles account, complete the booking immediately. Do not wait — the seat can be taken by another searcher.

LifeMiles charges low taxes and fees on most partner awards, typically $30-$100 depending on the route. Some carriers (notably British Airways) add fuel surcharges, but most Star Alliance carriers keep fees minimal through LifeMiles.

Yes, Lufthansa First Class is bookable through LifeMiles at 87,000 miles one-way from the US to Europe. Availability is limited and typically released at 14 days before departure for partner programs, though some space appears further out. Search on United.com first to confirm Lufthansa First saver space exists before transferring.

Transfer times vary by partner. Amex Membership Rewards transfers often post same-day. Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers typically take 1-2 business days. Citi ThankYou and Capital One transfers can take 1-3 days. Always account for transfer time when booking time-sensitive award space.

Most Star Alliance carriers booked through LifeMiles have low or no fuel surcharges. The notable exception is British Airways (a oneworld carrier, not bookable through LifeMiles). Taxes and fees on typical Star Alliance routes run $30-$100 per ticket, making LifeMiles one of the cheapest programs for out-of-pocket award costs.

If the booking fails because award space disappeared between your search and transfer, the miles sit in your LifeMiles account. They do not expire as long as you have account activity every 12 months. You can use them for a future booking, but you cannot transfer them back to your original program.

Avianca LifeMiles is the program that lets FI-community travelers fly the same premium cabins as frequent business travelers at a fraction of the points cost. By consistently underpricing Star Alliance awards, LifeMiles turns 63,000-87,000 transferable points into experiences worth $8,000 or more. The process requires discipline (never transfer before confirming availability), patience (searching for saver space takes time), and a willingness to navigate a less polished booking experience. But the value is real: 15-20 cents per point on aspirational flights that would be unreachable at cash prices.

#8612. My Unexpected Journey to Hormone Replacement (TRT)

As a man of Science, I’m supposed to hide my enthusiasm about this somewhat controversial subject, and instead direct you only to the peer-reviewed studies.

But man, I feel like I’ve stumbled upon the fountain of youth here. And the more I dig into the details and the hype and controversy surrounding the field of Hormone Replacement therapy, the more I need to share the word about it to my fellow middle-aged people (both men and women).

I’ve been interested in optimization and trying to get the most out of my body and mind since I was a little kid. I started vacuuming up all the training and nutrition books and magazines I could find while I was just a teenager, and that field still remains a favorite of mine over 30 years later. And if you’re a long-time reader here you’ve been reminded plenty of times of this interest, because health has always been the very heart of Mustachianism.

But a funny thing has been happening in the last ten years: even as I kept honing the healthy living habits and trying my best to improve, there seemed to be a force pulling me back almost as hard. So despite working a bit harder and smarter every year, I still felt myself riding a gradually declining tide of energy, motivation, and physical stamina.

“Perhaps this is just what it means to grow old”, I thought to myself,

Yet there was one thing that didn’t quite fit. Why was I having this decline in energy, when some of my older friends weren’t? And why was I still seeing people out there in their 50s, 60s and well beyond doing things that I felt too tired to do today?

One of these tireless friends is a guy named Kevin, who is the personification of the highly energetic successful middle-aged man. He’s a semi-retired serial entrepreneur (and extreme rock climber) who lives in Boulder.  And through an interesting twist of fate, in April of 2025 he invited me out for a hike right around the time I was doing all this wondering. And during this hike (and climb) he told me about his latest venture, a boutique men’s health company that specializes in helping men just like us get their youth back through the process of testosterone replacement therapy.

Long story short: his ideas planted a seed in my head, which led to a bunch of research and a growing interest in trying TRT myself. I had of course heard about the process, but for some reason never considered doing it until I heard Kevin’s enthusiasm: he had been on it for several years, and according to him it is a “night and day difference” in all the things you want in life: energy, focus, thinking speed, and of course physical health.

Another convenient twist of fate is that I happen to be dating an REI doctor – a Reproductive Endocrinologist and Infertility specialist who has two board certifications in exactly the relevant bodily systems that are affected by these hormones. And while she was initially skeptical that I needed more Testosterone (and in her practice she regularly sees the downsides of men taking the stuff too early in life and thus compromising their own fertility), she has followed along and helped me learn at each step of this process, eventually becoming fully in support of the program.

So I signed up as a test customer for Kevin’s new company, which is called Bolt Health. I worked with their doctor to get a baseline blood test and review my numbers compared to all the past tests I’ve collected, and as it turned out, my levels had been dropping consistently over the years, and the latest test was by far the lowest ever.

Even more telling, my age-related drop in Testosterone was correlating perfectly with my decline in energy and motivation:

The next step was a prescription for a tiny daily dose of supplemental T, which arrived at my house the next week along with instructions for how to use it. And so began the journey.

Now let’s jump forward seven months to the present day as I write this.

And wow, what a great year it has been! I only wish I had known and tried this a few years earlier, because I’m getting a lot more out of my life.

It’s not a night-and-day difference for me, but more like a 50% boost in overall youthfulness and energy. The biggest subjective change is that I just don’t have sucky tired days anymore, which was the main problem with my life before: wasting too much of my precious freedom due to not having the energy to enjoy it.

This is why I’ve become somewhat of an evangelist for hormone replacement therapy for people from about age 45 onwards. It won’t work for everyone – if your levels are already pretty high, you don’t get the same boost. Two of my male friends tried TRT and quit because they didn’t notice any benefit. But these same two guys already had plenty of energy to begin with, which is usually a sign that the body has what it needs.

It turns out I am very late to this party. Although Testosterone supplementation started out as a niche practice in the 1940s, from the 2010s onward it has been everywhere.

TRT is the reason you see every actor suddenly showing up buff overnight for their superhero roles and it’s also why so many of today’s CEOs don’t look anything like yesterday’s CEOs.

In many cases, it has gone too far with young men using it just to gain muscle for the beach or the football field, and questionable online providers (aka “Prescription Mills”) handing out prescriptions to anyone with a valid credit card – with profit as their sole motive. It became overhyped in certain pockets of Bro Culture, where every Bro eventually receives the advice “Bro! You need to get on the T!” from another Bro, and therefore does it. And some of this reputation surely contributed to my own skepticism.

But there’s a lot of valid science behind TRT, if you’re the right candidate and you take the right dosage. And because of that, I feel it is probably under-hyped in my own demographic, the Nerdy Tech Worker Semi Retired Dad contingent. And that’s why I’m writing this blog post, because there are a lot of us out there.

Many of us just tend to work with what we were given, and accept that aging means slowing down. And for those of us already enjoying an early retirement, we have the option of unlimited rest and recuperation time, so who really cares if we get tired a bit more often? After all, what better way to flex one’s wealth than with a decadent Tuesday Afternoon Nap while everyone else is stuck in the office?

While this seemingly healthy attitude has a lot of positive aspects, it can also mask a real problem which may be easily fixable. Because sometimes, the only thing that’s even better than an afternoon nap, is having the energy and motivation to go out for an afternoon hike, bike ride or adventure with friends. More energy is also pretty darned useful if you’re still raising kids or trying to do well in your career as a person over 45.

How it Actually Works (and What Happened to Me)

Distilling all of the fluffy discussion above into the simplest possible answer: TRT means using a tiny needle to inject a few drops of clear liquid just below the surface of your skin. And you do this by yourself at home, ideally once every morning.

Here’s one of the baby needles I use for my daily dose.The typical serving is less than one tenth of a milliliter, which is only a few drops.

And while the term “needle” sounds scary to some, this is very different from the monstrosities they use to draw blood from your veins. This one is so miniature that you don’t need special training to use it, and you usually don’t even feel it.

So I began doing this to myself on May 1st of this year, while keeping a daily journal of my results along the way. The results seemed to be almost immediate in all the promised areas, but I know how powerful the Placebo Effect can be so I kept my skeptic’s hat on to see what would happen in the long run.

I was seeing increased energy and motivation as well as lean weight gain through the whole spring and summer, but I remember the first truly shocking observation happened during a mountain vacation in July. I was part of a multi-family trip with lively adults, chaotic kids, early mornings, late nights with a few drinks, very intense high altitude sunshine and nonstop physical activities. It was just the type of situation that would drain my energy pretty quickly in the past.

But on day three I went out on a solo mountain bike ride to explore the area, and as I was climbing a long ascent with the blazing sun cooking me from every angle I just somehow kept having plenty of energy to keep climbing. Then I came down and joined the group for a few games of full-sun pickleball, biked back up the mountain to our cabin, and the story of unlimited energy went on from there.

“Hot Damn”, I thought to myself, “I don’t know whose youthful and tireless body I have inherited here but I’d sure like to keep it!”

In August, the Bolt Health program scheduled a follow-up blood test for me and sure enough, my Testosterone levels had been boosted from 415 to 730ng/dL, bringing me from the low side of normal to the higher side.

Many labs define “normal” as anywhere between 300 and 1000, which seems strange to me given the huge effect this hormone has on your wellbeing. It’s a bit like saying “Most cars have between 90 and 300 horsepower, so it doesn’t really matter what engine you have”

I mean yeah, either one will still get you down the road, but which one would you rather be driving?

Since then, it has just been more of the same good results. My improvements ramped up and then just stayed there – so I’m operating at a new, much higher and more enjoyable level of functioning. Energy and motivation are no longer a problem, and I even find myself willing to make longer-term plans again (before this everything beyond same-day planning felt overwhelming). And my body seems to just want to gain strength and size with any excuse. Heavy weights feel lighter and the hard manual labor I still like to spend my time on feels easier for longer. It’s nice to be young again!

When you dig into the details, hormone replacement is mired in a soup of both real and incorrect information about both its benefits and its risks. And then our well-meaning medical establishment locks this whole container of soup deep in the cabinet with a label that says, “Needs Further Study”. But if you summarize the findings on both sides of the issue, you’ll see this:

The modern American Lifestyle is a Testosterone and Health Crusher. It’s a miracle that anybody feels good ever with the crap that people do to their bodies. So if you’re not already doing all the simple, natural, outdoor things that naturally boost your health, energy, and hormone levels, you’ll want to start with these first. You can find a pretty complete list on my oft-cited Badassity Tracker page.

Since I was already doing all of these things pretty consistently, I felt ready to take the next step and at least consider hormone supplementation. But wait, there’s more!

Many of the problems above are more likely to appear when the body is flooded with too much testosterone. In the bad old days, TRT was administered by sticking a pellet beneath your skin or injecting a large amount into the butt which then gets used up over the next several weeks. One friend recounted a story of extreme moodiness when the pellet was first implanted, ramping down to tiredness by the time the hormone was all gone.

More modern providers like Bolt have fixed this problem by breaking the dose into much smaller servings which you administer each day. The idea is that your levels remain stable, and you need a lot less overall which reduces side effects.

For my part, I have not had any of the negative side effects because I was a pretty ideal candidate in the first place: 50 years old with depressed Testosterone levels but an otherwise healthy lifestyle and no risk factors.

My hope in sharing this article is to be transparent and hopefully take some of the stigma out of this subject of other people who might benefit. Because in our modern over-connected world, everybody has an opinion on your life, even when you didn’t ask them.

And it’s not just men – many women in this same age group benefit from Estrogen replacement (and there are even interesting stories about female testosterone supplementation in certain situations as this author shares). The point is that aging is normal, but in some cases there’s a pretty easy way to make it slower

The great news is that Testosterone itself is a cheap and widely available substance, typically under $50 per month even for people like me without conventional insurance or drug coverage. The expensive part (here in the US) is just the doctor stuff – consultations, blood tests, ongoing analysis and prescription renewals and so on.

The company that I used is positioned as a premium provider, bundling these services along with a bunch of other men’s health perks and deliveries for a few hundred dollars, which is expensive relative to most other parts of my budget, but still cheap if I consider the life and financial benefits of being 20-50% more energetic and productive.

If you want to be on this program, your final decision will hinge on your income, insurance coverage if applicable, whether your existing doctor can already help you, and how much service and advice you’re willing to pay for.

Note: I decided not to become a Bolt health affiliate because I wanted to write this article without conflict of interest. And I can honestly say, Bolt’s product and service seem great to me because I know and trust the people who run it. But  it’s also the only one I’ve tried. So I don’t know much about the competition and there may be other good options out there. At the very minimum, you can always try one service and switch to another if you don’t like the first one.

I’ve got lots more to say on money and early retirement, and lots of interesting projects in the works now too. So I’m thankful to have stumbled upon this booster for all aspects of life, so I can do more of everything else, for even more decades than I had expected.

I wish this same type of good fortune for you, however you create it.

In the Comments: Do you have questions about hormone replacement or anything else in this article? I’ll try to invite Kevin, Dr. Sean Bender and other knowledgeable people to contribute and answer questions as well.
