Interesting. I know very little about this topic, but as I read my thoughts immediately went to the evolutionary biologist Robert Sapolsky and his book The Trouble With Testosterone. I would encourage you to go down that pathway and add it into your thinking. I’m curious what the Bolt people would say to these arguments.

It has been some time since I read the book so I got some LLM summaries to refresh me on why many evolutionary biologist consider testosterone an expensive biological tax. I’m going to paste some of it here:

In the wild, maintaining high testosterone levels is akin to driving a car with the engine red-lining. It provides short-term power for mating and fighting, but it wears down the machinery (the body) much faster. Here is a breakdown of the specific evolutionary costs Sapolsky and other biologists highlight, focusing on the immune system and metabolic “taxes.” 1. The Immunocompetence Handicap This is the central theory explaining why high testosterone is costly. The “Handicap Principle” suggests that because testosterone suppresses the immune system, only males with superior genetics can afford to maintain high levels of it. The Trade-off: Energy is finite. The body must choose between investing in survival (immunity, cell repair) or reproduction (muscle mass, aggression, mating displays). Testosterone forces the body to prioritize reproduction at the expense of survival. The “Honest Signal”: High T features (like a peacock’s tail or a stag’s massive muscles) are “honest signals” to females because they are dangerous to possess. The male is essentially saying, “Look at how strong my genes are—I can handicap my own immune system with this much testosterone and still be standing.” Parasitic Load: In wild primate studies, males with the highest testosterone often have the highest burden of intestinal parasites. Their immune systems are less efficient at fighting off low-level infections because their energy is diverted elsewhere. 2. Metabolic & Physiological Costs Beyond just the immune system, high testosterone extracts a heavy toll on the body’s daily maintenance. Metabolic Burn: Testosterone is metabolically expensive. It forces the body to build and maintain lean muscle mass which burns calories at a much higher rate than fat. In a food-scarce environment (which is most of evolutionary history), having high T is a risk; you are more likely to starve during a famine. The “Good Cholesterol” Crash: Testosterone generally lowers HDL (good cholesterol). Sapolsky notes that this is one reason why males across many species die younger than females. The hormone that helps you win the fight today clogs your arteries for tomorrow. 3. Behavioral “Taxes” High testosterone lowers the threshold for risk-taking, which carries a direct survival cost. Injury and Mortality: High-T males are more conspicuous and more likely to engage in risky confrontations. In the wild, “winning” a fight often leaves a victor injured, making them susceptible to infection (which their T-suppressed immune system is now less equipped to fight). Parental Investment: Evolutionarily, there is often an inverse relationship between testosterone and parental care. High T drives mating effort (seeking new partners) rather than parenting effort (caring for offspring). In species where offspring need high investment, high T can actually be an evolutionary disadvantage if the offspring die from neglect. Summary of the Trap The “trouble” Sapolsky identifies is that while high testosterone might help a male pass on genes (by winning a mate), it actively works against his staying alive. The Irony: Pro-TRT (Testosterone Replacement Therapy) arguments often frame high T as the key to “health” and “vitality.” From an evolutionary standpoint, nature views high T as the exact opposite: a calculated health risk taken solely to reproduce before you die.

I hope this is good food for thought and discussion. Thanks for your years of great blogging MMM!

Testosterone cypionate (most common, what MMM is using) and enanthate (another commonly used ester) have a half-life of around 10 days, meaning that 10 days after your dose about half of it will be left. After a few weeks of weekly dosing the levels stabilize (you can math this out using mg if you want). There’s zero reason to dose daily. I actually tested twice-weekly dosing vs weekly with blood testing and there was no difference in my levels. Weekly is more than fine and you won’t notice any fluctuations. It’s pretty common for people to dose every other week, but weekly is more than sufficient to maintain consistent levels.

College students have a lot on their plate already, including the need to study to get good grades, participating in any number of on-campus activities and potentially working part-time to have some spending money.

That said, college students should also focus on their financial future, including steps they can take to build credit before they enter the workforce.

After all, having a credit history and a good credit score can mean being able to rent an apartment, finance a car or take out a loan, whereas having no credit at all can mean sitting on the sidelines until the situation changes.

Fortunately, there are all kinds of ways for young adults to build credit while they’re still in school. Some strategies require a little work on their part, but many are hands-off tasks that you only have to do once.

Make sure your student knows the basic cornerstones of credit building, including the factors that are used to determine credit scores. While factors like new credit, length of credit history and credit mix will play a role in their credit later on, the two most important issues for credit newcomers to focus on include payment history and credit utilization.

Payment history makes up 35% of FICO scores and credit utilization ratio makes up 30% of scores.

Generally speaking, college students and everyone else can score well in these categories by making all bill payments on time and keeping debt levels low. How low?

Most experts recommend keeping credit utilization below 30% at a maximum and below 10% for the best possible results. This means trying to owe less than $300 for every $1,000 in available credit limits at a maximum, but preferably less than $100 for every $1,000 in credit limits.

One step you can personally take to help a child build credit is adding them to your credit card account as an authorized user. This means they will get a credit card in their name and access to your spending limit, but you are legally responsible for any charges they make. Obviously, this move works best when you have excellent credit and a strong history of on-time payments and you plan to continue using credit responsibly .

While this step can be risky if you’re worried your college student will use their card to overspend, you don’t actually have to give them their physical authorized user credit card.

In fact, they can get credit for your on-time payments whether they have access to a card or not. If you do decide to give them their credit card, you can do so with the agreement they can only use it for emergency expenses.

Your child can build credit faster if they apply for a credit card and get approved for one on their own, yet this can be difficult for students who have no credit history. That said, secured credit cards require a refundable cash deposit as collateral are very easy to get approved for.

Some secured credit cards like the Ambition Card by College Ave even offer cash back1 on every purchase and don’t charge interest2. If your child opts to start building credit with a secured credit card, make sure they understand the best ways to build credit quickly — keeping credit utilization low and paying bills early or on time each month.

While secured credit cards are a good option for students with little to no credit get started on their journey to good credit, there are also credit cards specifically designed for college students. Student credit cards are unsecured cards, meaning they don’t require an upfront cash deposit as collateral, but charge interest on any purchases not paid in full each month.

Many student credit cards offer rewards for spending with no annual fee required as well, although these cards do tend to come with a high APR. The key to getting the most out of a student credit card is having your dependent use it only for purchases they can afford and paying off the balance in its entirety each billing cycle. After all, sky high interest rates don’t really matter when you never carry a balance from one month to the next.

“One of the safest ways for college student to build their credit by learning valuable money skills.”

While secured cards and student credit cards help young adults build credit with each bill payment they make, other payments they’re making can also help.

In fact, using an app like Experian Boost can help them get credit for utility bills they’re paying, subscriptions they pay for and even rent payments they’re making. This app is also free to use, and you only have to set up most bill payments in the app once to have them reported to the credit bureaus.

There are also rent-specific apps and tools students can use to get credit for rent payments, although they come with fees. Examples include websites like Rental Kharma and RentReporters.

The Fair Isaac Corporation (FICO) also notes that students can start building credit with their student loans during school, even if they’re not officially required to make payments until six months after graduation with federal student loans.

Their advice is to make interest-only payments on federal student loans along with payments on any private student loans they have during college in order to start having those payments reported to the credit bureaus as soon as possible.

“Making interest-only payments as a student will not only positively affect your credit history but will also keep the interest from capitalizing and adding to your student loan balance,” the agency writes.

Of course, interest capitalization on loans would only be an issue with private student loans and  Federal Direct Unsubsidized Loans since the U.S. Department of Education pays the interest on Direct Subsidized Loans while you’re in school at least half-time, for six months after you graduate and during periods of deferment.

College students don’t have to wait until they’re done with school to start building credit for the future, and it makes sense to start building positive credit habits early on regardless. Tools like a credit card can help students on their way, whether they opt for a secured credit card or a student card. Other steps like using credit-building apps can also help, and with little effort on the student’s part or on yours.

Either way, the best time to start building credit was a few years ago, and the second best time is now. You can give your student a leg up on the future by helping them build credit so it’s there when they need it.

#8610. 25 Legit Ways to Make Money From Home – and What Each Pays

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Legit ways to make money from home don’t pay alike. Remote jobs and freelance work pay a real hourly rate, while paid surveys add up to pocket change. Pick the one that fits the hours, skills, and space you have, and walk away from any job that asks you to pay up front.

In the Federal Reserve’s survey of household finances for 2024, 20% of adults had done some gig work in the month before, most often selling things. Only 21% of them called it their main job.

Which way fits depends on what you have most of: spare hours, a skill, or space and things to rent out. The kind of work sets the pay. A remote job or a freelance skill pays a real hourly rate, renting earns from space or a car you already own, selling pays item by item, and online gigs like paid surveys pay pocket change.

Freelance and gig pay arrives with no tax taken out, so set aside part of every payment for taxes on your self-employment side income.

Airbnb says the typical U.S. host earned about $15,600 in extra income in 2025. If you’d rather not host guests, Neighbor says an empty garage can bring in $100 to $600 a month, rented for storage or parking. Neighbor keeps 4.9% plus 30 cents of each payout. Before you list either one, confirm that your lease, your homeowners association, and your city allow it.

Neighbor says an empty parking space can rent for $50 to $300 a month, and listing one costs nothing. Price yours by checking what garages and lots nearby charge by the month.

Turo puts its U.S. hosts’ average at $10,489 a year per car. In most U.S. markets, hosts keep 70%, 80%, or 90% of each trip’s price, depending on the protection plan they choose. Run your car through Turo’s Carculator to see what yours could earn in your market.

Selling pays once, not every month. On eBay, the fee in most categories is 13.6% of the sale’s total plus 40 cents for an order over $10, and your first 250 listings each month are free. That makes the fee on a $50 sale $7.20. Start with the item that would sell for the most.

Etsy charges 20 cents to list an item and 6.5% of each sale, shipping included, plus a payment processing fee. On a $30 piece with free shipping, the first two fees come to $2.15. Price each piece to cover materials, those fees, and a fair rate for your hours.

Retail arbitrage means buying discounted products in stores and reselling them online for more. You earn only the gap between the two prices after the resale site’s fees, and your cash sits in stock until it sells. Before you buy, look up what the same item has actually sold for online.

In an Institute for Justice survey of 775 people who sell food made in their home kitchens, median profit was $500 for all of 2016, while producers averaged 15 hours of work a week. Check your state’s cottage food law, which sets the foods you may sell from a home kitchen.

Editorial freelancers charge median rates of $65 to $75 an hour for business and marketing writing and $50 to $60 for copyediting it, according to the Editorial Freelancers Association’s 2026 rate chart. Win your first clients on Upwork, which takes 0% to 15% of each contract.

Interpreters and translators earned a median $28.93 an hour in May 2025, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). Translate between the two languages you know best, starting with documents in a field you already work in, such as law or medicine.

A virtual assistant does an administrative assistant’s work from home. Secretaries and administrative assistants earned a median $23.23 an hour in May 2025, the BLS reports. Offer two or three tasks you already do well, such as scheduling, email, and travel booking.

Management consultants, whom the BLS counts as management analysts, earned a median $48.97 an hour in May 2025. Pitch your first project to a former employer or colleague who already knows your work.

Tutors earned a median $20.84 an hour in May 2025, according to BLS wage data. On Wyzant, tutors keep 75% of the hourly rate they post. Apply in the one or two subjects you know best.

Animal care and service workers earned a median $17.08 an hour in May 2025, per the BLS. On Rover, you set your own prices and, outside California, take home 80% of each booking. Offer to watch pets in your own home, so the work fits around the rest of your day.

These are jobs with an employer, and remote job websites list the openings you can do from home.

Customer service representatives earned a median $21.53 an hour in May 2025, and some employers let them work from home, the BLS says. Apply for remote openings listed on the company’s own careers page.

Computer support specialists earned a median $30.24 an hour in May 2025, and some can work from home, per the BLS. Look for remote help desk openings, and list every system and program you’ve fixed for others.

Data entry keyers earned a median $19.88 an hour in May 2025, per BLS wage data, and staffing agencies employ more of them than any other industry. Register with a staffing agency that places office workers.

Medical transcriptionists earned a median $19.43 an hour in May 2025, but the BLS expects jobs in the field to fall 4% by 2035 as speech recognition reduces the need for them. Start with a certificate program beyond high school, which the job typically requires.

These earn nothing until people find what you made, and the money grows with your audience.

A blog earns from ads and affiliate links once it has readers. The ad network Mediavine takes small blogs into its Journey program once they draw 1,000 visits in 30 days from countries such as the U.S. and Canada. Its main program waits until a site makes $5,000 a year from ads. Pick one topic you know well and publish on a schedule you can keep.

Amazon’s Kindle Direct Publishing offers a 70% royalty option on e-books priced $2.99 to $12.99. Audiobook narrators on ACX, Audible’s marketplace for them, are paid by the finished hour of audio, a share of royalties, or both. ACX says most narrators need 5 to 7 hours of work for each finished hour, so a rate of $100 per finished hour comes to $14 to $20 for each hour you work. Start with a short e-book on something you know well, priced inside that 70% band.

Udemy pays instructors 97% of the revenue from students who buy through the instructor’s own coupon or referral link and 37% from every other sale. Outline a course on a skill people already pay to learn, and send your own audience to it first.

Flippa suggests pricing a site at 2 to 2.5 times its net profit over the past 12 months, so a site netting $500 a month would list for $12,000 to $15,000. Build one that earns steadily for a year before you sell it.

These pay per task, and the work comes only when a company needs testers or survey takers.

Branded Surveys says members can expect $5 to $100 a month, depending on how often they take surveys and how many are available, which is pocket change. Most of its surveys run 5 to 20 minutes, so take them in spare minutes, and cash out once you reach 500 points, or $5.

User Interviews, which pays people for surveys, focus groups, and user tests, says its average study pays over $45, with payment within a few days of each session. Sign up and apply to studies about products you already use.

PlaytestCloud pays $5 to $9 for a typical 15-minute playtest and survey, and its onboarding session pays nothing. Sign up, finish the onboarding, and watch your email for invitations.

A real employer never charges you to get hired, the Federal Trade Commission warns, so anyone who does is running a scam. In a work-from-home scam, the charge comes as a starter kit, training, or a certification you have to buy first. Search the company’s name plus the word “scam” before you hand over money or personal details.

#8608. 33 Jobs That Need Little or No Experience – and Which Training Pays More

For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. You can get hired with little or no experience in dozens of jobs, so choose by how much training time you can give now. Restaurants, warehouses, and delivery companies train you within weeks, while a paid apprenticeship or a short certificate program takes longer and usually leads to higher pay.

Most U.S. jobs ask for no more than a high school diploma. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) puts 59% of U.S. jobs in 2025 in occupations that typically need a diploma or less to get in, including 23.6% that need no formal credential at all.

Jobs that need no credential paid a median $36,400 that year, and jobs that need a diploma, another 35.4% of the total, paid $48,050, against $50,980 for all jobs. Jobs that typically call for a certificate from a program after high school paid $49,910, or $13,510 a year more than jobs that need no credential.

Each job below shows its median pay in May 2025 and BLS’s projected change in jobs from 2025 to 2035, against 3.5% growth for all jobs. The pay figures count only workers on a payroll, so they leave out the self-employed, including most rideshare drivers.

This list is aimed at adults starting out or changing careers. If you’re in high school, summer jobs for high school students fit your schedule better, and if you need to work from home, look for remote jobs you can do from anywhere.

These typically ask for a high school diploma at most, and you learn on the job, in anything from a few days to a paid apprenticeship of several years. Longer training usually pays more. Servers learn in a month or less and earn a median $35,230 a year, while plumbers apprentice for four or five years and earn $63,800. The longest apprenticeships lead to high-paying jobs that don’t require a bachelor’s degree.

These also typically ask for a high school diploma at most, but before you can work you need a license, a certificate, or a registration, which usually takes a short course, an exam, or both.

BLS lists a certificate from a program after high school as the usual way into these jobs, and programs run from three to six months of truck-driving school to one or two years for medical assistants. If you’re weighing one against a four-year degree, compare trade school and college on total cost against the pay each path brings.

Before you accept any offer, ask how long training lasts and whether you’re paid during it.

#8607. Where Should I Live? – Weigh 14 Factors, Starting With What Your Pay Buys

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Choosing where to live is a money decision first, so screen each place on its prices, its state and local taxes, and what your job pays there. Then rank the other factors, from commute to climate, by how much each matters to you, and spend a month in your top pick before you sign a lease or buy.

California’s prices ran about 27% above Arkansas’s in 2024 (110.7 against 86.9), the widest gap between any two states in the Bureau of Economic Analysis’s regional price parities, which score each state’s prices against a national level of 100. For rents the gap was wider still, with California’s nearly three times those of West Virginia, the cheapest state for rent (154.3 against 54.2).

So the same paycheck buys about 27% more in Arkansas than in California, before taxes and before any difference in what your job pays in each state. That’s why the three money factors below come first: affordability, taxes, and jobs. Screen every place you’re considering on those three, then use the other 11 to choose among the places that pass.

If you don’t have a list yet, start with the best U.S. cities to live in, places where remote workers get more for their money, college towns worth moving to, or, for a move abroad, inexpensive countries.

Start with each state’s price parity, then look closer at housing. Census QuickFacts lists the median rent and home value for cities and counties side by side, though its figures average several recent years, so check current listings for the home you’d need too.

Then add up what housing would cost each month, rent or a mortgage payment plus utilities, and divide it by your monthly income. By the Department of Housing and Urban Development’s standard, which the Census Bureau uses, a household that spends more than 30% of its income on housing is cost-burdened.

Compare the whole state and local tax bill, not just the income tax. A state with no income tax can still cost you more overall if its sales and property taxes run high. The Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy’s Who Pays? report estimates the share of income that families at each income level pay in state and local taxes, state by state, so find the group closest to your income.

If you’ll keep a remote job based in another state, check your employer’s location rules and the tax bill before you move.

Look up what your occupation pays in each metro area and how many people do that work there. The Bureau of Labor Statistics’ occupational employment and wage estimates give both for every metro area.

To compare pay between states, divide it by the state’s price parity and multiply by 100. In a state at 110, for example, a $70,000 salary buys about what $63,600 buys at the national price level, before taxes. A state’s parity averages its cities and rural areas, so treat it as a rough guide.

If you plan to buy, look at how home prices have moved, not just where they stand. The Federal Housing Finance Agency’s House Price Index tracks single-family home prices by state, metro area, county, and ZIP code, so you can compare five or 10 years of history across your list. How long homes sit unsold in current listings shows how easily you could sell later. Buy only if you expect to stay long enough for owning to beat renting.

QuickFacts lists the average travel time to work for each city and county, a quick way to compare commutes across your list. If you’d rather not drive, check the transit agency’s routes and schedules to see that buses or trains go where and when you’d need them.

If you fly often, check the nearest airport’s nonstop destinations on its website against the cities you visit most, and count the drive and parking in every trip’s cost. A bigger airport an hour farther away can still save time if it flies nonstop where the closer one connects.

Look up reported crimes for each city or county police department in the FBI’s Crime Data Explorer, using the same year for every place on your list. A citywide total can hide big differences between neighborhoods, so treat it as a first screen.

Climate sets your heating and cooling bills and your insurance costs, not just how comfortable you are. FEMA’s National Risk Index shows which communities are most at risk from 18 natural hazards, from floods to wildfires, so check it for every place on your list. Where flood risk runs high, price flood insurance along with a home or renters policy.

List what you do with a free weekend, from concerts and pro sports to hiking and worship, and check that each place offers it within an easy drive. The city’s events calendar and local news show what’s on in a typical month.

Price your usual grocery list at the stores in each place on their apps or websites, and check how far the nearest full-size supermarket is. If eating out is a big part of your week, see what’s within a short drive and what it costs.

QuickFacts also shows each place’s population and how much it has grown or shrunk since 2020. Size sets how many jobs, stores, and services you can choose from, and how much traffic comes with them. A shrinking population can mean fewer of all three later, so weigh the trend along with the size. Whether the city, a suburb, or the country costs you less depends on housing, car, and commute costs added together.

Count the trips you’d make each year to see family and friends, and price them, time off included. The help you’d leave behind has a price too. If relatives watch your kids now, the Labor Department’s National Database of Childcare Prices lists paid child care prices by county.

If you have kids or plan to, compare the schools in each place on your list. GreatSchools, a nonprofit, rates schools from 1 to 10 against other schools in the same state using state data, so compare ratings within a state, never across state lines.

Check that doctors who take your insurance practice nearby, along with a hospital you’d trust. Medicare’s Care Compare lets you compare the quality of care at Medicare-certified hospitals near any address. If you buy your own coverage, HealthCare.gov previews plans and estimated prices by ZIP code before you apply.

Before you sign a lease, buy a home, or book the move, live in your top pick for a month. Airbnb hosts can discount stays of 28 nights or more, and Furnished Finder lists only rentals of 30 days or more, with no booking fee for renters.

Live an ordinary month, not a vacation. Drive or ride your commute at rush hour, shop where you’d shop, and walk the neighborhoods you’d live in at night and on a weekend.

Book the month for the season you’d like least there, such as July in Phoenix or January in Minneapolis, because you’ll live through it every year.

#8605. Price Comparison Websites – Search Now, Track What Can Wait, and Check at Checkout

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

No single price comparison site always finds the lowest price, because each kind works differently. Use a shopping search engine when you’re ready to buy, put a price tracker on anything you can wait for, and let a browser extension check for a lower price or a coupon code at checkout.

In the second quarter of 2026, online sales made up 17.1% of all U.S. retail sales, by the Census Bureau’s count, adjusted for seasonal swings. With that much buying done online, checking prices before you pay is a habit worth building.

Each kind of tool looks for a lower price at a different moment. A shopping search engine compares many stores at once and shows today’s prices side by side. A price tracker watches one item for days or weeks and alerts you when it falls to the price you set. A browser extension works while you shop and looks for a lower price or a working coupon code before you pay.

Deal websites work the other way around. They post whatever happens to be on sale, while a comparison site starts from the item you name.

Use one of these when you’re ready to buy. Search for the exact item, with its model number if it has one, and compare prices with shipping added. If the lowest price is at a store you’d rather not buy from, ask your usual store whether it matches competitors’ prices.

Google Shopping lists offers from stores that send Google their product details, so one search lines up many sellers’ prices for the same item. It can also tell you whether today’s price is low, typical, or high compared with the past three months. To have it watch a price, sign in, tap Track price, and set a target. Google then emails you and sends an alert through its app when the price drops below that target.

The catch is that offers labeled Sponsored are ads, and a store’s payment to Google can affect where they rank. A store that doesn’t list its products there won’t appear at all. Before you buy, check the final price, shipping included, on the store’s own site.

ShopSavvy compares prices at thousands of stores, online and nearby, and its free app scans a product’s barcode in a store to show whether another seller has it for less. It also charts how each product’s price has moved and can watch an item for a lower price or a restock.

Its alerts can lag. Re-checks run on the phones and computers of whoever is watching the item, and on ShopSavvy’s own servers for some large stores, so it never promises an alert the instant a price falls. A price it hasn’t seen for over 30 days carries a note that it may have changed.

Pricepirates sets eBay listings, auctions still running among them, beside offers from thousands of online stores. Its apps for Windows, Mac, iPhone, and Android are free and show no ads. Start with it for anything you’d buy used or from an eBay seller.

An auction’s price is only its current bid, which can climb before the auction ends.

A tracker suits a purchase that can wait. Tell it the price you’d pay, and it watches the price for you.

camelcamelcamel tracks prices on Amazon and emails you when an item drops to the price you name. Its charts show each item’s price history, so you can tell whether today’s price is near its recent low. The Camelizer, its free browser extension, puts the same chart on the Amazon product page.

It covers only Amazon, so it never tells you when another store sells the item for less.

BuyVia’s free app compares prices at online stores and local chains such as Walmart, Target, and Best Buy. Set an alert on an item, and it sends a push notification or an email when the item goes on sale online or in a store near you.

Its sale alerts skip Amazon, so put a camelcamelcamel alert on anything you might buy there.

An extension runs inside your web browser and reads the store page you’re on, so it can look for a better deal without a separate search. Many shopping extensions only pay cash back or test coupon codes, while these three also check what other sellers charge.

When you look at a product on Amazon, Capital One Shopping checks other sellers and shows a lower-priced match if it finds one, and at checkout it tests promo codes on its own. It also alerts you when something you viewed or bought drops in price, and a drop soon after you buy is the moment to ask the store for a price adjustment. You don’t need a Capital One card or bank account to use it.

In return, it records the pages you view, what you buy, and the price you paid. Its rewards are gift cards, not cash.

Honey, which PayPal owns, looks for coupon codes on more than 30,000 sites and tests them at checkout with one click. On Amazon, it compares sellers with shipping costs and Prime status counted, and its Droplist alerts you when an item you saved drops in price.

Droplist watches only the store you saved the item from. Honey also records the stores and pages you visit, and what you buy there, while you use it.

Price.com compares prices on new, used, and refurbished items. Its extension works at more than 100,000 stores, where it applies coupon codes and cash back at checkout, and its website can email you when the price of an item you want falls.

The extension asks for access to your data on every website you visit, not just stores.

Start with the next item on your shopping list. Search it on Google Shopping now, and if it can wait, tap Track price and set the price you’d pay.

#8604. Buy a New Car Only for a 0% Loan or a Must-Have Feature

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Buy a two- or three-year-old car rather than a new one, since a new car loses value fastest in its first years. Go new only when the automaker offers you 0% or a low-rate loan, or when you need a safety or fuel-saving feature no used car in your budget has.

The average new vehicle sold for a record $51,109 in October 2026, according to Kelley Blue Book (KBB). KBB estimates that a new car loses about 30% of its value in its first two years and 8% to 12% a year after that.

That early loss is why a two- or three-year-old car is the better buy for most people, and keeping a car for a decade doesn’t change that by itself. A 0% or low-rate loan from the automaker is what narrows the cost gap between new and used.

Take a $45,000 new car and its two-year-old twin at about $31,500, each financed in full for five years and kept for 10 years. The loans carry October’s average rates of 7.3% for new cars and 11% for used ones, according to Edmunds. Assume each car loses 10% of its remaining value a year once it’s two years old, the middle of KBB’s range. Counting interest and what each is worth at the end, the new car costs you about $40,300 over those 10 years and the twin about $30,100. Neither total counts insurance, fuel, or upkeep, the other parts of what a car costs to own.

With a 0% loan on the new car, its total falls to about $31,400, only about $1,300 more than the twin’s $30,100. That’s about $130 a year for a car two years newer with its full factory warranty, which makes new the better buy.

The other case for new is a safety or fuel-saving feature you need that no used car in your budget has. A new electric car no longer qualifies for the federal tax credit, which ended for those bought after Sept. 30, 2025.

Before you shop, get preapproved for a used-car loan and look up the automaker’s current financing offers on its website, then total both cars the same way over the years you plan to keep one.

#8603. Where to Get Quarters – 13 Places, Starting With Your Own Bank

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Get quarters where coins are kept in bulk. Ask a teller at your own bank or credit union for a $10 roll of 40 quarters, then try a store’s service desk or a laundromat or car wash change machine. Before you go looking, check whether the machine you need them for takes a card or an app instead.

Fewer quarters come back in change because fewer people pay with cash. The Federal Reserve’s 2026 Diary of Consumer Payment Choice found that cash made up 14% of consumer payments in 2025, about six cash payments a month per person, down from 14 a month in 2016.

A store’s register can spare only a few dollars’ worth, since it needs its coins to make change. Banks hand quarters out by the roll, and businesses whose machines run on quarters often keep a change machine. The 13 places below run from easiest to hardest.

Ask a teller, not the ATM, for a $10 roll, which holds 40 quarters, and take a few rolls if you’ll need more later. Customers usually pay just the face value, out of their account or in cash, though a few banks charge a small fee per roll. If you don’t bank there, call first, since some banks and credit unions offer coin services only to their own customers or members.

Skip the checkout lanes and ask at the customer service desk, where some stores will trade a $10 bill for a roll. Others make change only with a purchase, and then just a few dollars’ worth. A coin-counting kiosk like Coinstar won’t help, since it takes coins and pays out only a voucher for cash, an eGift card, or a donation receipt.

A big-box store’s service desk works the same way and often stays open after banks close. If the clerk needs a sale to open the register, buy something you’d use anyway, like a bottle of water, and ask for the change in quarters.

A laundromat with coin-operated washers often has a change machine that breaks bills into quarters, though a $10 or $20 bill may come back partly in smaller bills. Check the labels on its front before you feed it, since some take only certain bills and some pay out tokens that work only in that laundromat.

Self-serve car washes that take coins often keep a change machine near the bays. Check it the same way, since some pay out the car wash’s own tokens instead of quarters.

An arcade with coin-operated games usually keeps quarters in a change machine or behind the counter. Many arcades have switched to tokens or reloadable game cards, and neither works anywhere else, so check what you’ll get before you put in a bill.

Convenience stores ring up a lot of small cash sales, so their drawers usually hold quarters, and many are open late. Ask for a few dollars’ worth with a purchase, and expect less late at night, when the drawer has to last until morning.

Ask at the front register, where the line is often shorter than at a grocery store, and expect a few dollars’ worth of quarters at most, usually with a small purchase. Many drugstores stay open late, too.

Ask at the register inside, not at the pump. Buy a drink or a snack with a $5 bill and ask for your change in coins, which usually gets you a few dollars in quarters.

Ask at the counter when the line is short, and order something small if the cashier needs a sale to open the drawer. Expect a couple of dollars’ worth. If there’s a tip jar, ask whether you can trade a bill for its coins.

Pay with a bill and the change comes back in coins, often quarters, so a $1 bill for a 75-cent snack returns one quarter. Expect a quarter or two per purchase, and dimes and nickels when the machine runs low on quarters.

Any cashier has to make change when you pay with cash, so ask for yours in quarters. Pay for a $1.25 item with a $5 bill, and the $3.75 you get back can come as 15 quarters if the drawer can spare them.

Ask a friend, relative, or coworker to trade quarters for your bills, especially one who keeps a change jar or a stash for the office vending machine. Expect only what has piled up, often a few dollars’ worth.

Many washers, dryers, parking meters, and vending machines now take a card or a phone app, so check for a card reader or a sticker naming an app before you go looking for quarters. PayRange lets you pay at laundromats and vending machines from your phone, and ParkMobile does the same for street and garage parking in place of the meter. Download the app the sticker names and add a payment card at home, before you need it.

I recently completed three of the top Christian financial education programs for churches: SeedTime’s True Financial Freedom, Dave Ramsey’s Financial Peace University, and Crown Financial’s MoneyLife.

These popular programs all claim to help you get control of your finances from a biblical perspective. However, they go about it in different ways with varying teaching styles and philosophies.

In this post, I’ll provide an in-depth look at each program – breaking down the unique features, strengths, weaknesses, and what’s actually included when you buy in.

My goal is to give you the real deal on these courses so you can determine which one (if any) is the best fit for transforming your financial life in a way that aligns with your faith. Whether you’re deep in debt, building wealth, or simply trying to honor God with your money, this comparison will help guide your journey.

Let’s dive into the nitty-gritty details of each program:

When it comes to pricing, Financial Peace University from Dave Ramsey sits in the middle. For an individual membership, it’s $69.99. They also offer bulk pricing for churches starting at around $800 for 10 memberships.

On the higher end, Seedtime’s True Financial Freedom charges $149 for an individual/couple license with regular deals making it available as low as $74. But they have some solid deals for Churches – you can get a bulk student license for as low as $48 per person if you buy multiple licenses. Or there’s an annual church subscription starting as low as $750 per year based on average attendance.

The most affordable option is Crown Financial’s MoneyLife course at just $29.95 for an individual purchase. I couldn’t find any publicly listed bulk pricing for churches, but being a non-profit, I’d expect them to be the cheapest route for congregations.

But as you’ll see, there are plenty more differences beyond just the price tags when comparing what’s actually included in each program.

True Financial Freedom, created by Bob Lotich and his wife Linda from SeedTime, is a financial literacy video course designed for churches that strikes a beautiful balance between biblical wisdom and practical money management strategies. The program’s goal is to equip Christians with the tools and mindset they need to experience true financial freedom while making an eternal impact for God’s Kingdom.

One of the standout features of True Financial Freedom is the engaging and relatable teaching style of Bob and Linda. They share their own financial struggles and triumphs with humor, transparency, and grace, making participants feel like they’re learning from wise, caring friends rather than aloof experts. This approach creates a safe, non-judgmental environment where participants can openly discuss their financial challenges and celebrate their progress.

The program offers several unique benefits, such as the “Never 100” rule (their ‘done-is-better-than-perfect’ approach to adjust spending) and the “Straight A” strategy for automating finances. These concepts are not only memorable but also highly actionable in helping participants take control of their money and build lasting wealth.

Another strength of True Financial Freedom is its emphasis on creating a personalized financial strategy. Through interactive workshops, participants are guided in developing a custom blueprint that fits their unique situation, goals, and values. This approach recognizes that there’s no one-size-fits-all solution to personal finance and empowers participants to take ownership of their financial journey.

True Financial Freedom is perfect for Christians who want to learn how to thrive financially while staying grounded in the Bible. The program teaches participants how to avoid the extremes of being “so heavenly-minded they’re no earthly good” or becoming so focused on building worldly wealth that they lose sight of what truly matters.

With its grace-filled approach and practical tools, True Financial Freedom helps Christians find the balance needed to change their financial life and make a lasting difference in the world in the process.

Financial Peace University, created by Dave Ramsey and his team at Ramsey Solutions, is a highly popular financial education program that has helped countless individuals and families get out of debt and build wealth. The program’s primary goal is to guide participants through a proven, step-by-step approach to taking control of their money and achieving financial peace.

Dave Ramsey, the face of Financial Peace University, is known for his high-energy, tough love teaching style. He delivers hard-hitting truths about money with a sense of urgency and conviction that inspires participants to take action. However, some may find his approach a bit intense or even abrasive at times, likening it to going through bootcamp. While this style resonates with some, it may not be everyone’s preferred learning environment.

The cornerstone of Financial Peace University is the “Baby Steps” system, a clear, prescriptive plan for getting out of debt and building wealth. The program heavily emphasizes the debt snowball method, which involves paying off debts from smallest to largest, regardless of interest rates. This approach has proven highly effective in keeping participants motivated and helping them experience quick wins on their debt-free journey.

While Financial Peace University does incorporate some biblical principles, its overall approach is more secular in nature. The program focuses primarily on the practical nuts and bolts of money management, with less emphasis on exploring the deeper spiritual implications of financial stewardship.

Financial Peace University is best suited for individuals and families who are drowning in debt and need a clear, actionable plan to get back on track. The program’s structured approach and intense motivation can be a lifeline for those feeling overwhelmed by their financial situation. However, those seeking a more personalized, grace-filled approach that deeply integrates biblical wisdom may find other programs more appealing.

MoneyLife, offered by Crown Financial, is a financial education program that takes a deeply biblical approach to money management. The program’s primary goal is to guide Christians in understanding and applying God’s financial principles to their lives, emphasizing the importance of seeing God as the ultimate provider and owner of all resources.

One of MoneyLife’s distinguishing features is its strong focus on biblical teachings and spiritual practices related to money. The program dives deep into exploring how our financial decisions can reflect our faith and values, encouraging participants to align their money management with biblical principles. This emphasis on the spiritual aspects of finance sets MoneyLife apart from other programs that may focus more heavily on practical strategies.

The teaching style in MoneyLife tends to be more academic and classroom-like compared to other programs. Participants can expect a significant amount of reading materials and written assessments throughout the course. While this approach may appeal to those who prefer a studious learning environment, it may not be as engaging for individuals who thrive on interactive, video-based content.

MoneyLife offers some unique elements, such as personality assessments that help participants understand how their natural tendencies impact their financial decisions. The program also includes exercises like the transfer of ownership, which guides participants in acknowledging God’s ultimate ownership of their resources. These introspective activities can be powerful tools for reshaping participants’ mindsets and habits around money.

However, one potential drawback of MoneyLife is that its emphasis on biblical principles and spiritual practices may come at the expense of providing highly actionable, practical financial strategies.

MoneyLife is ideal for Christians who are seeking a deeply biblical understanding of money management and are willing to engage in a more studious, reflective learning process. The program is well-suited for those who want to explore the spiritual foundations of financial stewardship and align their money habits with their faith. However, those primarily looking for a simple and easy financial strategy or a more interactive learning experience may find other programs that better fit their needs.

Having gone through all 3 programs, here is my personal experience and recommendations:

I can honestly say that True Financial Freedom was a life-changing experience. Bob and Linda’s warm, relatable teaching style made me feel like I was learning from trusted friends who truly cared about my success. The program’s emphasis on creating a personalized financial strategy was a game-changer for me, as it helped me develop a plan that fit my unique situation and goals.

The “Never 100” rule and “Straight A” strategy have become cornerstones of my financial habits, helping me live below my means and automate my savings and giving. It was perfect for someone like myself who didn’t want a complicated, jargon-filled financial class – and wasn’t going to sign up for an intense ‘shame & blame’ session either.

Personally, True Financial Freedom struck that balance better than any of the other programs on the list and gave me the strategy to move forward. My savings, giving, and earning have all increased in significant ways since taking the program.

For those who are drowning in debt and need a clear, structured plan to get out, I highly recommend Financial Peace University. Dave Ramsey’s no-nonsense approach and the step-by-step “Baby Steps” system can provide the motivation and direction needed to tackle debt head-on. The debt snowball method, in particular, has helped countless people experience quick wins and build momentum on their debt-free journey. Just be prepared for a more intense, boot camp-style learning environment.

If you’re seeking a program that deeply explores the biblical principles behind money management, Crown’s MoneyLife might be the right fit for you. The program’s emphasis on spiritual practices and aligning your finances with your faith can be incredibly powerful for those who want to grow in their understanding of God’s perspective on wealth. However, be prepared for a more academic, reading-intensive learning experience and less focus on highly practical, actionable strategies.

Ultimately, the best program for you will depend on your unique financial situation, learning style, and personal goals. If you’re looking for a grace-filled, practical approach that helps you thrive in God’s Kingdom while making an eternal impact, I highly recommend True Financial Freedom. If you need a structured, intensive plan to get out of debt fast, Financial Peace University could be your best bet. And if you desire a deep dive into the biblical foundations of money management, MoneyLife is worth considering.

Regardless of which program you choose, the most important thing is to take action and invest in your financial education. By doing so, you’ll be better equipped to handle the resources God has entrusted to you and experience the joy and freedom that comes from aligning your finances with your faith.

Dylan is a devoted husband, father, and Christian leader who serves in lay-ministry at Calvary Chapel of Westmoreland County. With a background in marketing for influential organizations such as The Navigators ministry and Highmark Health, he brings a unique perspective to his passion for developing practical discipleship tools. He lives in Greensburg, PA with his wife and two children.

Business class hops across Europe for fewer points than most domestic economy awards

Picture this: you've just crossed the Atlantic on a long-haul award, touched down at London Heathrow, and now you need to get to Rome for the real adventure to begin. Most travelers at this point resign themselves to a cramped economy seat on a budget carrier, dragging luggage through a secondary terminal. But you? You're walking into the Virgin Atlantic clubhouse, sipping a Bloody Mary, and then settling into a proper business class seat for the 2.5-hour hop to Fiumicino. That's the magic of this redemption. Here's the math that should make your jaw drop. A business class seat on a short-haul European flight — London Heathrow to Rome, London to Athens, London to virtually any major European city — routinely retails for **$1,000 to $3,000 in cash**. Airlines know that business travelers on these routes are often on corporate accounts and will pay whatever it costs. The leisure traveler simply doesn't book business class on a two-hour flight because it feels absurd. And that's exactly the pricing inefficiency the ChooseFI community learns to exploit. Virgin Atlantic's Flying Club prices these short-haul European business class seats at a flat **17,500 miles one-way**. At the low end of that $1,000–$3,000 cash range, you're already extracting **5.7 cents per point** — well above what most programs deliver. At the high end, when those seats spike to $3,000 on peak travel dates, you're looking at a staggering **17.1 cents per point**. For context, most travel rewards experts consider 1.5–2 cents per point a solid redemption. This one can deliver *ten times* that. What makes this feel particularly right for the FI mindset is the positioning angle. This isn't just a standalone splurge — it's the finishing move on a transatlantic trip you've already largely funded with points. You've landed in London. You need to get to your final European destination. Instead of paying $200 for a budget airline seat that charges extra for your carry-on, you drop 17,500 Virgin miles and arrive refreshed, fed, and ready. The opportunity cost of those miles is low; the experiential upgrade is enormous. This is what travel rewards done right looks like: not flying business class because you're wealthy, but because you understood the system better than the airlines expected you to.

The core insight here is understanding how Virgin Atlantic prices its own metal versus partner awards — and then deliberately choosing the right one for the right job.

Virgin Atlantic's Flying Club is famous in the points community for two things. First, its partner award sweet spots: ANA First Class for as low as 55,000–60,000 miles one-way, Delta One at competitive rates. These are the headline acts. But quietly sitting in the same award chart is a genuinely underappreciated gem — Virgin's own short-haul European business class, priced at a flat 17,500 miles regardless of the specific route within that distance band.

Why does Virgin price it this way? Virgin Atlantic operates as a premium carrier and sets its award chart to reflect aspirational redemptions — the kind that make Flying Club membership feel worthwhile. For long-haul routes on their own metal, their pricing is competitive but not exceptional. For short-haul Europe, however, the fixed pricing creates an opportunity: a two-hour flight to Rome or Athens costs the same 17,500 miles as a cheaper, shorter hop, but those premium routes have cash prices that routinely spike into the thousands. The chart wasn't built to be a loophole — it's just that cash prices for short-haul business class in Europe are genuinely volatile and often extraordinary.

The fuel surcharge reality check. Here's where you need to pay close attention. Virgin Atlantic is known for passing fuel surcharges onto award redemptions on their own flights. This is the opposite of what happens on ANA or Delta partner awards booked through Flying Club (which carry zero surcharges). On a short-haul European route, those surcharges are real but typically far more manageable than on a transatlantic segment — often in the $50–$150 range rather than $500+. The CPP math still works strongly in your favor, but you should go in with eyes open: this is not a zero-cash-outlay redemption.

The transfer path is exceptional. This is where the ChooseFI community has a serious structural advantage. Virgin Atlantic Flying Club accepts transfers from essentially every major points currency:

Every major transferable currency gets you there at a 1:1 ratio with instant speed. That means if you're holding Chase points from your Sapphire Reserve or Preferred, Amex points from your Gold or Platinum, or Citi points from your Premier card, you have a direct, frictionless pipeline to 17,500 Virgin miles within minutes of finding availability. This is critical because, as you'll learn in the booking section, Virgin availability on its own short-haul European routes can be limited, and you want to be able to move fast when a seat opens up.

The booking window opens 331 days in advance — use it. Miles don't expire as long as you have account activity within 36 months, so there's no pressure to burn them before you're ready.

Free calculator shows when you could reach financial independence — plus a savings rate tracker, expense audit, and more.

Before you touch a single website, clarify your mission: you're looking for Virgin Atlantic-operated business class availability on short-haul European routes departing from London Heathrow (LHR). This is not a search for partner award space — this is VS metal, VS availability, VS seats. Your most common target routes will be LHR → FCO (Rome), LHR → ATH (Athens), and similar European city pairs. Build your itinerary around where VS actually flies in Europe, not every possible destination.

Go to virginatlantic.com and use the award search tool. Select "Book with miles" and enter your route. Virgin shows its own availability directly here — you don't need a third-party search engine for this specific redemption. Search one-way rather than round-trip so you can see each direction independently. If your target dates show no availability, flex by ±3 days. Business class award seats on short-haul routes are typically released in small batches.

Open a second browser tab and search the same route and date on Google Flights or directly on virginatlantic.com for a revenue ticket. Note the cash price for business class. This is your CPP sanity check — if the cash price is $1,200 and you're spending 17,500 miles plus ~$100 in surcharges, you're at roughly 6.3 cents per point. If the cash price is $2,500, your CPP jumps dramatically. This step helps you prioritize which dates to target.

Log into your Virgin Atlantic Flying Club account. If you don't have 17,500 miles already, check your transferable points balances:

Do NOT transfer points until you have confirmed award availability on your target date. Transfers to Virgin are one-directional and cannot be reversed.

Once you've confirmed a seat is available, transfer your points from your chosen program. For Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt transfers, the miles land in your Flying Club account instantly. Refresh your Flying Club account, confirm the miles are there, and complete the booking before the seat disappears. Enter your payment details for the taxes and surcharges (typically $50–$150 on short-haul European routes).

If you're struggling to find seats close to your travel dates, shift your strategy to the booking window's leading edge. Virgin opens award availability 331 days in advance. Set a calendar reminder 331 days before your ideal travel date, log in at that exact time, and book the moment inventory releases. Peak-season seats to popular destinations like Rome and Athens move quickly.

After booking, screenshot your confirmation, note your booking reference, and verify the routing, cabin class, and surcharge amounts. Add the flight to your calendar with the Virgin Atlantic booking reference. Sign up for flight notifications.

Virgin Atlantic operates its own short-haul flights from London Heathrow to destinations across Europe including Amsterdam, Paris, Edinburgh, Geneva, and Athens. These are different from partner codeshare flights. The 17,500-point price applies specifically to Virgin Atlantic-operated short-haul business class. Partner flights (booked through Flying Club but operated by Delta, KLM, or Air France) use a different award chart and typically cost significantly more. When searching, filter for Virgin Atlantic flight numbers (VS prefix) to find the sweet spot pricing. The business class product on short-haul includes a dedicated cabin, lounge access at Heathrow, priority boarding, and meal service.

Let's walk through a real scenario that illustrates exactly what this redemption looks like in practice.

The Setup: You've just arrived at London Heathrow on a transatlantic award — perhaps an ANA First Class redemption through the very same Flying Club program. You have a few days in London, and now you need to get to Athens, Greece, where your Mediterranean adventure begins. You check flights: a business class seat on Virgin Atlantic's LHR → ATH route on your target date is priced at $2,200 cash.

The Redemption: You log into virginatlantic.com and find a business class award seat on that same flight: 17,500 Virgin miles + approximately $120 in taxes and fuel surcharges. You have 20,000 Citi ThankYou Points sitting in your ThankYou account from your Citi Premier card. You initiate the transfer — 1:1, instant — and within minutes, your Flying Club account reflects 17,500 miles (with 2,500 to spare for future use). You complete the booking.

The Experience: On the day of travel, you access the Virgin Clubhouse at Heathrow — one of the most celebrated airport lounges in the world. The cocktail bar, the à la carte dining, the spa treatments available before departure — this is the part that makes the ChooseFI community members shake their heads in disbelief when they first experience it. Then you board and settle into Virgin's short-haul business class: a proper dedicated seat, a full meal service, attentive cabin crew. For a two-and-a-half-hour flight, it's a genuinely elevated experience.

You land in Athens refreshed, fed, and without having spent thousands of dollars. That's the positioning flight done right — and it's what separates travelers who understand the travel rewards system from those who are still paying cash for European business class.

Do this: Use it as a positioning flight on a broader trip This redemption was practically designed for trip architecture. If you're already planning a transatlantic journey — coming into London on a long-haul award — the 17,500-mile European hop becomes the natural, high-value conclusion. You're not just booking a short flight; you're completing a fully points-funded journey across two continents. Think of this as the last domino.

Do this: Search 331 days out for peak season Virgin's booking window opens exactly 331 days before departure. For summer travel to Athens, Rome, or other peak European destinations, business class award inventory gets claimed early. Set a phone reminder 331 days before your ideal travel date. Log in that morning. The seats that seem impossible to find in the 60-day window are often available the moment the calendar rolls over.

Do this: Compare cash prices before transferring Not all dates are created equal. A Tuesday in November to Rome might retail for $800 in business class — still a reasonable 4.6 CPP — while the same route on a Friday in July might hit $2,800, delivering 17+ CPP. Run the cash price check on Google Flights before you commit your miles. Target the high-cash-price windows for maximum value extraction.

Avoid this: Transferring points before confirming availability This is the single most common mistake. Transferring miles to Virgin Atlantic is a one-way street. If you send 17,500 Chase points over and then discover the seat isn't actually available (or you misread the cabin class), those miles are stuck in Flying Club. Always — always — confirm the specific flight and cabin availability first, THEN transfer.

Avoid this: Confusing this with partner award bookings Virgin's zero-surcharge policy applies to partner airlines like ANA and Delta. On Virgin Atlantic-operated flights (which this redemption is), expect fuel surcharges of $50–$150. Budget for these. They don't destroy the CPP math, but they're a genuine cash cost you need to plan around.

Do this: Hold Virgin miles for multiple redemptions Because miles don't expire with account activity every 36 months, there's no reason to hoard and rush. Keep Flying Club active by earning miles through their shopping portal or partners, and wait for the right route and cash price moment to pounce.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

This redemption is built for a specific type of ChooseFI traveler: the intermediate-to-advanced points strategist who thinks in itineraries, not individual flights.

The ideal candidate is someone who's already planning a trip that routes through London Heathrow — perhaps on a transatlantic award — and needs an elegant, high-value way to reach their final European destination. Solo travelers and couples benefit most here. At 17,500 miles per person, a couple needs 35,000 Virgin miles, which is completely achievable with a single transfer from a combined Chase or Amex balance.

Families should approach with caution. This redemption scores a 2/5 for family-friendliness for good reason. Multiplying 17,500 miles per person across four or more travelers creates a significant points requirement, and availability for multiple seats on the same flight is far from guaranteed. The fuel surcharges also multiply with passenger count. Families are better served by other redemption strategies.

This is NOT for beginners. The overall score of 2.7/5 and beginner-friendliness rating of 1/5 signal real complexity. If you're just starting your travel rewards journey, build your foundation with simpler redemptions first. But if you've got a year of points accumulation behind you and you're ready to think architecturally about trip planning, this sweet spot can be a revelatory experience.

This redemption is rated **Hard** — and that rating is earned honestly. The difficulty isn't in the math or the concept; it's in three very real execution challenges. **Challenge 1: Finding award availability.** Virgin Atlantic doesn't release enormous quantities of business class award seats on its own short-haul European flights. You may search a dozen dates before finding a seat. This is the primary friction point. The fix: use the 331-day advance booking window religiously, and be genuinely flexible on your travel dates by at least ±3 days. **Challenge 2: Navigating the Virgin Atlantic booking interface.** Compared to programs like Chase's travel portal, Flying Club's award search tool is clunkier and less intuitive. It occasionally shows availability that isn't actually bookable through to completion. The fix: search virginatlantic.com directly, be patient with the interface, and have your payment information ready to move quickly when a seat surfaces. **Challenge 3: Understanding the surcharge reality.** New points enthusiasts sometimes expect zero out-of-pocket on award bookings. Virgin's fuel surcharges on its own metal are real, and they'll surprise you if you're not expecting them. The fix: budget $50–$150 per person in cash costs as a baseline assumption. The good news: the **transfer path is as easy as it gets** in the points world. Instant 1:1 transfers from Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt mean that once you find availability, you can have miles in your account and a booking confirmed in under 10 minutes. If you're willing to invest the search time and approach with patience, this is one of those redemptions that fundamentally changes how you see the travel rewards system. The payoff — business class in Europe for 17,500 miles — is worth the effort.

This redemption works best as part of a larger trip. If you are flying transatlantic to or from Europe, route through London Heathrow. Then use the short-haul award to connect to your final European destination at a fraction of the cost of a separate ticket.

Log into VirginAtlantic.com and search for reward flights in Upper Class (business) on your desired European route. Look for VS-coded flights only. Ignore partner-operated results, which will price differently.

Midweek flights (Tuesday through Thursday) and shoulder season dates offer the best availability. Peak summer weekends and holiday periods are harder to find. Build flexibility into your schedule if possible.

Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers to Flying Club are instant, making Chase the preferred transfer partner for time-sensitive bookings. Amex Membership Rewards also transfers 1:1 but may take 1-2 days.

Complete the booking on VirginAtlantic.com. Your business class ticket includes access to the Virgin Atlantic Clubhouse at Heathrow, one of the best airport lounges in Europe. Arrive early and enjoy it as part of the experience.

Virgin Atlantic operates short-haul flights from London Heathrow to destinations including Amsterdam, Paris CDG, Edinburgh, Geneva, Athens, Tel Aviv, and several others. Routes change seasonally, so check VirginAtlantic.com for current schedules. The 17,500-point sweet spot applies to all Virgin Atlantic-operated short-haul business class flights.

Yes, Virgin Atlantic Flying Club prices awards as one-way, so you can book a single short-haul business class segment for 17,500 points. This makes it ideal for positioning flights where you only need one direction covered by points.

The flight itself is short, but the value extends beyond the seat. You get dedicated check-in, priority boarding, the Heathrow Clubhouse lounge (which is excellent), a meal service, and a more relaxed travel experience. At 17,500 points, the per-point value (3-5 cents) makes it a strong redemption even for a short flight.

Virgin Atlantic does add taxes and fees to award tickets, including some carrier-imposed surcharges. On short-haul European routes, total out-of-pocket costs typically run $50-$150 depending on the route and departure airport taxes. This is higher than some programs but still reasonable given the business class product.

The Virgin Atlantic short-haul European business class sweet spot is the perfect complement to a transatlantic award trip. At just 17,500 points, it costs less than most domestic economy awards while delivering business class service, Heathrow Clubhouse lounge access, and a stress-free connection to destinations across Europe. It is not the flashiest redemption in travel rewards, but it is one of the most practical: a building block that makes multi-city European itineraries accessible and affordable for the FI community.
